outside.caption: One dosa. The outside range is up to 1.9 times the batter, plus up to a teaspoon of butter.
outside.basis: USDA FNDDS lists dosas at 35 g (small), 80 g (medium) and 155 g (large); 155 / 80 = 1.9, used as the top size. Butter up to a teaspoon is a stated assumption.
text: Restaurant plain dosas and paper dosas are often much bigger than home ones, and many places finish them with butter or ghee. USDA's survey data lists dosas from 35 g for a small one to 155 g for a large one.
The range below runs from a dosa like this one up to one about 1.9 times the size, with up to a teaspoon of butter on top.

changes: Fat on the tawa is the biggest variable. Each teaspoon of oil adds about 40 calories, and a teaspoon of ghee about 45.
A bigger or thicker dosa uses more batter. Paper dosa is thin but large, so it often has more than a home dosa.
Sambar and chutney are separate dishes. ICMR-NIN counts a cup of sambar at about 110 calories and 2 tablespoons of coconut chutney at about 120.
Rava dosa, neer dosa and pesarattu use different batters and have their own values. Masala dosa adds a potato filling: see [masala dosa](/calories/masala-dosa/).
method: The recipe is the plain dosa in Basic Food Preparation, a standard Indian cookery manual (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 50 g raw rice, 50 g parboiled rice, 30 g urad dal and a little fenugreek, making 4 dosas, cooked with 1 tablespoon of oil or butter between them. That's about ¾ teaspoon (3.4 g) per dosa. Values are from IFCT 2017.
Fermenting and cooking change the water in the batter, not the calories, so each dosa is counted as a quarter of the batter plus the fat on the tawa.

range.text: Published figures for one dosa differ because dosas differ in size. ICMR-NIN counts a dosa at 125 calories, and USDA's survey data puts a medium 80 g dosa at about 170. A home plain dosa usually lands between {{kcal:dry}} and 170, depending on size and oil.
range.reason: USDA FNDDS medium dosa (80 g, 168 kcal) is 17% above this page's textbook dosa; NIN's 125 is 13% below. Size differs. Shown as a range.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 plain dosa?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for a home dosa cooked with ¾ teaspoon of oil, and about {{kcal:dry}} without oil. A large restaurant dosa can be close to twice that.

faq.q: How many calories are in a dosa with ghee?
faq.a: About {{kcal:ghee}} with a teaspoon of ghee on the tawa.

faq.q: How many calories are in dosa with sambar and chutney?
faq.a: Add them separately. ICMR-NIN counts a cup of sambar at about 110 calories and 2 tablespoons of coconut chutney at about 120, so a dosa with both is about 375 to 400.

faq.q: Which has fewer calories, dosa or idli?
faq.a: Per piece, an [idli](/calories/idli/) at about {{kcal@idli:medium}} calories, because a dosa uses more batter and is cooked with oil. Two idlis are about {{kcal@idli:two}}, a little less than one dosa.

faq.q: How much protein is in a plain dosa?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g, from the rice and urad dal. Sambar adds a few grams more.

faq.q: How many calories are in dosa with sambar?
faq.a: About {{kcal:with_sambar}} calories for one dosa and a 200 ml katori of [sambar](/calories/sambar/), with about {{protein:with_sambar}} g of protein.

foods.answer: One onion tomato uttapam (about 40 g of rice and urad dal, 1½ teaspoons of oil) has about {{kcal:one}} calories. With a teaspoon of ghee on top it's about {{kcal:one_ghee}}, and with sambar about {{kcal:with_sambar}}. Thickness and size matter most: a thick uttapam holds twice the batter of a dosa. Udupi restaurant uttapams run about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Uttapam is made from the same kind of rice and urad dal batter as dosa, but it's poured thick, topped with onion, tomato, chilli and coriander, and cooked slowly on both sides with oil. It's a breakfast and tiffin dish across Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, and a standard on Udupi restaurant menus.
Because it's thick, one uttapam holds more batter than a home dosa. The toppings add little; the batter and the oil on the tawa make up most of the number.
foods.portionsCaption: Made as below, with the tawa oil counted in. Sambar and chutney are not included.

text: Restaurant uttapams are often thicker and wider than home ones, and some places finish them with butter or serve a ghee version. The toppings are similar.
We found no lab measurement of restaurant uttapam, so the range below assumes one up to 1.5 times this size, with up to a teaspoon of butter.

changes: Thickness and size matter most. A thick uttapam can hold twice the batter of a home dosa.
Each teaspoon of oil on the tawa adds about 40 calories. Uttapam is cooked on both sides, so it usually takes more oil than a dosa.
The onion and tomato topping adds under 20 calories an uttapam.
Cheese or paneer uttapam adds more: a 20 g grating of cheese is about 60 calories.
Rava uttapam uses semolina and curd instead of rice and dal, and has its own values.
method: The recipe is the onion tomato uttapam in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 60 g rice, 20 g urad dal, 50 g each of onion and tomato and green chilli, cooked with 3 teaspoons of oil, making 2 uttapams. Values are from IFCT 2017.
The databank also lists a cup of oil 'for frying', which would make each uttapam over 600 calories. Uttapam is cooked on a tawa, so only the 3 teaspoons are counted here.

range.text: Basic Food Preparation, another standard manual, makes a smaller mixed-vegetable uttapam at about 175 calories. Uttapams vary in size and oil, so most come to between about 175 and {{kcal:one}}.
range.reason: INDB's per-uttapam value for Basic Food Preparation's uttapam (BFP152, 174 kcal) is 19% below this page's ASC148 uttapam. That uttapam uses about 33 g of grain each against 40 g here. Shown as a range.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 uttapam?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for an onion tomato uttapam made at home with 1½ teaspoons of oil. A mini uttapam is about {{kcal:mini}}.

faq.q: Which has more calories, uttapam or dosa?
faq.a: Usually the uttapam, because it's thicker and holds more batter and oil. A home [plain dosa](/calories/plain-dosa/) is about {{kcal@plain-dosa:one}} calories against about {{kcal:one}} for an uttapam.

faq.q: How much protein is in an uttapam?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g, from the rice and urad dal.

faq.q: Is uttapam batter the same as dosa batter?
faq.a: Very close. Many homes use leftover dosa batter for uttapam, often after it's turned a little sour. The calories per gram of batter are about the same.

faq.q: How many calories are in uttapam with sambar?
faq.a: About {{kcal:with_sambar}} calories for one uttapam and a 200 ml katori of [sambar](/calories/sambar/).

foods.description: A 200 ml katori of dal fry has about {{kcal:k200}} calories, with 10 g of ghee in the pot. Dhaba dal fry and dal fry vs dal tadka compared.
foods.answer: A 200 ml katori of home dal fry has about {{kcal:k200}} calories; it's thicker than dal tadka, so a katori holds more dal. With 2 rotis it's about {{kcal:with_roti}}, with a katori of rice about {{kcal:with_rice}}. Each teaspoon of ghee in the masala adds about 45 calories. Dhaba dal fry, with extra ghee, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Dal fry is toor dal, cooked soft and then stirred into onion, tomato, green chilli and spices fried in ghee, with a jeera tempering. In dhabas and on restaurant menus it sits next to dal tadka; the difference is that the masala is cooked into the dal rather than poured over at the end, and dal fry is usually thicker.
Most of the calories come from two things in roughly equal parts: the dal and the ghee.

text: Dhaba dal fry is often thicker than home dal fry and finished with an extra spoon of ghee or butter, sometimes a second tadka with dry red chillies.
No lab has measured a dhaba dal fry, so the range below assumes a katori up to 1.5 times as thick, with up to half as much ghee again.

changes: Each teaspoon of ghee or oil in the masala or the tempering adds about 45 calories to the pot.
Thickness decides how much dal is in a katori. This dal fry is about half water by weight; a runnier one has fewer calories per katori.
Onion and tomato add little: under 15 calories for the whole bowl here.
Dal fry made with moong or masoor is within a few percent of toor per gram in IFCT 2017, so the fat and thickness matter more than the dal.
method: No standard textbook has a single dal fry recipe, so this one combines three from Basic Food Preparation, a standard Indian cookery manual (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 30 g of toor dal as in its arhar dal, its onion-tomato masala (20 g onion, 15 g tomato, 5 g ghee) and its jeera tempering (5 g ghee). Values are from IFCT 2017.
The water is half that of the dal tadka page, for a thicker dal. That's an assumption, and the range below shows what thickness does.

range.text: Dal thickness varies more than anything else here. ICMR-NIN counts half a cup of plain dal at 100 calories, close to this page's {{kcal:half}}, while USDA's survey value for dal is about 145 per 100 g. A 200 ml katori of dal fry can be anywhere from about {{kcal:k200}} to 290, depending on how thick it is.
range.reason: USDA FNDDS 'Dal' (41305050, 145 kcal per 100 g) is 62% above this page's dal fry; NIN's plain dal is within 12%. The difference is thickness. Shown as a range.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 bowl of dal fry?
faq.a: A bowl made from 30 g of dry toor dal with 10 g of ghee has about {{kcal:bowl}} calories. A 200 ml katori is about {{kcal:k200}}.

faq.q: What's the difference between dal fry and dal tadka?
faq.a: In dal fry the onion-tomato masala is cooked into the dal; in dal tadka a ghee tempering is poured on at the end. Dal fry is usually thicker, so a 200 ml katori is about {{kcal:k200}} calories here against about {{kcal@dal-tadka:k200}} for [dal tadka](/calories/dal-tadka/).

faq.q: How much protein is in dal fry?
faq.a: About {{protein:k200}} g in a 200 ml katori, and about {{protein:bowl}} g in a bowl made from 30 g of dry dal.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of dal fry?
faq.a: About {{per100}} calories per 100 g of this dal fry. A thinner dal has less, a thicker one more.

faq.q: How many calories are in dal fry and rice?
faq.a: A 200 ml katori of dal fry is about {{kcal:k200}}, and a 200 ml katori of [plain rice](/calories/plain-rice/) about {{kcal@plain-rice:k200}}.

faq.q: How many calories are in dal fry with rice?
faq.a: About {{kcal:with_rice}} calories for a 200 ml katori of dal fry with a 200 ml katori of [rice](/calories/plain-rice/). With 2 medium [rotis](/calories/roti/) instead, about {{kcal:with_roti}}, with about {{protein:with_roti}} g of protein.

A teaspoon of ghee on top adds about 45, taking it to about {{kcal:bowl_ghee}}. Thali dal, with ghee poured on at the table, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Toor dal (arhar, tuvar) is split pigeon pea, the everyday dal across Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Andhra. It's eaten plain as varan or pappu with rice and ghee, sweet and sour as Gujarati dal with jaggery and kokum, and as the base of sambar and dal tadka.
Cooked dal is mostly water, so the useful number is the dry dal that went into the pot. ICMR-NIN's standard pulse portion is 30 g of dry dal, and that's the bowl this page counts.

We found no lab figure for thali dal, so the range below adds half to one teaspoon of ghee to the same bowl.

changes: A teaspoon of ghee on top adds about 45 calories, almost half the bowl again.
Gujarati dal adds jaggery, about 18 calories a teaspoon, and often a ghee tadka with mustard, methi and curry leaves.
The water doesn't change the bowl's total, only how many katoris it fills. Count by the dry dal when you can.
Dal cooked with vegetables, as in sambar or dal palak, adds a little for the vegetables. See [sambar](/calories/sambar/).
method: The bowl is ICMR-NIN's standard pulse portion of 30 g of dry dal, cooked in a cup (240 ml) of water with turmeric, as in the plain dals of The Art & Science of Cooking. Values are from IFCT 2017: raw toor dal has {{ing:toor_dal}} calories, 21.7 g of protein and 1.6 g of fat per 100 g.

intro: Dhuli moong dal is split, skinned green gram. It cooks quickly to a soft, light dal and is the one most homes make for children, for someone unwell, or with rice as khichdi. It's tempered simply with jeera and a teaspoon of oil or ghee.
The dal itself is close to toor dal in calories. The tadka is what changes the number from one home to the next.

Whole green moong (sabut moong) has the skin and a little more fibre, and is within a few percent per gram.
Palak or lauki added to moong dal adds very few calories and a lot of volume.
Moong dal cooked with rice is khichdi: see [khichdi](/calories/khichdi/).

The fat is counted per portion here, so you can see the dal with and without it. Values are from IFCT 2017.

intro: Chana dal is split Bengal gram, the small brown chickpea with its skin removed. It holds its shape when cooked, so chana dal is usually thick, often cooked with lauki, and finished with an onion-tomato masala. Ground, it becomes besan.
Per gram, chana dal has a little more fat than other dals, about 5%. A katori of it is thicker than most dals too, which is why it comes out higher.

foods.name: Dal makhani
foods.title: Dal makhani calories: home katori and restaurant
foods.description: A 200 ml katori of home dal makhani has about {{kcal:k200}} calories; a restaurant katori with butter and cream about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
foods.answer: A 200 ml katori of home dal makhani has about {{kcal:k200}} calories. A textbook bowl from 40 g of dry dal and rajma is about {{kcal:bowl}}. Butter and cream matter most: a teaspoon of butter adds about 35 and a tablespoon of cream about 30. A restaurant katori, finished with both, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Dal makhani is whole black urad with a little rajma, simmered for hours with tomato, ginger and garlic, then finished with butter and cream. It was made famous by Moti Mahal in Delhi and is on almost every north Indian restaurant menu, often as the richest dal on it.
At home it's usually made with less butter and cream than in restaurants. The dal and beans give it body; the fat decides how far the number climbs.
foods.portionsCaption: Home dal makhani, made as below.

recipe.label: Recipe: one bowl, 30 g whole urad and 10 g rajma with curd, cream and 1 tablespoon of oil

outside.basis: No analysed value for restaurant dal makhani was found. The Indian Nutrient Databank's open-source dal makhani (OSR139) uses 3 tablespoons of butter and 2.5 of cream for 180 g of dal; restaurant finishes vary, so 1 to 2 teaspoons of butter and 1 to 2 tablespoons of cream per katori are a stated assumption.
text: Restaurant dal makhani is finished with a lot more butter and cream than most home versions, often with a swirl of cream on top as it's served.
No lab has measured a restaurant katori, so the range below adds 1 to 2 teaspoons of butter and 1 to 2 tablespoons of cream to this one.

changes: Butter and cream are the biggest variables. A teaspoon of butter adds about 35 calories, and a tablespoon of cream about 30.
Long simmering thickens the dal. The same pot boiled down further has more in each katori.
Dal makhani without cream or butter, tempered with a little oil, is close to a thick [rajma](/calories/rajma/) per katori.
Rice or naan with it are counted separately.
method: The recipe is the Moti Mahal dal in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 30 g whole urad and 10 g rajma with tomato, onion, ginger, garlic, curd, a teaspoon of cream and a tablespoon of oil. Values are from IFCT 2017, with curd and cream from USDA.
The textbook adds 1.5 cups of water and simmers it down. The databank records half a cup left in the dish, and this page uses that for the cooked weight.

range.text: The databank's open-source dal makhani, with more water, works out to about 74 calories per 100 g, against about {{per100}} here. Thickness and the amount of butter and cream vary a lot, so a home katori can be anywhere from about 150 to {{kcal:k200}}.
range.reason: INDB's OSR139 dal makhani (74 kcal per 100 g) is 27% below this page's ASC160 dal. OSR139 uses 4 cups of water for 180 g of dal. Shown as a range.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 katori of dal makhani?
faq.a: About {{kcal:k200}} for a 200 ml katori made at home, and about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} in a restaurant, depending on the butter and cream.

faq.q: How many calories are in dal makhani without cream?
faq.a: This home recipe has only a teaspoon of cream in the whole bowl, about 10 calories. Taking it out changes little; leaving out butter on top matters more.

faq.q: How much protein is in dal makhani?
faq.a: About {{protein:k200}} g in a 200 ml katori, from the urad and rajma.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of dal makhani?
faq.a: About {{per100}} for this home version. Restaurant dal makhani with more butter and cream is higher.

faq.q: Which has more calories, dal makhani or dal tadka?
faq.a: Dal makhani, usually by a lot. A 200 ml katori here is about {{kcal:k200}} against about {{kcal@dal-tadka:k200}} for a thin [dal tadka](/calories/dal-tadka/).

foods.title: Chole calories: per katori, per 100 g and with bhature
foods.description: A 200 ml katori of home chole has about {{kcal:k200}} calories, made from 40 g of dry kabuli chana. Chole bhature and restaurant chole compared.
foods.answer: A 200 ml katori of home chole, from about 40 g of dry kabuli chana, has about {{kcal:k200}} calories. Chole with 2 rotis is about {{kcal:with_roti}}, and a bhatura adds about {{kcal@bhatura:one}}. Oil is the main variable after the chana: each teaspoon adds about 40. Stall or restaurant chole, cooked with more oil, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} a katori.
intro: Chole is white kabuli chana, soaked overnight, boiled soft and cooked in an onion, tomato, ginger and spice gravy. Punjabi and Pindi chole are dark and tangy with amla or tea; it's eaten with bhature, kulche, puri or rice, and as a filling for tikki chaat.
Kabuli chana has a little more fat than most beans, about 6%. A thick chole holds a lot of chana in each katori, so it counts for more than a thin dal.

text: Chole from a chole bhature stall or a restaurant is usually cooked with more oil, often with oil floating on top, and sometimes finished with butter.

No lab figure exists for street chole, so the range below assumes 1.5 to 2 times the oil of this home recipe. The bhatura is extra: see [bhatura](/calories/bhatura/), or the whole plate on [chole bhature](/calories/chole-bhature/).

changes: Oil is the main variable after the chana. Each teaspoon adds about 40 calories to the pot.
A thicker chole holds more chana per katori. Mashing some chana to thicken the gravy doesn't add calories.
Kala chana has a little less per gram dry: IFCT 2017 puts it at {{ing:kala_chana}} calories per 100 g, against {{ing:kabuli_chana}} for kabuli chana (USDA).
Onion, lemon and green chilli on top add almost nothing. Chole tikki and chole kulche add their own.
method: The recipe is the kabuli channa curry in Basic Food Preparation, a standard Indian cookery manual (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 40 g of dry kabuli chana with tomato, onion, ginger, garlic, a teaspoon of curd, spices and 2 teaspoons of oil. IFCT 2017 has no kabuli chana, so chana values are from USDA; everything else is IFCT 2017.
Cooked weight follows the rajma page: the chana's cooked weight from water content (2.32 times dry), plus the other ingredients.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 katori of chole?
faq.a: About {{kcal:k200}} in a 200 ml katori of home chole, and about {{kcal:k150}} in a 150 ml one.

faq.q: How many calories are in chole bhature?
faq.a: A 200 ml katori of chole is about {{kcal:k200}}, and each home [bhatura](/calories/bhatura/) about {{kcal@bhatura:one}}. Two bhature and a katori of chole come to about {{kcal@chole-bhature:plate}}, before onion and pickle: see [chole bhature](/calories/chole-bhature/).

faq.q: How much protein is in chole?
faq.a: About {{protein:k200}} g in a 200 ml katori.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of chole?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}} for this home chole.

faq.q: Which has more calories, chole or rajma?
faq.a: Chole, per katori here: about {{kcal:k200}} against about {{kcal@rajma:k200}} for [rajma](/calories/rajma/). Kabuli chana has more fat than rajma, and this chole is thicker.

faq.q: How many calories are in chole with rice?
faq.a: About {{kcal:with_rice}} calories for a 200 ml katori of chole with a 200 ml katori of [rice](/calories/plain-rice/). With 2 medium [rotis](/calories/roti/) instead, about {{kcal:with_roti}}, with about {{protein:with_roti}} g of protein.

foods.title: Kadhi calories: with and without pakora, per katori
foods.description: A 200 ml katori of kadhi without pakoras has about {{kcal:k200}} calories. A bowl with its share of fried pakoras is about {{kcal:bowl_pakora}}.
foods.answer: A 200 ml katori of kadhi without pakoras has about {{kcal:k200}} calories, and kadhi with 2 rotis about {{kcal:with_roti}}. Pakoras change it most: a bowl with its share of fried pakoras is about {{kcal:bowl_pakora}}, against {{kcal:bowl}} without. The tadka oil comes next, about 40 calories a teaspoon. Dhaba kadhi pakora, with more pakoras, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Kadhi is curd whisked with besan, simmered until it thickens and tempered with mustard or cumin, methi seeds, dry red chillies and curry leaves. Punjabi kadhi is thick and comes with fried besan pakoras; Gujarati kadhi is thin, white and a little sweet, eaten with khichdi.
The kadhi itself is light: mostly water and curd. The tadka oil and, above all, the fried pakoras are where most of the calories in a bowl of kadhi pakora come from.

outside.basis: No analysed value for restaurant kadhi was found. The pakoras here already use the fat content of street pakoras measured by Gupta et al. 2016 (30.6%); a serving up to 1.3 times as big is a stated assumption.
text: At a dhaba, kadhi pakora is usually served with more pakoras in a bigger bowl, and the pakoras are fried in oil that's been used many times.
The pakoras on this page already use the fat content of street pakoras measured in a lab, so the range below only allows for a serving up to 1.3 times as big.

changes: Pakoras are the biggest variable. A bowl's share of fried pakoras adds more than the kadhi itself: about {{kcal:bowl_pakora}} for the bowl with them, against {{kcal:bowl}} without.
The tadka oil is next: each teaspoon adds about 40 calories to the pot.
Thin Gujarati kadhi has less besan per katori and often a teaspoon of sugar, about 16 calories.
Full-fat curd and sour curd count about the same. Low-fat curd lowers it a little.
method: The recipe is the besan kadhi with pakodies in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 100 g curd, 20 g besan and 2 glasses of water for 2 bowls, with a tablespoon of oil in the tadka. Its pakoras use 30 g besan with spinach and onion. Values are from IFCT 2017, with curd and chilli powder from USDA.

The databank counts all the pakora frying oil as eaten. This page instead assumes the pakoras end up 30.6% fat, the figure a lab measured in street pakoras in Delhi. That's about 19 g of oil per bowl's share of pakoras.

faq.q: How many calories are in kadhi without pakora?
faq.a: About {{kcal:k200}} in a 200 ml katori, and about {{kcal:bowl}} in a bowl of half this recipe.

faq.q: How many calories are in kadhi pakora?
faq.a: About {{kcal:bowl_pakora}} for a bowl with its share of pakoras. The pakoras are most of it.

faq.q: How much protein is in kadhi?
faq.a: About {{protein:bowl}} g in a bowl without pakoras, from the curd and besan, and about {{protein:bowl_pakora}} g with them.

faq.q: How many calories are in kadhi chawal?
faq.a: About {{kcal:with_rice}} calories for a 200 ml katori of kadhi with a 200 ml katori of [rice](/calories/plain-rice/). With 2 medium [rotis](/calories/roti/) instead, about {{kcal:with_roti}}, with about {{protein:with_roti}} g of protein.

judgement: ASC168 lists besan twice (20 g and 30 g). The 20 g is taken as the kadhi and the 30 g, with spinach and onion, as the pakoras.

Pakora oil: fat set to 30.6% of the raw batter (besan 30 + spinach 20 + onion 15 + about 25 g water) plus oil, from Gupta et al. 2016's urban pakora (16.57 g fat in 54.16 g). (1.6 + x) / (90 + x) = 0.306 gives x = 37.4 g for the batch, 18.7 g per bowl.
No independent analysed value for kadhi was found (IFCT, NIN Annexure 8, USDA FNDDS, Europe PMC). INDB counts 480 ml of frying oil (2,367 kcal per bowl), so its values aren't used.
Asafoetida, cumin and coriander seeds (0.25 tsp each) left out.

foods.title: Sambar calories: per katori, cup and 100 g
foods.description: A 200 ml katori of textbook sambar with coconut has about {{kcal:k200}} calories; a thin everyday sambar is closer to 110. With idli, dosa and rice.
foods.answer: A 200 ml katori of thick sambar made with coconut has about {{kcal:k200}} calories. A thinner everyday sambar without coconut is closer to 110, ICMR-NIN's figure for a cup. Coconut is the biggest single variable: the 30 g here adds about 120 calories to the pot. Udupi restaurant or canteen sambar runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} a katori.
intro: Sambar is toor dal cooked with tamarind, sambar powder and vegetables such as drumstick, brinjal, okra and shallots, tempered with mustard seeds and curry leaves. It's eaten across south India with rice, idli, dosa and vada, and every state and family makes it differently.
This textbook sambar grinds roasted coconut into the masala, as in many Kerala and Udupi homes. The coconut is about a quarter of its calories, so whether yours has it matters.

text: Sambar from an Udupi restaurant or an office canteen is usually thinner than this textbook one and refilled freely, so the katori matters less than how many you have.
We found no lab figure for restaurant sambar, so the range below runs from a thinner sambar, close to ICMR-NIN's 110 calories a cup, up to one as thick as this.

changes: Coconut is the biggest single variable. The 30 g of fresh coconut here adds about 120 calories to the pot, about a quarter of the total.
Thickness decides how much dal is in a katori. A thin, everyday sambar has about half of this one per katori.
The tadka oil adds about 40 calories a teaspoon to the pot. Some homes finish with a spoon of ghee.
Vegetables add little: drumstick, brinjal, okra and tomato together are about 30 calories in the whole pot.
method: The recipe is the sambar in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 50 g toor dal with a teaspoon each of roasted chana and urad dal, 30 g fresh coconut, tamarind, drumstick, brinjal, okra, tomato and onion, cooked in a cup of water with 2 teaspoons of oil, for 2 bowls. Values are from IFCT 2017.
The cooked weight is the ingredients added together, and katoris are worked out at 1 g per ml.

range.text: ICMR-NIN counts a cup of sambar at 110 calories, about half this page's {{kcal:cup}}. Most of the difference is thickness and the coconut. Depending on how it's made, a 200 ml katori of sambar can be anywhere from about 110 to {{kcal:k200}}.
range.reason: NIN's 110 kcal per cup is 45% below this page's thick, coconut sambar (ASC167). USDA FNDDS sambar (86 kcal per 100 g) sits in between. Shown as a range.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 cup of sambar?
faq.a: About 110 for a thin everyday sambar, ICMR-NIN's figure, and about {{kcal:cup}} for this thick sambar with coconut.

faq.q: How many calories are in idli sambar?
faq.a: About {{kcal@idli-sambar:two}} calories for 2 medium [idlis](/calories/idli/) with a 200 ml katori of this sambar; a thinner sambar brings it down. The [idli sambar](/calories/idli-sambar/) page has 1 to 4 idlis and the restaurant range.

faq.q: How much protein is in sambar?
faq.a: About {{protein:k200}} g in a 200 ml katori of this sambar, mostly from the toor dal.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of sambar?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}} for this thick sambar with coconut, and about 55 for a thin one. USDA's survey value is 86.

faq.q: Which has more calories, sambar or rasam?
faq.a: Sambar, by a lot. Rasam has very little dal and no coconut: a 200 ml katori of [rasam](/calories/rasam/) is about {{kcal@rasam:k200}} calories.

foods.name: Rasam
foods.title: Rasam calories: per katori and with rice
foods.description: A 200 ml katori of tomato rasam has about {{kcal:k200}} calories. With a katori of rice it's about {{kcal:rasam_rice}}. Worked out from a textbook recipe.
foods.answer: A 200 ml katori of tomato rasam has about {{kcal:k200}} calories, and a 150 ml tumbler to drink about {{kcal:tumbler}}. Rasam rice, with a 200 ml katori of rice, is about {{kcal:rasam_rice}}. The tadka is nearly all of it: a teaspoon of ghee or oil adds about 40 to 45. Restaurant rasam runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Rasam is a thin, peppery soup of tamarind and tomato, with a little cooked toor dal and a spice powder of coriander, cumin, pepper and dry red chilli, tempered with mustard, garlic and curry leaves. It's served with rice in Tamil, Andhra and Karnataka meals, and drunk on its own from a tumbler.
It's one of the lightest things in a south Indian meal. Most of the calories in a katori come from the tadka oil and the small amount of dal.
foods.portionsCaption: Tomato rasam, made as below.

recipe.label: Recipe: one bowl, 10 g toor dal with tomato, tamarind and ½ teaspoon of oil
recipe.yieldNote: the ingredients added together, with no allowance for water boiled off, as the Indian Nutrient Databank does
recipe.densityNote: rasam taken as 1 g per ml, like water

portions.label: 200 ml rasam with a 200 ml katori of rice

outside.label: Restaurant or meals hotel
outside.caption: One 200 ml katori. The outside range adds up to a teaspoon of ghee or oil to the tadka.
outside.basis: No analysed value for restaurant rasam was found. Up to an extra NIN teaspoon of ghee or oil in the tadka is a stated assumption.
text: Rasam in a meals hotel or restaurant is much like home rasam. Some places temper it with ghee, and it's usually refilled freely.
With no lab figure to go on, the range below adds up to a teaspoon of ghee to the tadka for each katori.

changes: The tadka is most of a katori's calories. A teaspoon of ghee or oil adds about 40 to 45.
Dal rasam with more toor dal has more: each extra 10 g of dal adds about 35 calories to the pot.
Lemon rasam and pepper rasam are close to tomato rasam per katori.
Rice with rasam usually counts for far more than the rasam itself.
method: The recipe is the tamarind rasam in Basic Food Preparation, a standard Indian cookery manual (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 10 g toor dal, 50 g tomato, tamarind, dry and green chilli, ginger, coriander seed and pepper, in 1.25 cups of water with half a teaspoon of oil. Values are from IFCT 2017.
The rasam rice row adds a 200 ml katori of rice from the plain rice page, which is about 45 g of raw rice.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 cup of rasam?
faq.a: About {{kcal:k200}} in a 200 ml katori, and about {{kcal:tumbler}} in a 150 ml tumbler.

faq.q: How many calories are in rasam rice?
faq.a: About {{kcal:rasam_rice}} for a 200 ml katori of rasam with a 200 ml katori of [plain rice](/calories/plain-rice/). Most of that is the rice.

faq.q: How much protein is in rasam?
faq.a: About {{protein:k200}} g in a 200 ml katori. Rasam has little dal, so it's not a large source.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of rasam?
faq.a: About {{per100}}.

judgement: No independent analysed value for rasam was found (IFCT, NIN Annexure 8, USDA FNDDS). INDB's per-bowl value (104.3 kcal) is from the same textbook recipe.
Rice: a 200 ml katori of cooked rice is 134 g on the plain rice page (density 0.67), from 45 g raw rice (yield 2.98).
Mustard seeds, cumin, garlic, asafoetida, coriander and curry leaves (under 1 g each) left out; together under 5 kcal.

foods.name: Khichdi
foods.title: Khichdi calories: per katori, plate and 100 g
foods.description: A 200 ml katori of moong dal khichdi with a teaspoon of ghee in the pot has about {{kcal:k200}} calories. With extra ghee, curd and kadhi.
foods.answer: A 200 ml katori of moong dal khichdi has about {{kcal:k200}} calories, with a teaspoon of ghee in the pot. A whole plate is about {{kcal:plate}}. Ghee on top is the biggest variable: each teaspoon adds about 45, taking a katori to about {{kcal:k200_ghee}}. Thali or restaurant khichdi, with ghee poured over, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Khichdi is rice and moong dal cooked together until soft, with ginger, jeera and a little ghee. It's the comfort food of most Indian homes: Gujarati khichdi with kadhi, Bengali khichuri at pujas, and Tamil ven pongal with pepper and ghee are all versions of it.
Rice is about two thirds of khichdi's calories here. How much water it's cooked with changes what a katori holds, and the ghee on top is the other big variable.
foods.portionsCaption: Soft khichdi with the water absorbed, made as below.

recipe.label: Recipe: 60 g rice and 20 g moong dal with ginger, jeera and 5 g ghee
recipe.yieldNote: the recipe's solids (78.5 g) at the 67.2% water of USDA's rice with lentils, so 78.5 / 0.328
recipe.densityNote: USDA's rice with lentils: 207 g per cup (236.6 ml)

portions.label: 200 ml katori, 1 tsp ghee on top

outside.label: Restaurant or thali
outside.caption: One 200 ml katori. The outside range adds 1 to 2 teaspoons of ghee.
outside.basis: No analysed value for restaurant khichdi was found. Restaurant and thali khichdi is usually served with ghee poured over; 1 to 2 NIN teaspoons per katori is a stated assumption.
text: Khichdi in a Gujarati thali or a restaurant usually comes with ghee poured over the top, sometimes more than once.
No lab has measured restaurant khichdi, so the range below adds 1 to 2 teaspoons of ghee to a 200 ml katori.

changes: Ghee on top is the biggest variable. Each teaspoon adds about 45 calories.
A soft, porridge-like khichdi with more water has fewer calories per katori; the pot's total stays the same.
More dal and less rice changes the calories very little, since dal and rice are close per gram, but it adds protein.
Vegetable khichdi with peas, carrot and potato adds a little. Kadhi on the side is counted separately: see [kadhi](/calories/kadhi/).
method: The recipe is the plain khichdi in Basic Food Preparation, a standard Indian cookery manual (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 60 g rice and 20 g moong dal cooked in 2 cups of water with ginger, jeera and 5 g of ghee. Values are from IFCT 2017.

The databank adds all the water to the cooked weight, which makes a very thin khichdi. This page instead uses the water content of USDA's rice cooked with lentils, 67%, which is a soft khichdi with the water absorbed. Katoris use USDA's 207 g per cup.

range.text: ICMR-NIN counts a cup of khichdi at 200 calories, a little under this page's {{kcal:k200}}. Khichdi ranges from fluffy to porridge-thin, so a 200 ml katori can be anywhere from about 200 to {{kcal:k200}}, and less again if it's very watery.
range.reason: NIN's 200 kcal per cup is 16% below this page's katori; a wetter khichdi explains it. Shown as a range.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 katori of khichdi?
faq.a: About {{kcal:k200}} for a 200 ml katori of soft khichdi, and about {{kcal:k150}} for a 150 ml one.

faq.q: How many calories are in khichdi with ghee?
faq.a: About {{kcal:k200_ghee}} for a 200 ml katori with an extra teaspoon of ghee on top.

faq.q: How much protein is in khichdi?
faq.a: About {{protein:k200}} g in a 200 ml katori, and about {{protein:plate}} g in a plate of the whole recipe.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of khichdi?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}} for this soft khichdi.

faq.q: Which has more calories, khichdi or rice?
faq.a: Khichdi, per katori: about {{kcal:k200}} against about {{kcal@plain-rice:k200}} for a 200 ml katori of [plain rice](/calories/plain-rice/). Soft khichdi packs more into a katori than fluffy rice, and it has ghee.

crossCheck.source: ICMR-NIN, Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2011), Annexure 8: khichdi, 1 cup
USDA FNDDS 2021-2023, Rice, white, with lentils, fat added (58160805)

judgement: Yield from water content rather than INDB's sum of ingredients (572 g), which ignores evaporation and absorption: solids = rice 53.9 + moong 18.0 + ginger 0.6 + cumin 0.9 + ghee 5 = 78.5 g; at FNDDS 58160805's 67.2% water, 239 g.
Density 0.875 g per ml from FNDDS 58160805 (207 g per cup of 236.6 ml).
Rice is parboiled (A014), as INDB maps 'rice' in this recipe.

foods.name: Palak paneer
foods.title: Palak paneer calories: home bowl, katori and restaurant
foods.description: A home bowl of palak paneer with 40 g of paneer has about {{kcal:bowl}} calories; a 200 ml katori about {{kcal:k200}}. With cream and restaurant style.
foods.answer: A bowl of home palak paneer (150 g spinach, 40 g paneer) has about {{kcal:bowl}} calories. A 200 ml katori is about {{kcal:k200}}, and the bowl with a tablespoon of cream about {{kcal:bowl_cream}}. Paneer is the biggest part: each extra 25 g adds about 65 calories. Restaurant palak paneer, richer with cream, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Palak paneer is spinach cooked down with onion, tomato, ginger and garlic, puréed into a smooth green gravy, with cubes of paneer stirred in. Restaurants often finish it with cream or butter; at home it's usually plainer.
Spinach adds very few calories. Paneer is about half of this bowl's calories and the oil most of the rest, so the amount of paneer and fat decides the number.
foods.portionsCaption: Home palak paneer, made as below.

recipe.label: Recipe: one bowl, 150 g spinach and 40 g paneer with ½ tablespoon of oil
recipe.yieldNote: the ingredients added together, with no allowance for water boiled off, as the Indian Nutrient Databank does
recipe.densityNote: taken as 1 g per ml; a stated assumption

outside.label: Restaurant
outside.caption: One 200 ml katori. The outside range has 1.5 to 2 times the oil, plus up to a tablespoon of cream.
outside.basis: USDA's palak paneer (FNDDS 72125310) is 7.0% fat against 4.8% here, in line with richer restaurant versions. Up to twice the oil and up to a tablespoon of cream per katori are stated assumptions.
text: Restaurant palak paneer usually has more fat than home versions: more oil or butter in the masala and often a swirl of cream. USDA's survey value for palak paneer is half as fatty again as this home bowl, per gram.
No lab has measured an Indian restaurant palak paneer, so the range below allows 1.5 to 2 times the oil, plus up to a tablespoon of cream per katori.

changes: Paneer is the biggest part. Each extra 25 g of paneer adds about 65 calories.
A tablespoon of cream adds about 30 calories, and a teaspoon of butter about 35.
Spinach barely counts: the 150 g in this bowl is under 40 calories.
Low-fat paneer, or tofu in its place, lowers the number. Full-fat malai paneer raises it.
method: The recipe is the spinach paneer in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 150 g spinach, 40 g paneer, tomato, onion, ginger, garlic and spices, cooked with half a tablespoon of oil. Values are from IFCT 2017.
The cooked weight is the ingredients added together, and katoris are worked out at 1 g per ml.

range.text: USDA's survey value for palak paneer is about 101 calories per 100 g, against about {{per100}} here, because it's made with more fat. Depending on the paneer, oil and cream, a 200 ml katori is anywhere from about {{kcal:k200}} to 200.
range.reason: USDA FNDDS palak paneer (101 kcal per 100 g) is 29% above this textbook bowl, with more fat (7.0% against 4.8%). Shown as a range.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 bowl of palak paneer?
faq.a: About {{kcal:bowl}} for a home bowl with 40 g of paneer, and about {{kcal:bowl_cream}} with a tablespoon of cream stirred in.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of palak paneer?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}} for this home version. USDA's survey value, closer to restaurant style, is 101.

faq.q: How much protein is in palak paneer?
faq.a: About {{protein:bowl}} g in a bowl with 40 g of paneer, most of it from the paneer.

faq.q: Which has more calories, palak paneer or paneer butter masala?
faq.a: Paneer butter masala, usually by a lot, because of the butter, cream and larger amount of paneer. A 200 ml katori of [paneer butter masala](/calories/paneer-butter-masala/) is about {{kcal@paneer-butter-masala:k200}}, against about {{kcal:k200}} here.

crossCheck.source: USDA FNDDS 2021-2023, Palak Paneer (72125310)

judgement: Range top: about 100 kcal per 100 g x 200 g = 200 kcal, in line with FNDDS.
Garam masala (0.25 tsp) left out.
Cream 1 tbsp = 15 g of USDA light cream (19% fat).

foods.name: Matar paneer
foods.title: Matar paneer calories: per katori and per bowl
foods.description: A 200 ml katori of home matar paneer has about {{kcal:k200}} calories, from peas, paneer and a tablespoon of oil. Restaurant matar paneer compared.
foods.answer: A 200 ml katori of home matar paneer has about {{kcal:k200}} calories. A full textbook bowl, with 50 g of paneer and 100 g of peas, is about {{kcal:bowl}}. Paneer matters most, about 65 calories per extra 25 g; each teaspoon of oil adds about 40. Restaurant matar paneer, richer, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} a katori.
intro: Matar paneer is green peas and paneer cubes in an onion and tomato gravy, cooked with ginger, garlic and garam masala. It's one of the most common paneer dishes in north Indian homes and on dhaba menus, eaten with roti or rice.
Paneer and oil carry most of the calories; the peas add protein and fibre and a smaller share. This textbook gravy is thick, made without added water.
foods.portionsCaption: Thick gravy, made as below.

recipe.label: Recipe: one bowl, 100 g peas and 50 g paneer with 1 tablespoon of oil
recipe.yieldNote: the ingredients added together, as the Indian Nutrient Databank does; the textbook adds no water
recipe.densityNote: taken as 1 g per ml; a stated assumption

outside.label: Dhaba or restaurant
outside.caption: One 200 ml katori. The outside range has up to half as much fat again, plus up to a tablespoon of cream.
outside.basis: No analysed value for restaurant matar paneer was found. Up to 1.5 times the oil and up to a tablespoon of cream per katori are stated assumptions.
text: Restaurant matar paneer often has a richer gravy, with cream, cashew paste or butter, and sometimes fried paneer.
With no lab figure to go on, the range below allows up to half as much oil again and up to a tablespoon of cream per katori.

changes: Paneer is the main variable. Each extra 25 g adds about 65 calories.
Oil comes next: each teaspoon in the masala adds about 40 calories to the pot.
Peas add less than you might think: 50 g is about 40 calories, with about 4 g of protein.
A thinner gravy with water added fills more katoris with the same total.
method: The recipe is the matar paneer in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 100 g peas and 50 g paneer with tomato, onion, ginger, garlic, green chilli and spices, cooked in a tablespoon of oil. Values are from IFCT 2017.
The textbook adds no water, so this is a thick gravy, and katoris are worked out at 1 g per ml.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 katori of matar paneer?
faq.a: About {{kcal:k200}} in a 200 ml katori, and about {{kcal:k150}} in a 150 ml one.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of matar paneer?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}} for this thick home version.

faq.q: How much protein is in matar paneer?
faq.a: About {{protein:k200}} g in a 200 ml katori, from the paneer and peas.

faq.q: Which has more calories, matar paneer or palak paneer?
faq.a: Matar paneer here, about {{kcal:k200}} per 200 ml katori against about {{kcal@palak-paneer:k200}} for [palak paneer](/calories/palak-paneer/). It has more paneer, more oil and peas instead of spinach.

judgement: The textbook says 100 g peas (unshelled); INDB counts all 100 g as peas. Followed here; if it means pods, the peas would be about half and the bowl about 40 kcal lower.
No independent analysed value for matar paneer was found (IFCT, NIN Annexure 8, USDA FNDDS).
Garam masala (0.25 tsp) left out.

foods.name: Chicken curry
foods.title: Chicken curry calories: per katori, bowl and 100 g
foods.description: A bowl of home chicken curry with 125 g of chicken has about {{kcal:bowl}} calories; a 200 ml katori about {{kcal:k200}}. Restaurant curry compared.
foods.answer: A bowl of home chicken curry with 125 g of chicken has about {{kcal:bowl}} calories. A 200 ml katori is about {{kcal:k200}}. The share of chicken matters most: a katori of mostly pieces has more than one of mostly gravy. Restaurant or dhaba chicken curry, cooked with more oil, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Home chicken curry is chicken cooked in a masala of fried onion, tomato, ginger, garlic and whole spices, with a little curd. Every region has its own, from Punjabi tari wala chicken to Bengali kosha mangsho-style curries and Kerala versions with coconut.
Chicken is about two thirds of the calories in this recipe and the oil most of the rest. The share of chicken to gravy in your katori makes a big difference.
foods.portionsCaption: Home chicken curry, made as below, with chicken and gravy together.

recipe.label: Recipe: 250 g chicken with onion, tomato and 1 tablespoon of oil, for 2 bowls
recipe.yieldNote: the ingredients added together, as the Indian Nutrient Databank does; the textbook adds no water
recipe.densityNote: taken as 1 g per ml; a stated assumption

outside.label: Restaurant or dhaba
outside.caption: One 200 ml katori. The outside range has 1.5 to 2 times the oil.
outside.basis: No analysed value for restaurant chicken curry in India was found. 1.5 to 2 times this recipe's oil is a stated assumption; restaurant gravies are commonly finished with more oil or butter.
text: Restaurant and dhaba chicken curries are usually cooked with more oil, often with a layer of it on top, and some add cream or butter.
No lab has measured one, so the range below assumes 1.5 to 2 times the oil of this home recipe for the same katori.

changes: The share of chicken matters most. A katori that's mostly pieces has more than one that's mostly gravy.
Each teaspoon of oil adds about 40 calories to the pot. Skimming oil off the top takes some away.
Chicken with skin, or thighs and legs, have more fat than skinless breast.
Coconut-based curries add more: 60 g of coconut milk is about 140 calories.
method: The recipe is the chicken curry in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 250 g chicken with 100 g each of onion and tomato, ginger, garlic, curd and whole spices, cooked in a tablespoon of oil, for 2 bowls. Values are from IFCT 2017.
IFCT 2017's chicken breast has more fat than USDA's (9 g per 100 g against 3 g), so these figures are at the higher end. The textbook adds no water; katoris are worked out at 1 g per ml.

range.text: Published figures differ with the oil and the share of chicken. ICMR-NIN counts ¾ cup of chicken curry at 240 calories, above this page's {{kcal:cup3}}, while USDA's survey puts 100 g at 107, below this page's {{kcal:g100}}. A 200 ml katori of chicken curry can be anywhere from about 215 to 320.
range.reason: NIN's chicken curry (240 kcal per 3/4 cup) is 24% above this page's 150 ml; USDA FNDDS chicken curry (107 kcal per 100 g) is 17% below. Shown as a range.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 bowl of chicken curry?
faq.a: About {{kcal:bowl}} for a home bowl with 125 g of chicken, and about {{kcal:k200}} for a 200 ml katori.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of chicken curry?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}} for this home curry. Values from other sources run from about 107 to 160, depending on oil and how much is chicken.

faq.q: How much protein is in chicken curry?
faq.a: About {{protein:bowl}} g in a bowl with 125 g of chicken, and about {{protein:k200}} g in a 200 ml katori.

faq.q: How many calories are in chicken curry and rice?
faq.a: Add about {{kcal@plain-rice:k200}} for a 200 ml katori of [plain rice](/calories/plain-rice/) to the curry: about {{kcal:k200}} for a 200 ml katori.

faq.q: Which has more calories, chicken curry or butter chicken?
faq.a: Restaurant butter chicken, usually, because of the butter and cream. Made at home from textbook recipes the two are close: about {{kcal:k200}} per 200 ml katori here and about {{kcal@butter-chicken:k200}} for [butter chicken](/calories/butter-chicken/).

foods.name: Butter chicken
foods.title: Butter chicken calories: home serving and restaurant
foods.description: A home serving of butter chicken with 125 g of chicken has about {{kcal:serving}} calories. Restaurant butter chicken is about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
foods.answer: A home serving of butter chicken, 125 g of chicken with its share of butter and cream, has about {{kcal:serving}} calories. A 200 ml katori is about {{kcal:k200}}. Butter and cream matter most: a tablespoon of butter adds about 100, a tablespoon of cream about 30. A restaurant serving, richer and larger, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Butter chicken, or murgh makhani, is chicken in a smooth tomato gravy enriched with butter and cream, lightly sweet and spiced with garam masala and kasuri methi. It came out of Delhi's Moti Mahal kitchen and is now the most ordered chicken curry on Indian delivery apps and restaurant menus.
In this textbook version the chicken is about 60% of the calories and the butter and cream about 30%. Restaurants use a lot more of both, which is where the big numbers come from.
foods.portionsCaption: Home butter chicken, made as below, with chicken and gravy together.

recipe.label: Recipe: 250 g chicken in tomato gravy with 1½ tablespoons of butter and 1½ of cream, for 2 servings
recipe.yieldNote: the ingredients added together, as the Indian Nutrient Databank does; the textbook adds no water
recipe.densityNote: taken as 1 g per ml; a stated assumption

outside.label: Restaurant or delivery
outside.caption: One serving. The outside range has 1.5 to 2 times the butter and cream, in a serving up to 1.5 times as big.
outside.basis: No analysed value for restaurant butter chicken was found. Up to twice the butter and cream and a serving up to 1.5 times as big are stated assumptions, in line with the restaurant range on the paneer butter masala page.
text: Restaurant butter chicken is usually made with far more butter and cream than a home or textbook version, often finished with another knob of butter and a swirl of cream, and delivery portions tend to be large.
No lab has measured one, so the range below allows 1.5 to 2 times the butter and cream, in a serving up to 1.5 times as big.

changes: Butter and cream are the biggest variables. A tablespoon of butter adds about 100 calories, and a tablespoon of cream about 30.
Serving size comes next. Delivery boxes often hold more chicken and gravy than a home serving.
Thigh meat or chicken with skin has more fat than breast. Tandoori chicken pieces, marinated in curd first, add a little.
Naan or rice is extra: a home [butter naan](/calories/butter-naan/) is about {{kcal@butter-naan:one_tsp}}.
method: The recipe is the butter chicken in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 250 g chicken with fresh tomato, tomato purée, onion, ginger, green chilli and pepper, finished with 1½ tablespoons each of butter and cream, for 2 servings. Values are from IFCT 2017, with butter, cream, purée and sugar from USDA.

intro: Egg curry is hard-boiled eggs simmered in an onion and tomato masala with ginger, garlic and ground coriander. Bengali dim kosha fries the eggs first, South Indian muttai kuzhambu adds tamarind or coconut, and dhaba anda curry is often oilier and spicier.

method: The recipe is the egg curry in Basic Food Preparation, a standard Indian cookery manual (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 1 egg with tomato, onion, ginger, garlic, green chilli and ground coriander, cooked in 2 teaspoons of oil. Values are from IFCT 2017.

intro: Aloo sabzi is potato cooked with tomato, onion, ginger, garlic and ground coriander, with a jeera tempering. Some homes make it dry, others with a thin gravy for puri or kachori. Gujarati batata nu shaak is often sweet and sour, and the halwai version served with puri is usually oilier.
Potato itself is a moderate starch, about 70 calories per 100 g raw in IFCT 2017. The oil in the pot adds about as much again.

intro: Bhindi sabzi is okra cut into rounds and stir-fried with onion, turmeric, chilli and coriander until it loses its stickiness. Bhindi do pyaza adds more onion, Gujarati bhinda nu shaak is often cooked with a little besan or peanut, and kurkuri bhindi is deep-fried.

foods.answer: A 200 ml katori of home baingan bharta has about {{kcal:k200}} calories. A textbook bowl, made from 200 g of brinjal with a tablespoon of oil, is about {{kcal:bowl}}. Oil or ghee is the biggest part, about 40 to 45 calories a teaspoon. Dhaba bharta, with more oil and ghee on top, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Baingan bharta is a large brinjal roasted over a flame until the skin chars, then peeled, mashed and cooked with onion, tomato, green chilli and ginger. Punjabi bharta is cooked in oil or ghee, Bihari chokha is mixed with mustard oil raw, and Gujarati ringan no olo and Maharashtrian bharit are close cousins.
Brinjal is one of the lightest vegetables, about 25 calories per 100 g. Over half of this bowl's calories come from the oil.

recipe.yieldNote: the ingredients added together, as the Indian Nutrient Databank does; water lost in roasting isn't counted

text: Dhaba bharta is often cooked in more oil and finished with ghee or butter on top, and a roasted bharta that's cooked down further holds more in each katori.
No lab has measured it, so the range below allows up to twice this recipe's fat.

changes: Oil or ghee is the biggest part. Each teaspoon adds about 40 to 45 calories to the pot.
Roasting drives water out of the brinjal, so a well-roasted bharta packs more into a katori than this recipe suggests.
Bihari chokha uses a spoon of raw mustard oil instead of frying; the calories per teaspoon are the same.
Peas in matar baingan bharta add a little, about 40 calories per 50 g.

The cooked weight is the ingredients added together, with no allowance for water lost in roasting, so the katori figures are on the low side for a dry bharta.

range.text: ICMR-NIN's general figure for a cup of dry vegetable dish is 150 calories, a little above this page's {{kcal:k200}}. A drier, well-roasted bharta, or one with more oil, comes closer to that, so a 200 ml katori is usually between {{kcal:k200}} and 150.
range.reason: NIN's dry vegetable (150 kcal per cup) is 15% above this page's katori, which ignores water lost in roasting. Shown as a range.

intro: Upma is roasted semolina (rava, suji) cooked in water with a tempering of mustard seeds, urad dal, curry leaves, green chilli, ginger and onion. It's a quick breakfast across south and west India, made plain or with peas, carrot and beans, and in Karnataka it's uppittu or kharabath.
Semolina and oil make up most of upma's calories, in about equal parts in this textbook recipe. How much water it's cooked with changes what a katori holds.

text: Upma in a darshini or Udupi restaurant is usually a generous plate, often with ghee on top and cashews in the tempering.
No lab has measured it, so the range below allows a plate up to 1.5 times this one, with up to a teaspoon of ghee.

changes: Oil or ghee matters as much as the rava. Each teaspoon adds about 40 to 45 calories.
Vegetables like peas, carrot and beans add volume and a few calories, so a vegetable upma has less per katori.
Cashews in the tempering add about 60 calories per 10 g.
Wetter upma fills more katoris with the same calories. Count by the rava when you can.
method: The recipe is the semolina upma in Basic Food Preparation, a standard Indian cookery manual (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 40 g coarse semolina with 5 g urad dal, onion, green chilli, ginger, curry leaves, mustard seeds and lemon, cooked in 15 g of oil and 100 ml of water, for 2 small bowls. Values are from IFCT 2017.
The cooked weight is the ingredients added together. Katoris use USDA's 170 g per cup for upma.

range.text: Upma varies a lot with the water. ICMR-NIN counts a cup at 270 calories, above this page's {{kcal:k200}}, while USDA's much wetter upma is about 87 per 100 g against {{kcal:g100}} here. A 200 ml katori can be anywhere from about 125 to 270.
range.reason: NIN's upma (270 kcal per cup) is 26% above this page's katori; USDA FNDDS upma (87 kcal per 100 g) is 42% below. Water content differs. Shown as a range.

intro: Besan chilla is a thin savoury pancake of gram flour batter with onion, tomato, green chilli, ginger, coriander and ajwain, cooked on a tawa. In Gujarat it's pudla, and many homes stuff it with grated paneer or add vegetables to the batter.
Besan is higher in protein than wheat flour, about 22 g per 100 g in IFCT 2017. The oil on the tawa is what changes the number most.

intro: Dhokla, as most of India knows it, is the soft, yellow besan cake from Gujarat: gram flour and curd batter, leavened with soda and steamed, then tempered with mustard seeds, green chillies and curry leaves. In Gujarat the besan one is called khaman, and dhokla usually means a fermented rice and dal version.
It's steamed, so most of its calories come from the besan. Farsan shops pour a sweetened oil tempering over it, which adds more.

Values are from IFCT 2017, with curd from USDA.
Steaming keeps the water in, so the cooked weight is the ingredients added together: about 40 g a piece. Besan is valued as ground Bengal gram dal.

Two vadas, the usual plate, are about {{kcal:two}} before sambar and chutney, and about {{kcal:two_sambar}} with sambar. Size matters most: a vada from 20 g of dal has a third more. intro: Medu vada is a ring-shaped fritter of ground urad dal batter, deep-fried until crisp outside and soft inside. It's a breakfast staple in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala and Andhra, eaten with sambar and coconut chutney, or soaked in sambar as sambar vada.
Urad dal is high in protein for a fried snack. Oil taken up in frying is about a third of each vada's calories.

recipe.label: Recipe: 60 g urad dal, ground and deep-fried into 4 vadas

ingredients.note: Taken up in frying: a stated assumption, so a vada is about 10% fat

recipe.yieldNote: the dal's non-fat solids (53.5 g) at USDA's vada composition, 42% water and 9.7% fat, so 53.5 / 0.4827

outside.basis: Fat up to 1.22 times: Jain et al. 2024 found total fat in Indian fried foods rose from a mean of 22.5% to 27.4% of dry weight between the 1st and 32nd frying in the same oil. Vadas up to 1.5 times as big are a stated assumption.
text: Vadas from an Udupi restaurant or a stall are often bigger than home ones and fried in oil that's been used many times, which raises the fat they take up.
A lab study found fried foods took up about a fifth more fat after 32 fryings in the same oil. The range below uses that, with vadas up to 1.5 times this size.

changes: Size is the main variable. A vada from 20 g of dal has a third more than one from 15 g.
Oil that's been used many times leaves more fat in each vada.
Sambar and chutney are separate. ICMR-NIN counts a cup of sambar at about 110 calories and 2 tablespoons of coconut chutney at about 120.
Sambar vada soaks two vadas in sambar: count the sambar too, see [sambar](/calories/sambar/).
method: The recipe is the plain urad dal vada in Basic Food Preparation, a standard Indian cookery manual (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 60 g of urad dal ground with a little water and deep-fried, making 4 vadas. Values are from IFCT 2017.

The databank counts all the frying oil as eaten, which is far too high. This page assumes a vada ends up with the composition of USDA's vada, 42% water and 9.7% fat, which works out to about 2.5 g of oil per vada and a vada of about 28 g. ICMR-NIN's 140 calories for 2 vadas agrees.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 medu vada?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for a home vada made from 15 g of urad dal.

faq.q: How much protein is in medu vada?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g in one vada and about {{protein:two}} g in two, from the urad dal.

faq.q: Which has more calories, medu vada or idli?

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 medu vada with sambar?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two_sambar}} calories: 2 vadas at {{kcal:two}} and a 200 ml katori of [sambar](/calories/sambar/). Two tablespoons of coconut chutney add about 120.

Cooked vada about 27.7 g, close to FNDDS's 30 g per vada.
INDB counts 240 ml of frying oil (746 kcal per 100 g), so its values aren't used.

outside.label: Street stall
outside.caption: One vada pav. The outside range has up to about a fifth more frying oil, in a vada up to 1.3 times as big.
outside.basis: Fat up to 1.22 times: Jain et al. 2024 found total fat in Indian fried foods rose from a mean of 22.5% to 27.4% of dry weight between the 1st and 32nd frying in the same oil. A vada pav up to 1.3 times as big is a stated assumption.
text: Street vadas are fried in oil that's used all day, and stall sizes vary from small to large. Some stalls brush the pav with butter or add cheese.
A lab study found fried foods took up about a fifth more fat after 32 fryings in the same oil. The range below uses that, with a vada pav up to 1.3 times this size.

changes: Butter on the pav adds about 35 calories a teaspoon, and a slice of cheese about 60 to 70.
Dry garlic chutney has coconut, peanuts or sesame in it and adds a little; green chutney adds almost nothing.
A bigger vada, or oil that's been used many times, means more fat in each vada.
Without the pav, the vada alone is about {{kcal:vada}}.
method: The vada follows the potato bonda in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 100 g potato, 20 g peas, onion, ginger, green chilli and cashew, coated in a batter of 2 tablespoons of besan and 2 teaspoons of rice flour. The textbook makes 4 small bondas; a Mumbai vada is bigger, so this page makes 2. Values are from IFCT 2017.

The databank counts all the frying oil as eaten. ICMR-NIN counts a potato bonda at 100 calories, so this page sets the oil taken up to match that: about 10 g per vada. The pav is 43 g, the size in the databank's pav bhaji recipe, valued from USDA's soft dinner roll.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 vada pav?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for a vada pav made at home with a 43 g pav, and about {{kcal:butter}} with a teaspoon of butter.

faq.q: How many calories are in vada pav without pav?
faq.a: About {{kcal:vada}} for the batata vada on its own.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 vada pav?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two}} for two.

faq.q: How much protein is in vada pav?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g, from the pav, the besan and the peas.

faq.q: Which has more calories, vada pav or samosa?
faq.a: A vada pav, because of the pav. A home [samosa](/calories/samosa/) is about {{kcal@samosa:one}}, against about {{kcal:one}} for a vada pav.

judgement: Oil taken up: set so the textbook's 4 bondas are 100 kcal each, ICMR-NIN's potato bonda (2 for 200 kcal). Before frying the recipe is 221.5 kcal, so (400 - 221.5) / 8.843 = 20.2 g of oil. Because NIN is used to set the oil, it isn't listed as a separate check.
Besan 2 tbsp = 15 g; rice flour 2 tsp = 5 g (USDA). Cashew 2 nuts = 2.5 g (INDB).
Pav 43 g: INDB's OSR112 pav bhaji lists 12 pav at 516 g. Valued as USDA FDC 172793, dinner rolls.
Chana and urad dal (0.125 tsp each), mustard seeds, curry leaves, coriander and soda left out.
Cheese slice in the changes list: 20 g at about 300 to 340 kcal per 100 g.

foods.name: Pav bhaji
foods.title: Pav bhaji calories: per plate, with 1, 2 or 4 pav
foods.description: A plate of pav bhaji with 2 butter pav has about {{kcal:plate2}} calories; the bhaji alone is about {{kcal:bhaji}}. With extra pav and street butter.
foods.answer: A plate of pav bhaji with 2 butter-toasted pav has about {{kcal:plate2}} calories. The bhaji alone is about {{kcal:bhaji}}, each butter pav adds about {{kcal:pav}}, and a plate with 4 pav is about {{kcal:plate4}}. Butter matters most: each teaspoon adds about 35. Street pav bhaji, with a cube of butter on the tawa, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Pav bhaji is a thick, spiced mash of potato, peas, tomato, cauliflower, capsicum and carrot, cooked on a big tawa with butter and pav bhaji masala, served with soft pav toasted in more butter, chopped onion and lemon. It started as a quick meal for Mumbai's mill workers and is now sold everywhere.
Butter is the key number. In this recipe the butter in the bhaji and on the pav is close to half of a plate's calories.
foods.portionsCaption: Home pav bhaji as below. Each pav is 43 g, toasted in a teaspoon of butter.

recipe.label: Recipe: about 1.1 kg of vegetables cooked with 4¾ tablespoons of butter, for 5 plates of bhaji
recipe.yieldNote: no cooked weight used; a plate of bhaji is a fifth of the recipe

outside.label: Street or restaurant
outside.caption: One plate with 2 pav. The outside range adds 10 to 25 g more butter (about 2 to 5 teaspoons).
outside.basis: No analysed value for street pav bhaji was found. Street stalls are known for adding a block of butter to the bhaji and pav; 10 to 25 g more per plate is a stated assumption.
text: Street pav bhaji is known for its butter: a cube melted into each plate's bhaji on the tawa, and pav toasted in more of it. Amul-style butter pav bhaji can carry a lot more than this home plate.
No lab has measured it, so the range below adds 10 to 25 g more butter to one plate with 2 pav.

changes: Butter is the biggest variable. Each teaspoon adds about 35 calories, and street plates often have several more.
Each extra butter pav adds about {{kcal:pav}}. A plain pav without butter is about 135.
More potato in the bhaji raises it a little; more cauliflower, capsicum or peas changes it little.
Without butter, a plate of bhaji is about 95 calories lighter.
method: The recipe is the pav bhaji in the Indian Nutrient Databank's open recipe set: potato, tomato, peas, carrot, cauliflower, capsicum, beans and onion with pav bhaji masala, cooked with 3 tablespoons of butter, for 5 plates, with 12 pav and 5 to 7 more tablespoons of butter for topping and toasting. This page uses 6 tablespoons: a teaspoon for each pav and the rest on top of the bhaji. Values are from IFCT 2017, with butter and pav from USDA.
Whole spices that aren't eaten, and those under 1 g, are left out. Each pav is 43 g, as in the recipe (12 pav weighing 516 g).

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 plate of pav bhaji?
faq.a: About {{kcal:plate2}} for a plate of bhaji with 2 butter pav, and about {{kcal:plate4}} with 4 pav.

faq.q: How many calories are in pav bhaji without pav?
faq.a: About {{kcal:bhaji}} for a plate of the bhaji alone.

faq.q: How many calories are in pav bhaji without butter?
faq.a: Leaving out all the butter takes off about 95 calories from the bhaji and about 35 from each pav, so a plate with 2 plain pav is about 385.

faq.q: How much protein is in pav bhaji?
faq.a: About {{protein:plate2}} g in a plate with 2 pav, mostly from the pav and the peas.

useCase.label: Calories in restaurant and delivery food

judgement: Open-source recipe OSR112 (INDB), 5 servings. Butter: 3 tbsp in the bhaji plus 6 tbsp (85.2 g) of the 5 to 7 tbsp for topping and toasting, split as 5 g per pav (12 pav, 60 g) and 25 g on top of the bhaji.
Lemon '1 no' taken as 48 g juice (USDA FDC 167747). Ginger-garlic paste 1 tsp each = 5 g. Coriander 3.5 tbsp = 3.5 g (INDB's 0.25 cup = 4 g).
Left out: black cardamom, cloves, mace, nutmeg, cinnamon, star anise, amchur and dried ginger powder (under 15 kcal together for 5 plates).
No independent analysed value for pav bhaji was found (IFCT, NIN Annexure 8, USDA FNDDS). INDB's per-serving value (561 kcal) is from this recipe with hamburger buns as the pav.
Without butter: bhaji butter (67.6 g, 485 kcal) / 5 = 97 kcal per plate; pav butter 5 g = 36 kcal. Plate with 2 plain pav: bhaji 213 - 97 + 2 x 133 = 382, about 385.

foods.name: Pani puri
foods.title: Pani puri calories: per puri and per plate of 6
foods.description: A plate of 6 pani puri with potato, chana and sweet chutney has about {{kcal:plate}} calories, about {{kcal:one}} each. Shells, pani and fillings compared.
foods.answer: A plate of 6 pani puri with potato, chana and sweet chutney has about {{kcal:plate}} calories, about {{kcal:one}} a puri. Ten come to about {{kcal:ten}}. The fried shells are most of it; sweet chutney adds about 20 calories a tablespoon. A street plate, 5 to 8 puris with more or less chutney, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Pani puri is a round, hollow, fried shell of semolina or wheat, cracked open and filled with potato, chana or ragda, sweet tamarind chutney and spiced mint-tamarind water, eaten in one bite. It's golgappa in Delhi, puchka in Kolkata and gupchup in Odisha.
The shells are fried, so they carry most of the calories. The pani itself is mostly water with a little tamarind; the potato and chutney add the rest.
foods.portionsCaption: A plate as below: 6 puris with potato, chana, sweet chutney and pani.

recipe.label: One plate: 6 puris with potato, chana, a tablespoon of sweet chutney and 150 ml pani

ingredients.note: 6 puris with their boondi, at the packet's 39 g for 5
dry weight, boiled, about 10 g cooked

recipe.yieldNote: no cooked weight used; the recipe is one plate of 6

outside.label: Street stall
outside.caption: A plate of 6. The outside range is 0.9 to 1.3 times this plate.
outside.basis: No analysed value for street pani puri was found. Shell size and filling vary by stall; 0.9 to 1.3 times this plate is a stated assumption. Ragda (white peas) in place of potato and more sweet chutney are common.
text: Street pani puri varies with the stall: shell size, how much potato or ragda goes in, and how much sweet chutney you ask for. Most vendors give 5 to 8 to a plate and keep going if you want more.
We found no lab measurement of street pani puri, so the range below runs from 0.9 to 1.3 times this plate.

changes: The shells are most of it. Each puri with its share of the plate is about {{kcal:one}}.
Sweet chutney adds about 20 calories a tablespoon; asking for extra adds up.
Ragda (white peas) in place of potato adds a little more protein and about the same calories.
The pani itself, mint, tamarind and spices in water, is about 15 calories for a whole plate.
method: No standard recipe for this plate exists in the Indian Nutrient Databank, so the plate is assembled from typical amounts, each stated below and valued from IFCT 2017. Shells are a packaged pani puri's own label values (puris and boondi, 39 g for 5), since IFCT 2017 has no puri shells.

Sweet chutney as The Art & Science of Cooking's saunth chutney (ASC281: 25 g tamarind and 50 g jaggery in 100 ml water), so 1 tablespoon (15 g) holds 2.1 g tamarind and 4.3 g jaggery, about 21 kcal. The pani is 150 ml of water with 3 g tamarind and 10 g of mint and coriander.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 pani puri?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for one puri with its potato, chutney and pani.

faq.q: How many calories are in a plate of pani puri?
faq.a: About {{kcal:plate}} for a plate of 6, and about {{kcal:ten}} for 10.

faq.q: How many calories are in pani puri water?
faq.a: Very few. A plate's 150 ml of pani, with tamarind, mint and coriander, is about 15 calories. Sweet chutney adds more.

faq.q: How much protein is in pani puri?
faq.a: About {{protein:plate}} g in a plate of 6, from the shells and chana.

faq.q: Which has more calories, pani puri or bhel puri?
faq.a: A plate of [bhel puri](/calories/bhel-puri/) is about {{kcal@bhel-puri:plate}}, a little more than a plate of 6 pani puri at about {{kcal:plate}}.

useCase.label: Calories in restaurant and delivery food

judgement: Assembled plate; all amounts other than the shells and chutney are typical amounts, stated as assumptions: potato 30 g, kala chana 4 g dry, onion 10 g, pani 150 ml with 3 g tamarind and 5 g each of mint and coriander.

Shells: USDA FDC 1913634 (branded label, packaged pani puri kit): 39 g = 5 puris with boondi, 125 kcal, 2 g protein, 18 g carbohydrate (1.01 g fibre), 5 g fat. Carbohydrate taken as 18 - 1.01 g. 6 puris = 46.8 g.
Sweet chutney as The Art & Science of Cooking's saunth chutney (ASC281: 25 g tamarind and 50 g jaggery in 100 ml water), so 1 tablespoon (15 g) holds 2.1 g tamarind and 4.3 g jaggery, about 21 kcal.
No independent analysed value for pani puri was found (IFCT, NIN Annexure 8, USDA FNDDS, Europe PMC).
Pani alone: tamarind 3 g (8.7 kcal) + mint 5 g (1.9) + coriander 5 g (1.6) = about 12 kcal, about 15 with spices.

foods.title: Bhel puri calories: per plate and per 100 g
foods.description: A plate of bhel puri has about {{kcal:plate}} calories, from puffed rice, sev, papdi, potato, peanuts and chutneys. Dry bhel and street plates compared.
foods.answer: A plate of bhel puri, 25 g of puffed rice with sev, papdi, potato, onion, peanuts and chutneys, has about {{kcal:plate}} calories. Half a plate is about {{kcal:half}}, and 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}. Sev is the most calorie-dense part, about 55 calories per 10 g. A street plate, mixed to order, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Bhel puri is puffed rice tossed with fine sev, crushed papdi, boiled potato, onion, tomato and peanuts, dressed with sweet tamarind chutney and green chutney and finished with lemon and coriander. It's the Mumbai beach snack, and Kolkata's jhal muri and Karnataka's churmuri are close cousins.
Puffed rice is light by volume, so a plate looks bigger than its calories. The fried sev and papdi, and the peanuts, are where most of the fat comes from.

recipe.yieldNote: the ingredients added together, with sev and papdi at their fried weight

outside.basis: No analysed value for street bhel puri was found. Stall plates vary, often with more sev; 0.9 to 1.4 times this plate is a stated assumption.
text: Street bhel is mixed to order, and plates vary a lot, especially in how much sev goes on top. Some stalls add raw mango, boiled chana or more peanuts.
No lab has measured street bhel, so the range below runs from 0.9 to 1.4 times this plate.

changes: Sev is the most calorie-dense part: 10 g is about 55 calories, so a heavy hand with it adds up.
Peanuts add about 25 calories per 5 g, and each papdi about 20.
Sweet chutney adds about 20 calories a tablespoon. Dry bhel without it is a little lighter.
More onion, tomato, cucumber or raw mango adds volume and very few calories.
method: No standard recipe for this plate exists in the Indian Nutrient Databank, so the plate is assembled from typical amounts, each stated below and valued from IFCT 2017. The puffed rice and peanuts follow the proportions of the databank's open-source bhel puri (60 g puffed rice and 2 tablespoons of peanuts for 2 to 3 plates).

Sev valued as besan plus oil at 39.6% fat, the fat content Gupta et al. 2016 measured in bhujia (fried besan noodles) from a Delhi vendor. Papdi valued as maida plus oil at 38.5% fat, the fat content Gupta et al. 2016 measured in mathri (fried wheat crackers) from a Delhi vendor. 4 g per papdi is an assumption. Sweet chutney as The Art & Science of Cooking's saunth chutney (ASC281: 25 g tamarind and 50 g jaggery in 100 ml water), so 1 tablespoon (15 g) holds 2.1 g tamarind and 4.3 g jaggery, about 21 kcal.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 plate of bhel puri?
faq.a: About {{kcal:plate}} for a plate with 25 g of puffed rice, 10 g of sev and two papdis.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of bhel puri?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}} for this mix, chutneys included.

faq.q: How much protein is in bhel puri?
faq.a: About {{protein:plate}} g in a plate, from the puffed rice, sev and peanuts.

faq.q: Which has more calories, bhel puri or sev puri?
faq.a: A plate of [sev puri](/calories/sev-puri/) is about {{kcal@sev-puri:plate}}, a little more than bhel at about {{kcal:plate}}, because it has more papdi and sev.

useCase.label: Calories in restaurant and delivery food

judgement: Assembled plate. OSR114 (INDB open-source bhel puri) makes its own sev and papdi in bulk and counts all frying oil, so its totals (3,574 kcal per plate) aren't used; its puffed rice (60 g for 2 to 3 plates) and peanuts (2 tbsp) guide the amounts.
Sev 10 g = besan 6.0 g + oil 4.0 g; papdi 2 x 4 g = maida 4.9 g + oil 3.1 g. Moisture lost in frying isn't counted.
Amounts of potato (20 g), onion (15 g), tomato (15 g), coriander (5 g) and lemon (3 g) are typical amounts, stated as assumptions.
No independent analysed value for bhel puri was found (IFCT, NIN Annexure 8, USDA FNDDS).

foods.description: A home khasta kachori has about {{kcal:one}} calories; street kachoris tested in a lab came to about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}. With aloo sabzi.
foods.answer: A small home khasta kachori has about {{kcal:one}} calories, and 2 kachoris about {{kcal:two}}. Two with a 200 ml katori of aloo sabzi are about {{kcal:with_sabzi}}. Size and frying matter most: street kachoris tested in a lab were one and a half times this size, with two to three times the fat, and came to about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Khasta kachori is a flaky maida pastry, rubbed with plenty of oil or ghee, filled with spiced urad or moong dal and deep-fried slowly until it puffs and crisps. Matar kachori is filled with peas, and Rajasthani pyaz kachori with onion. In north India it's a breakfast with aloo sabzi.
Even before frying, oil in the dough and filling is about a third of a home kachori's calories, and after frying it's close to half. Street kachoris hold much more.
