outside.basis: Calibrated to Gupta et al. 2016, which bought and analysed kachoris from vendors: a village kachori of 55.70 g with 17.82 g fat, and a Delhi urban slum kachori of 53.83 g with 25.09 g fat. Size factor = vendor weight against about 35 g here; fat factor chosen so total fat matches the measured fat.
text: A peer-reviewed study bought kachoris from vendors in Delhi and a nearby village and tested them in a lab. They weighed 54 to 56 g, about one and a half times this home kachori, and held 32% and 47% fat.
The range below uses those two measured kachoris. Oil used again and again, and a thick, oil-rich crust, are the usual reasons street kachoris hold so much.

changes: Size and frying matter most. A street kachori can be one and a half times this one, with two to three times the fat.
The oil or ghee rubbed into the dough (moyan) makes it flaky and adds about 40 to 45 calories per teaspoon to the batch.
Matar and pyaz kachori fillings are a little lighter than dal; raj kachori, filled with curd and chutneys, is much more.
Aloo sabzi with it is a separate dish: see [aloo sabzi](/calories/aloo-sabzi/).
[Mathri](/calories/mathri/) and [namak para](/calories/namak-para/), the dry Diwali snacks, are about {{kcal@mathri:one}} a piece and {{kcal@namak-para:ten}} for 10 pieces.
method: The recipe is the khasta kachori in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 100 g maida rubbed with 1½ tablespoons of oil, filled with 30 g of spiced urad dal cooked in 2 teaspoons of oil, making 7 kachoris. Values are from IFCT 2017.

The databank counts all the frying oil as eaten. This page assumes a fresh home kachori ends up about 18% fat, the oil content measured in lab-fried samosa pastry (18.3%), which works out to about 2 g of oil taken up per kachori.

range.text: ICMR-NIN counts 2 pea kachoris at 380 calories, 190 each, between this small home kachori and the street ones measured in Delhi. Depending on size and oil, a kachori is anywhere from about {{kcal:one}} to {{outHi}} calories.
range.reason: NIN's pea kachori (190 kcal each) is 57% above this page's small home kachori; Gupta et al.'s street kachoris are higher again. Size and fat differ. Shown as a range.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 kachori?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for a small home khasta kachori, and about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} for a street kachori.

faq.q: How many calories are in kachori with aloo sabzi?
faq.a: About {{kcal:with_sabzi}} for 2 home kachoris with a 200 ml katori of aloo sabzi.

faq.q: How much fat is in a kachori?
faq.a: About {{fat:one}} g in this home kachori. Street kachoris tested in a lab held 17.8 g and 25.1 g.

faq.q: Which has more calories, kachori or samosa?
faq.a: A home [samosa](/calories/samosa/), about {{kcal@samosa:one}}, is bigger than this small khasta kachori at about {{kcal:one}}. Street versions of both are much higher.

judgement: Home oil uptake: fat set to 18.3% of raw dough, filling and oil (Sakhale et al. 2011, lab-fried samosa pastry). Own fat = 30.9 g; (30.9 + x) / (230.8 + x) = 0.183 gives x = 13.9 g for 7 kachoris. Moisture lost in frying isn't counted.

Street kachoris (Gupta et al. 2016, Tables 1 and 2): village 55.70 g, 17.82 g fat; urban 53.83 g, 25.09 g fat. Size 55.70 / 34.96 = 1.59 and 53.83 / 34.96 = 1.54; fat factors 1.77 and 2.60 solve for the measured fat.
Lemon '0.5 lemon' = 24 g juice (USDA). Asafoetida left out. INDB counts 480 ml frying oil (713 kcal per 100 g), so its values aren't used.
Aloo sabzi row: a 200 ml katori from the aloo sabzi page's recipe, 100 g potato, 50 g tomato, 30 g onion and 9 g oil (spices left out).

foods.name: Momos
foods.title: Momos calories: per piece and per plate, steamed or fried
foods.description: One steamed veg momo (25 g) has about {{kcal:one}} calories, so a plate of 6 is about {{kcal:plate6}}. Fried momos and chicken momos compared.
foods.answer: One steamed veg momo, about 25 g, has about {{kcal:one}} calories, so a plate of 6 is about {{kcal:plate6}} before the chutney or mayonnaise. A plate of 8 is about {{kcal:plate8}}, and 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}. Frying changes it most, and mayonnaise adds about 100 calories a tablespoon. A street plate of 6 runs about {{outLo}} steamed to {{outHi}} fried.
intro: Momos are dumplings of thin maida dough filled with cabbage, carrot, onion and ginger, or with minced chicken, then pleated and steamed. They came from Tibet and Nepal through Darjeeling and Sikkim, and are now sold at street carts across north India, steamed, fried or tandoori.
The maida wrapper is about four fifths of a veg momo's calories. Frying adds a lot; the red chutney adds little, and mayonnaise adds a lot.
foods.portionsCaption: Steamed veg momos, 25 g each, made as below. Chutney not included.

recipe.label: Recipe: 200 g maida dough with 225 g vegetable filling and 3 teaspoons of oil

ingredients.note: for the dough: an assumption, no calories

recipe.yieldNote: the ingredients added together; at 25 g a momo, the size USDA lists for a dumpling, that's about 22 momos

outside.label: Street cart, steamed or fried
outside.caption: A plate of 6. The outside range runs from steamed to fried, adding up to 11.6 g of oil, at USDA's fried dumpling fat.
outside.basis: USDA FNDDS lists a fried dumpling at 11.1 g fat per 100 g against 3.4 g for a steamed one with no meat, so frying adds about 7.7 g of fat per 100 g, or 11.6 g for 150 g of momos.
text: Street carts sell momos steamed, fried, or tossed in sauce. Frying adds a lot: USDA's fried dumplings have about three times the fat of steamed ones. Mayonnaise on the side adds about 100 calories a tablespoon.
The range below runs from a steamed plate of 6 to the same plate fried, using USDA's figures for steamed and fried dumplings.

changes: Fried or tandoori momos have much more fat than steamed ones.
Mayonnaise adds about 100 calories a tablespoon; the red chilli-garlic chutney adds very little.
Chicken momos are close per piece: USDA's steamed dumplings with meat are 113 calories per 100 g, against 125 without.
Paneer and cheese momos have more fat in the filling.
method: No standard textbook in the Indian Nutrient Databank has momos, so this uses a published dietitian's recipe from NephroPlus: 200 g maida with 100 g each of cabbage and carrot, 25 g spring onion, garlic, ginger, green chilli and pepper, cooked in 3 teaspoons of oil. Values are from IFCT 2017.
The recipe's water isn't stated; 100 ml is assumed for a stiff dough and only affects weight. Each momo is taken as 25 g, the size USDA lists for a dumpling.

range.text: USDA's steamed dumpling with no meat is about 125 calories per 100 g, below this page's {{kcal:g100}}, because its wrapper is thinner. A plate of 6 steamed veg momos is usually between about 190 and {{kcal:plate6}}.
range.reason: USDA FNDDS dumpling, no meat (125 kcal per 100 g) is 23% below this page's momos, which have a thicker maida wrapper. Shown as a range.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 momo?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for a 25 g steamed veg momo.

faq.q: How many calories are in a plate of momos?
faq.a: About {{kcal:plate6}} for 6 steamed veg momos, {{kcal:plate8}} for 8 and {{kcal:plate10}} for 10, before chutney or mayonnaise.

faq.q: How many calories are in fried momos?
faq.a: About {{outHi}} for a plate of 6 fried, against {{kcal:plate6}} steamed.

faq.q: How much protein is in momos?
faq.a: About {{protein:plate6}} g in a plate of 6 veg momos. Chicken momos have more.

judgement: Recipe: NephroPlus vegetable steamed momos (maida 1 cup = 200 g as stated, carrot 100 g, cabbage 100 g, spring onion 25 g, garlic 2 cloves, ginger 1 inch, green chilli 1, pepper 0.5 tsp, oil 3 tsp). Spring onion valued as onion. Ginger 1 inch = 10 g, as on the thepla page.
Water 100 ml (half the flour) is an assumption; with it the recipe weighs 554 g, about 22 momos at USDA's 25 g per dumpling.
Fried range: FNDDS 58111120 fried dumpling, no meat, 11.1 g fat per 100 g; FNDDS 55610300 steamed, 3.37 g. (11.1 - 3.37) x 1.5 = 11.6 g oil for 150 g.
Range low end: 125 kcal per 100 g x 150 g = 188 kcal.
Mayonnaise in the changes list: USDA 1 tbsp = 13.8 g (INDB unit table) at about 680 kcal per 100 g, about 94 kcal.

foods.name: Sabudana khichdi
foods.title: Sabudana khichdi calories: per plate and per bowl
foods.description: A plate of sabudana khichdi with peanuts, potato and ghee has about {{kcal:plate}} calories. Fasting-day portions, with and without peanuts.
foods.answer: A plate of sabudana khichdi (50 g dry sabudana, potato, peanuts, a tablespoon of ghee) has about {{kcal:plate}} calories. A small bowl from 25 g is about {{kcal:small}}. Peanuts add about 125 a plate, and each tablespoon of ghee in the pot about 38. A stall or fasting-thali plate, bigger, with more ghee, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Sabudana khichdi is soaked tapioca pearls tossed with crushed roasted peanuts, potato, green chilli, cumin and curry leaves in ghee, finished with lemon and sugar. It's the standard Navratri, Ekadashi and Mahashivratri food in Maharashtra, Gujarat and much of north India.
Sabudana is almost pure starch, and the peanuts and ghee add a lot of fat, so a plate is more filling in calories than it looks: in this recipe the ghee and peanuts together are close to half of it.
foods.portionsCaption: Sabudana khichdi made as below.

recipe.label: Recipe: 150 g sabudana with potato, peanuts, coconut and 3 tablespoons of ghee, for 3 plates

ingredients.note: half a cup, roasted and crushed

recipe.yieldNote: no cooked weight used; each plate is a third of the recipe

outside.label: Fasting thali or stall
outside.caption: One plate. The outside range is 1 to 1.3 times the size, with up to half as much ghee again.
outside.basis: No analysed value for stall or restaurant sabudana khichdi was found. A plate up to 1.3 times as big with up to 1.5 times the ghee is a stated assumption.
text: Sabudana khichdi from a Navratri stall or a fasting thali is often a bigger plate, cooked in more ghee or oil.
No lab has measured it, so the range below allows a plate up to 1.3 times this one, with up to half as much ghee again.

changes: Ghee is a big part: each tablespoon across the pot adds about 113 calories, about 38 to each plate.
Peanuts add about 125 calories a plate here. Fewer peanuts lowers it noticeably.
More potato and less sabudana lowers it a little; both are starch, but potato holds more water.
Coconut adds about 40 calories a plate.
method: The recipe is the sabudana khichdi in the Indian Nutrient Databank's open recipe set: 1 cup (152 g) of sabudana with 2 medium potatoes, half a cup of peanuts, grated coconut and 3 tablespoons of ghee, for 3 plates. Values are from IFCT 2017, with sabudana from USDA's tapioca pearls since IFCT 2017 has no sago.
Soaking adds water, not calories, so each plate is a third of the recipe.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 plate of sabudana khichdi?
faq.a: About {{kcal:plate}} for a plate made from 50 g of dry sabudana with its share of potato, peanuts and ghee.

faq.q: How many calories are in sabudana khichdi without peanuts?
faq.a: About 125 fewer per plate: the peanuts are about a quarter of it.

faq.q: How much protein is in sabudana khichdi?
faq.a: About {{protein:plate}} g in a plate, almost all from the peanuts. Sabudana itself has almost no protein; curd on the side adds more.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of dry sabudana?
faq.a: {{ing:sabudana}} calories, according to USDA's values for tapioca pearls.

judgement: Open-source recipe OSR099 (INDB). INDB's serving count of 3 is marked as guessed; kept.
Sabudana valued as USDA tapioca pearl, dry (FDC 169717). INDB maps it to its own sago entry.
Ghee 3 tbsp = 38.4 g (USDA tbsp of ghee, 12.8 g). Sugar 0.75 tsp = 3.2 g. Coconut grated 0.25 cup = 20 g dry (INDB).
No independent analysed value for sabudana khichdi was found (IFCT, NIN Annexure 8, USDA FNDDS). NIN's sago vada is a different dish.
Changes list: peanuts 73 / 3 = 24.3 g per plate = 126 kcal; coconut 20 / 3 = 6.7 g = 42 kcal; ghee per tbsp 12.8 x 8.84 = 113 kcal.

foods.name: Kuttu puri
foods.title: Kuttu puri calories: 1, 2 or 4 puris
foods.description: One kuttu puri made with about 13 g of buckwheat flour has about {{kcal:one}} calories once fried; 4 puris have about {{kcal:four}}. For Navratri.
foods.answer: One kuttu puri, about 13 g of kuttu atta with a little potato, deep-fried, has about {{kcal:one}} calories. Four come to about {{kcal:four}}, or about {{kcal:four_sabzi}} with a 200 ml katori of aloo sabzi. Size and the frying oil decide the number. Sweet-shop or thali puris, bigger and oilier, run about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Kuttu puri is made from buckwheat flour, which has no gluten, so the dough is bound with boiled potato and rolled out between sheets before deep-frying. It's eaten on Navratri and other fasting days with aloo sabzi and curd, when wheat and rice are avoided.
Kuttu flour has about the same calories per gram as wheat atta. As with any puri, the oil it takes up in frying is about half its calories.
foods.portionsCaption: Fried at home in fresh oil, as below.

recipe.label: Recipe: 80 g kuttu atta and 40 g boiled potato, deep-fried into 6 puris

ingredients.note: boiled and mashed, to bind the dough: an assumption
Taken up in frying: a stated assumption, so a puri is about 25% fat

recipe.yieldNote: the flour and potato's non-fat solids (76.7 g) at USDA's puri composition, 28% water and 24.9% fat, so 76.7 / 0.4706

portions.label: 4 puris with a 200 ml katori of aloo sabzi

outside.label: Fasting thali or sweet shop
outside.caption: One puri. The outside range is up to 1.3 times the size, with up to about a fifth more oil.
outside.basis: Fat up to 1.22 times: Jain et al. 2024 found total fat in Indian fried foods rose from a mean of 22.5% to 27.4% of dry weight between the 1st and 32nd frying in the same oil. Puris up to 1.3 times as big are a stated assumption.
text: Kuttu puris from a sweet shop or a Navratri thali are often a little bigger, and fried in oil that's been used many times.
A lab study found fried foods took up about a fifth more fat after 32 fryings in the same oil. The range below uses that, with puris up to 1.3 times this size.

changes: As with any puri, size and frying oil decide the number.
Kuttu flour is close to wheat atta per gram: USDA puts it at {{ing:kuttu}} calories per 100 g, against {{ing:atta}} for atta in IFCT 2017.
Singhara (water chestnut) and rajgira (amaranth) puris are similar per gram.
Aloo sabzi and curd with it are counted separately.
method: No standard textbook in the Indian Nutrient Databank has kuttu puri, so this follows the textbook puri on the puri page with kuttu atta in place of wheat, bound with 40 g of boiled potato (an assumption, since buckwheat has no gluten). Kuttu values are from USDA's buckwheat flour; potato and oil from IFCT 2017.
As on the puri page, the oil taken up is set so the puri matches USDA's puri composition, 24.9% fat, which is about 6 g per puri.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 kuttu puri?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for a home kuttu puri made with about 13 g of flour.

faq.q: How many calories are in 4 kuttu puris?
faq.a: About {{kcal:four}} for 4, and about {{kcal:four_sabzi}} with a 200 ml katori of aloo sabzi cooked in ghee.

faq.q: Is a kuttu puri lighter than a wheat puri?
faq.a: No, about the same. A home [puri](/calories/puri/) of a similar size is about {{kcal@puri:one}}; the oil decides most of the difference.

faq.q: How much protein is in a kuttu puri?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g.

judgement: Adapted recipe: the puri page's ASC107 structure (80 g flour for 6 puris) with kuttu atta (USDA FDC 170687) and 40 g boiled potato as a binder (assumption).

Oil taken up: non-fat solids = kuttu 80 x (1 - 0.112 - 0.031) = 68.6 g + potato 40 x (1 - 0.795 - 0.002) = 8.1 g = 76.7 g. Fat = 76.7 x 24.94 / 47.06 = 40.6 g; minus own fat 2.6 g = 38 g of oil for 6 puris.
No analysed value for kuttu puri was found (IFCT, NIN Annexure 8, USDA FNDDS).
Aloo sabzi row: a 200 ml katori of fasting aloo sabzi, 100 g potato, 50 g tomato and 9 g ghee (no onion or garlic).

foods.name: Makhana
foods.title: Makhana calories: per cup, 20 g, 50 g and roasted in ghee
foods.description: A cup of plain makhana (32 g) has about {{kcal:cup}} calories; 30 g roasted in a teaspoon of ghee about {{kcal:ghee30}}. Per 100 g and packaged.
foods.answer: A cup of plain makhana, about 32 g, has about {{kcal:cup}} calories, and a small 15 g katori about {{kcal:katori}}. Roasted in a teaspoon of ghee, 30 g comes to about {{kcal:ghee30}}. Ghee or oil for roasting adds about 45 calories a teaspoon. Packaged or shop-roasted makhana, with more oil, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} per 30 g.
intro: Makhana, or phool makhana, is the popped seed of the fox nut, a water lily grown mostly in Bihar's ponds and wetlands. It's eaten roasted with a little ghee and salt as a snack, in kheer, and in curries, and it's a common fasting-day food.
Makhana is very light by volume: a full cup weighs only about 32 g. Per gram it's a dry starch, about the same as rice, and roasting it in ghee adds to it.
foods.portionsCaption: Dry makhana, plain unless stated.

recipe.label: 100 g of dry makhana
recipe.yieldNote: dry makhana, not cooked; roasting doesn't change the weight much

outside.label: Packaged or shop-roasted
outside.caption: 30 g. The outside range adds 2.5 to 10 g more oil, so 1.5 to 3 times the fat of a teaspoon of ghee.
outside.basis: No analysed value for packaged flavoured makhana was used. Packaged makhana is roasted in oil with seasoning; 1.5 to 3 times the fat of 30 g roasted in a teaspoon of ghee is a stated assumption. Check the packet's label.
text: Packaged and shop-roasted makhana is usually roasted in more oil, with flavourings such as peri peri, cheese or pudina, and the label often lists more fat than home-roasted makhana.
The range below allows 1.5 to 3 times the fat of a teaspoon of ghee on 30 g. Your packet's label will be more exact.

changes: Ghee or oil for roasting adds about 45 calories a teaspoon.
Makhana is light by volume, so a big bowl can still be under 100 calories. Weigh it once to see what your bowl holds.
Makhana kheer adds milk and sugar: count those too.
Per gram, makhana is close to rice and wheat: USDA puts it at {{ing:makhana}} calories per 100 g.
method: Values are USDA's for dried lotus seeds, the closest analysed match, since IFCT 2017 has no makhana: {{ing:makhana}} calories, 15.4 g of protein and 2 g of fat per 100 g. USDA lists a cup at 32 g.
The ghee row adds a teaspoon (5 g) of ghee, from IFCT 2017, to 30 g of makhana. The katori row is an assumption of 15 g for a loosely filled 150 ml katori, half of USDA's cup by weight.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of makhana?
faq.a: {{ing:makhana}} calories in 100 g of dry makhana, according to USDA's values for dried lotus seeds.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 cup of makhana?
faq.a: About {{kcal:cup}} for a cup (about 32 g) of plain makhana.

faq.q: How many calories are in roasted makhana with ghee?
faq.a: About {{kcal:ghee30}} for 30 g roasted in a teaspoon of ghee.

faq.q: How much protein is in makhana?
faq.a: About {{protein:cup}} g in a cup, and about 15 g per 100 g.

faq.q: How many calories are in 50 g of makhana?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g50}} for 50 g of plain makhana, and about {{kcal:g20}} for 20 g.

judgement: Makhana valued as USDA FDC 170149, lotus seeds, dried (332 kcal, 15.4 g protein, 1.97 g fat, 64.5 g carbohydrate per 100 g; no fibre value, so carbohydrate is by difference). Makhana is the seed of Euryale ferox, a different water lily from the lotus; USDA's dried lotus seed is the closest analysed match. IFCT 2017 has no entry.
Katori 15 g is an assumption (half of USDA's 32 g cup, scaled for a 150 ml katori).
No second analysed source for makhana was found in IFCT 2017, NIN Annexure 8 or USDA FNDDS.

foods.name: Gulab jamun
foods.title: Gulab jamun calories: per piece, with syrup, per 100 g
foods.description: One khoa gulab jamun (about 43 g, drained) has about {{kcal:one}} calories, and more with a spoon of syrup. Based on a lab analysis and IFCT 2017.
foods.answer: One home gulab jamun made with khoa, about 43 g drained of syrup, has about {{kcal:one}} calories, and 2 about {{kcal:two}}. A tablespoon of syrup adds about 45, taking one to about {{kcal:one_syrup}}. Size matters most: a large sweet-shop gulab jamun can be half as big again. Sweet-shop or wedding ones run about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} each, before syrup.
intro: Gulab jamun is a soft ball of khoa and a little maida, fried slowly in ghee or oil until dark brown, then soaked in warm sugar syrup flavoured with cardamom and rose water. It's the sweet at most Indian weddings and festivals, and kala jamun and Bengal's lal mohan are close cousins.
About half of a gulab jamun's weight is sugar it has soaked up. That sugar is close to half its calories, and the khoa and the frying fat most of the rest.
foods.portionsCaption: Home gulab jamun, lifted out of the syrup.

recipe.label: Recipe: 100 g khoa and 25 g maida, fried and soaked in syrup, making 6 gulab jamuns

ingredients.note: Taken up in frying: set from a lab analysis, so a gulab jamun is about 12% fat
Taken up from the syrup: set from the same analysis, about 48% sugar

recipe.yieldNote: from protein: the dough's 19.1 g of protein is 7.35% of the finished gulab jamuns in a lab analysis, so 19.1 / 0.0735

outside.label: Sweet shop or wedding
outside.caption: One gulab jamun. The outside range is 1 to 1.5 times the size.
outside.basis: No analysed value for sweet-shop gulab jamun per piece was found. Pieces up to 1.5 times this size are a stated assumption; market brands analysed in the Indian Journal of Dairy Science had 6.5% to 12.3% fat, at or below this page's 12.3%.
text: Sweet-shop and wedding gulab jamuns are often bigger than home ones, and they're usually served with more syrup. Brands analysed in a dairy science study had no more fat than this one, between about 6.5% and 12.3%.
The range below allows a gulab jamun up to 1.5 times this size. Syrup on top is extra.

changes: Size matters most: a large sweet-shop gulab jamun can be half as big again.
Each tablespoon of syrup poured over adds about 45 calories, almost all sugar.
Gulab jamun made from a packet mix with milk powder is close per gram.
Served warm with a scoop of ice cream, add about 100 to 140 calories for the ice cream.
[Rasmalai](/calories/rasmalai/), chhena in sweetened milk, is about {{kcal@rasmalai:one}} a piece with its milk; a [peda](/calories/peda/) about {{kcal@peda:one}}.
method: The recipe is the gulab jamun in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 100 g khoa, 25 g maida and a teaspoon of milk, making 6 gulab jamuns, fried and soaked in a syrup of 200 g sugar in 125 ml water. Values are from IFCT 2017, with sugar from USDA.

The databank counts all the frying fat and all the syrup as eaten, which is far too high. A lab analysis of khoa gulab jamun found 7.35% protein, 12.3% fat and 48.2% total sugar. This page uses the dough's protein to work out the finished weight, then sets the fat and sugar taken up to match: about 2 g of fat and 18 g of sugar per gulab jamun.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 gulab jamun?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for a home gulab jamun of about 43 g, drained, and about {{kcal:one_syrup}} with a tablespoon of syrup.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 gulab jamuns?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two}} for two, drained.

faq.q: How much sugar is in a gulab jamun?
faq.a: About 18 g of added sugar in a 43 g gulab jamun, close to 4 teaspoons, plus the milk sugar in the khoa.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of gulab jamun?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}} for 100 g, drained of syrup.

judgement: Finished weight from protein: khoa 16.34 + maida 2.59 + milk 0.16 = 19.09 g protein; at 7.35% (Rahuri 2020 control) that's 259.7 g for 6.
Fat taken up: 12.32% x 259.7 = 32.0 g total; dough fat 21.0 g; so 11.0 g fried fat (ghee, as the textbook's 'fat').
Sugar taken up: 48.16% x 259.7 = 125.1 g total sugar; minus milk sugar in khoa and milk (about 16.8 g, IFCT carbohydrate) = 108.3 g sucrose.
Syrup on top: 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the textbook syrup (200 g sugar in 125 ml water, about 61.5% sugar, about 1.26 g per ml) = 11.6 g sugar, 45 kcal.
No independent kcal figure for gulab jamun was found (IFCT, NIN Annexure 8, USDA FNDDS). Market brands' fat (6.47% to 12.32%, IJDS) brackets this page's 12.3%.
Ice cream in the changes list: NIN counts half a cup of ice cream at 200 kcal; a scoop is about half to two thirds of that.

foods.name: Rasgulla
foods.title: Rasgulla calories: per piece, with syrup, per 100 g
foods.description: One rasgulla (about 36 g, squeezed) has about {{kcal:one}} calories; with a spoon of syrup about {{kcal:one_syrup}}. From a lab analysis and IFCT 2017.
foods.answer: One rasgulla, about 36 g lightly squeezed of syrup, has about {{kcal:one}} calories, and 2 rasgullas about {{kcal:two}}. With a tablespoon of syrup one is about {{kcal:one_syrup}}, and 100 g squeezed about {{kcal:g100}}. Syrup is the main variable: each tablespoon adds about 45 calories. Tinned and sweet-shop rasgullas, usually sweeter, run about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} each.
intro: Rasgulla is a spongy ball of chhena, fresh cheese made by curdling milk, kneaded smooth and cooked in light sugar syrup until it swells. It comes from Bengal and Odisha, where it's rosogolla and rasagola, and it's sold in tins and clay pots across India.
It isn't fried, so it has much less fat than gulab jamun. Most of its calories are the sugar it soaks up, and a rasgulla eaten straight from the syrup carries more.
foods.portionsCaption: Lightly squeezed of syrup, as below.

recipe.label: Recipe: chhena from 265 ml cow's milk, cooked in syrup, making 4 rasgullas

ingredients.note: Chhena from 265 ml cow's milk, valued as IFCT paneer
Taken up from the syrup: set from a lab analysis, about 35% sugar

recipe.yieldNote: from protein: the chhena's 6.9 g of protein is 4.8% of the finished rasgullas in a lab analysis, so 6.9 / 0.048

outside.label: Tinned or sweet shop
outside.caption: One rasgulla. The outside range is 1 to 1.4 times this one.
outside.basis: Aavin's rasgulla label (273 kcal per 100 g) is about 1.4 times this page's value per gram, mainly from more sugar; tinned and shop rasgullas also vary in size. 1 to 1.4 times is used.
text: Tinned and sweet-shop rasgullas are often sweeter than home ones. The label on Aavin's rasgulla, from Tamil Nadu's milk co-operative, lists 273 calories for 100 g, more than this page's {{kcal:g100}}, mostly from sugar.
The range below runs from this rasgulla up to 1.4 times it, in line with that label.

changes: Syrup is the main variable. Squeezing a rasgulla before eating takes off much of the sugar; a tablespoon of syrup adds about 45 calories.
Rasgullas made from full-fat milk or buffalo milk have more fat than those from toned milk.
[Rasmalai](/calories/rasmalai/) soaks the same chhena in thickened sweet milk instead of syrup, and comes to about {{kcal@rasmalai:one}} a piece with its milk, close to twice a rasgulla.
Low-sugar rasgullas made with sweeteners have far fewer calories.
method: The recipe is the rasgulla in Basic Food Preparation, a standard Indian cookery manual (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): chhena from 265 ml of cow's milk, kneaded with half a tablespoon of maida and cooked in a syrup of 150 g sugar. IFCT 2017 has no chhena, so it's valued as paneer, the closest match. The chhena's weight is worked out from the milk's protein, taking about 80% of milk protein as the casein that stays in the chhena (an assumption).
A lab analysis of rasgulla found 4.8% protein and 35% total sugar. This page uses the chhena's protein to work out the finished weight, then sets the sugar taken up to match, about 11 g per rasgulla.

range.text: Aavin's label lists 273 calories per 100 g of its rasgulla, against about {{kcal:g100}} here, because it holds more sugar. Depending on the syrup, 100 g of rasgulla is usually 200 to 275 calories.
range.reason: Aavin's label (273 kcal, basis taken as 100 g) is 38% above this page's rasgulla, which is set to a lab analysis at 35% sugar. Shown as a range.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 rasgulla?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for a home rasgulla of about 36 g, squeezed, and about {{kcal:one_syrup}} with a tablespoon of syrup.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 rasgullas?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two}} for two, squeezed of syrup.

faq.q: Which has more calories, rasgulla or gulab jamun?
faq.a: A [gulab jamun](/calories/gulab-jamun/), about {{kcal@gulab-jamun:one}} against about {{kcal:one}} for a rasgulla. The gulab jamun is fried and soaks up more sugar.

faq.q: How much protein is in a rasgulla?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g, from the chhena.

crossCheck.source: Aavin rasgulla label, per 100 g (basis taken from the values)

judgement: Chhena: milk protein 265 x 3.26% = 8.64 g; casein about 80% of milk protein (assumption) = 6.91 g, as paneer (IFCT L003, 18.86% protein) = 36.6 g.
Finished weight: 6.91 / 0.048 (VNMKV control rasgulla, 4.80% protein) = 144 g. Sugar: 34.96% x 144 = 50.3 g total; minus paneer's carbohydrate (4.5 g) = 45.8 g sucrose taken up.
Fat check: 5.4 g / 144 g = 3.8%, against 4.5% in the analysis.
4 rasgullas of 36 g is an assumption; BFP392's serving count (2) is marked as guessed in INDB.
Syrup on top: 1 tbsp of a 61.5% syrup = 11.6 g sugar, as on the gulab jamun page.

foods.name: Jalebi
foods.title: Jalebi calories: per piece, per 100 g, an estimate
foods.description: One 30 g jalebi has about {{kcal:one}} calories and 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}, estimated from frying and syrup data. No lab analysis of jalebi exists.
foods.answer: A 30 g jalebi has roughly {{kcal:one}} calories, 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}, and 250 g by weight about {{kcal:g250}}. This is an estimate: we found no lab analysis of jalebi. Syrup is the biggest unknown: a jalebi left to soak longer takes up more sugar. From a halwai, 2 jalebis run about {{outLo}} alone to {{outHi}} with rabri.
intro: Jalebi is a fermented maida batter piped in spirals into hot ghee or oil, fried crisp, then dipped in warm sugar syrup with saffron and cardamom. It's eaten hot for breakfast with poha in Indore, with rabri in north India, and at every festival in between.
Two things decide its number: the oil the spirals take up in frying and the syrup they soak up afterwards. Both vary from one halwai to the next, so treat the figures here as a guide.
foods.portionsCaption: Estimated values; see how they were worked out below.

recipe.label: Recipe: 100 g maida batter with curd, fried and soaked in syrup

ingredients.note: Taken up in frying: assumed at USDA's puri composition, 24.9% fat
From syrup equal to the fried weight, at the textbook syrup's 61.5% sugar: an assumption

recipe.yieldNote: fried weight (191.5 g, from the batter's solids at USDA's puri composition) plus an equal weight of syrup

outside.label: Halwai, with rabri
outside.caption: Two jalebis. The outside range adds up to 50 g of rabri.
outside.basis: Rabri is thickened sweetened milk. 50 g of rabri is modelled as 25 g khoa and 5 g sugar (a stated assumption) on top of 2 jalebis.
text: From a halwai, jalebis are often eaten hot with rabri or with poha, and sold by weight, so a plate can be anywhere from two pieces to a quarter kilo.
The range below runs from two jalebis on their own to two with about 50 g of rabri.

changes: Syrup is the biggest unknown. A jalebi that's left to soak longer takes up more sugar.
Oil taken up in frying is the next. Thin, crisp spirals take up more for their size than thick ones.
Rabri on top adds about 100 calories per 50 g; poha on the side is counted separately.
Imarti, made from urad dal batter, is similar per gram.
method: No standard textbook in the Indian Nutrient Databank has jalebi, and we found no lab analysis of it, so this is an estimate built in two steps, each stated. The batter is 100 g maida with 25 g curd and water. Values are from IFCT 2017, with curd and sugar from USDA.

First, the fried spirals are taken to have the composition of USDA's measured puri (24.9% fat, 28% water), another fried wheat dough. Second, they're taken to soak up their own weight of syrup made as in The Art & Science of Cooking's gulab jamun (200 g sugar in 125 ml water, about 61.5% sugar). The 30 g piece is a typical size, also an assumption.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 jalebi?
faq.a: Roughly {{kcal:one}} for a 30 g jalebi, an estimate. Thin, small jalebis have less; thick, syrupy ones more.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of jalebi?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}}, and about {{kcal:g250}} for a quarter kilo.

faq.q: How much sugar is in a jalebi?
faq.a: About 9 g of added sugar in a 30 g jalebi by this estimate, a little over 2 teaspoons.

faq.q: How many calories are in jalebi with rabri?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two}} for 2 jalebis on their own, and up to about {{outHi}} with 50 g of rabri.

judgement: No analysed value for jalebi was found (IFCT 2017, NIN Annexure 8, USDA FNDDS, Europe PMC, web search). Consumer calorie databases list figures that don't reconcile and aren't used.

Step 1, frying: batter non-fat solids = maida 100 x (1 - 0.1134 - 0.0076) = 87.9 g + curd 25 x (1 - 0.879 - 0.0325) = 2.2 g = 90.1 g. At FNDDS puri composition (24.94% fat, 27.99% water), fat = 90.1 x 24.94 / 47.07 = 47.7 g; minus own fat 1.6 g = 46.2 g oil; fried weight 90.1 / 0.4707 = 191.5 g.
Step 2, syrup: 191.5 g of syrup at 200 / 325 = 61.5% sugar = 117.8 g sugar and 73.7 g water. Equal weight of syrup is an assumption.
Rabri modelled as 25 g khoa + 5 g sugar per 50 g; an assumption.
Piece weight 30 g is an assumption.

intro: Kaju katli is ground cashews cooked with sugar syrup into a smooth dough, rolled thin, cut into diamonds and often topped with silver leaf. It's the most gifted sweet at Diwali and keeps for days without refrigeration.
Cashews and sugar are roughly equal by weight, but cashews carry more of the calories because of their fat. Per gram, kaju katli is one of the richest common sweets.

faq.q: How much protein is in kaju katli?

intro: Besan ladoo is gram flour roasted slowly in ghee until it smells nutty, then mixed with powdered sugar and cardamom and shaped into balls. It's a Diwali and festival sweet in most of north and west India, and it keeps for weeks.
A ladoo is about a fifth ghee by weight, so it's rich for its size.

Values are from IFCT 2017, with sugar from USDA.
Besan is valued as ground Bengal gram dal, since IFCT 2017 has no separate besan entry.

foods.title: Gajar halwa calories: per bowl and per katori

Ghee is a big part: each tablespoon across the pot adds about 113 calories. Wedding or sweet-shop halwa, richer, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} a bowl.
intro: Gajar halwa is grated red winter carrots cooked slowly in milk until it's absorbed, then with ghee, sugar and khoa, finished with cardamom and nuts. It's the north Indian winter sweet, made at home when Delhi carrots are in season and served warm at weddings.
Carrots themselves are light. The ghee, sugar and khoa make up about four fifths of a bowl's calories.
foods.portionsCaption: Home gajar halwa made as below.

recipe.label: Recipe: 200 g carrots with 40 g khoa, 40 g sugar and 20 g ghee, for 2 bowls
recipe.yieldNote: no measured cooked weight; carrots lose a lot of water as they cook

text: Wedding and sweet-shop gajar halwa is usually richer, with more ghee and khoa, and sometimes condensed milk.
No lab has measured it, so the range below allows up to 1.5 times the ghee and up to 20 g more khoa per bowl.

changes: Ghee is a big part: each tablespoon across the pot adds about 113 calories.
Khoa adds about 125 calories per 40 g; halwa made with only milk, cooked down, has less fat.
Sugar adds about 16 calories a teaspoon. Gajar halwa needs less than you'd think, since carrots are sweet.
Nuts on top add about 60 calories per 10 g.
A katori of [kheer](/calories/kheer/) is lighter, about {{kcal@kheer:k200}} for 200 ml, because it is mostly milk.
method: The recipe is the carrot halwa in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 200 g carrots cooked with 30 ml milk, 40 g khoa, 40 g sugar and 20 g ghee, finished with almonds, cashews and cardamom, for 2 bowls. Values are from IFCT 2017, with sugar from USDA.
Carrots lose much of their water as they cook, so this page counts halwa by its share of the recipe rather than by weight.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 bowl of gajar halwa?
faq.a: About {{kcal:bowl}} for a bowl made from 100 g of carrots, and about {{kcal:small}} for a small katori.

faq.q: How many calories are in gajar halwa with ice cream?
faq.a: Add about 100 to 140 calories for a scoop of vanilla ice cream to the bowl's {{kcal:bowl}}.

faq.q: How much sugar is in gajar halwa?
faq.a: About 20 g of added sugar in a bowl, 5 teaspoons, plus the natural sugar in the carrots and khoa.

faq.q: How much protein is in gajar halwa?
faq.a: About {{protein:bowl}} g in a bowl, mostly from the khoa.

foods.name: Filter coffee
foods.title: Filter coffee calories: with sugar, without, toned milk
foods.description: A tumbler of filter coffee with whole milk and 2 teaspoons of sugar has about {{kcal:two_tsp}} calories; without sugar, about {{kcal:no_sugar}}.
foods.answer: A tumbler of filter coffee, 50 ml of decoction with 100 ml of whole milk and 2 teaspoons of sugar, has about {{kcal:two_tsp}} calories. Without sugar it's about {{kcal:no_sugar}}, and with toned milk and 2 teaspoons about {{kcal:toned}}. Sugar matters most, about 16 calories a level teaspoon. Darshini coffee, sweeter and sometimes bigger, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Filter coffee is a strong decoction, dripped slowly through a brass or steel filter from ground coffee and chicory, mixed with hot milk and sugar, and frothed by pouring between a tumbler and davara. It's the morning drink across Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Kerala.
The decoction itself has almost no calories. The milk and the sugar are the whole number.
foods.portionsCaption: One tumbler: 50 ml decoction with 100 ml milk.

recipe.label: One tumbler: 50 ml coffee decoction with 100 ml whole milk
recipe.yieldNote: the decoction and milk together

outside.label: Darshini or Udupi hotel
outside.caption: One tumbler. The outside range adds up to a teaspoon more sugar, in a tumbler up to 1.2 times as big.
outside.basis: No analysed value for hotel filter coffee was found. Up to a teaspoon more sugar and a serving up to 1.2 times as big are stated assumptions.
text: Filter coffee in a darshini or Udupi hotel is usually sweeter than home coffee, and sometimes a little bigger, made with full-cream milk.
No lab has measured it, so the range below allows up to a teaspoon more sugar and a serving up to 1.2 times as big.

changes: Sugar is the main variable: each level teaspoon adds about 16 calories.
Toned milk instead of whole milk saves about 15 calories a tumbler; buffalo milk adds about 35.
More decoction and less milk lowers it; the decoction itself is close to zero.
Chicory in the coffee powder adds nothing measurable to the cup.
method: One tumbler is taken as 50 ml of decoction and 100 ml of whole milk. ICMR-NIN counts a cup of coffee with 2 teaspoons of sugar and 100 ml (taken here as the milk) at 110 calories. Milk values are from IFCT 2017; coffee and sugar from USDA. A level teaspoon of sugar is 4.2 g (USDA).
The toned-milk row uses Amul Taaza's label, 3% fat, as on the masala chai page.

faq.q: How many calories are in filter coffee?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two_tsp}} for a tumbler with whole milk and 2 teaspoons of sugar, and about {{kcal:no_sugar}} without sugar.

faq.q: How many calories are in filter coffee with toned milk?
faq.a: About {{kcal:toned}} with toned milk and 2 teaspoons of sugar.

faq.q: Which has more calories, filter coffee or chai?
faq.a: Filter coffee, usually, because it has more milk. A cup of [masala chai](/calories/masala-chai/) with 2 teaspoons of sugar is about {{kcal@masala-chai:cup2}}.

faq.q: How many calories are in black filter coffee?
faq.a: About 1 calorie in 50 ml of decoction. Sugar adds about 16 per teaspoon.

foods.name: Chaas
foods.title: Chaas calories: per glass, masala chaas and buttermilk
foods.description: A 200 ml glass of chaas made from curd and water has about {{kcal:k200}} calories. Thicker chaas, masala chaas and packed buttermilk compared.
foods.answer: A 200 ml glass of home chaas, curd whisked with about three times as much water, has about {{kcal:k200}} calories. A large 250 ml glass is about {{kcal:k250}}. The curd is the whole number: a 200 ml glass made thick, with about 100 g of curd, is about {{kcal:thick}}. Restaurant or packed chaas, often thicker, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Chaas is curd whisked with water and salt, often with roasted cumin, ginger, green chilli, mint or coriander as masala chaas. It's drunk with lunch across Gujarat, Rajasthan and Punjab, and in the south as majjige or neer mor.
Most of a glass is water, so chaas is one of the lightest drinks there is. The amount of curd in it sets the number.
foods.portionsCaption: 100 g curd in about 320 ml of water and ice, as below.

recipe.label: Recipe: 100 g curd whisked with about 320 ml water and ice, with cumin

ingredients.note: half a cup of water and 4 to 5 ice cubes

recipe.yieldNote: the ingredients added together
recipe.densityNote: taken as 1 g per ml, like water

portions.label: 200 ml chaas made thick (about 100 g curd)

outside.label: Restaurant or packed
outside.caption: One 200 ml glass. The outside range has 1 to 2 times the curd.
outside.basis: No analysed value for restaurant or packed chaas in India was found. Up to twice the curd per glass is a stated assumption; packed buttermilk labels vary.
text: Restaurant and packed chaas is sometimes thicker than home chaas, with more curd per glass. A thali restaurant's chaas is often refilled freely.
We found no lab figure for it, so the range below allows up to twice the curd in a 200 ml glass.

changes: The curd is the whole number. More water lowers it; a thick chaas can be twice as much.
Curd from toned or skimmed milk lowers it further.
Cumin, ginger, mint, coriander and salt add almost nothing.
Sweet lassi adds sugar: see [lassi](/calories/lassi/).
method: The recipe is the salted lassi in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 100 g curd whisked with half a cup of water and 4 to 5 ice cubes, with roasted cumin. Curd values are from USDA's whole-milk yogurt, since IFCT 2017 has no curd.
The thick chaas row adds curd so a 200 ml glass is half curd and half water.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 glass of chaas?
faq.a: About {{kcal:k200}} in a 200 ml glass, and about {{kcal:thick}} for thick chaas made with equal curd and water.

faq.q: How much protein is in chaas?
faq.a: About {{protein:k200}} g in a 200 ml glass.

faq.q: Is chaas the same as buttermilk?
faq.a: In India, yes: chaas is diluted curd. Western cultured buttermilk is thicker and has more per glass.

faq.q: Which has fewer calories, chaas or lassi?
faq.a: Chaas, by a lot. A glass of sweet [lassi](/calories/lassi/) has more curd and sugar, about {{kcal@lassi:glass}}.

foods.title: Sweet lassi calories: per glass, with malai
foods.description: A glass of sweet lassi with 100 g curd and 4 teaspoons of sugar has about {{kcal:glass}} calories; 200 ml about {{kcal:k200}}, as ICMR-NIN says.
foods.answer: A glass of home sweet lassi (240 ml, 100 g of curd, 4 teaspoons of sugar) has about {{kcal:glass}} calories. With a tablespoon of malai it's about {{kcal:malai}}. Sugar is the biggest part, about 16 a teaspoon: the same glass with 2 teaspoons is about {{kcal:less_sugar}}. A dhaba glass, bigger and topped with malai, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Sweet lassi is curd churned with sugar and a little water or ice until frothy, sometimes with cardamom or rose water. In Punjab and at dhabas it's thick, served in tall steel glasses with a layer of malai on top.
Sugar is a little over half its calories in this recipe, and the curd the rest. Malai on top adds a lot.

recipe.label: Recipe: 100 g curd with 20 g sugar and 120 ml water

text: A Punjabi dhaba or lassi shop serves lassi in big steel glasses, thick with curd and topped with a layer of malai, sometimes with dry fruit.
No lab has measured one, so the range below allows a glass 1.5 to 2.5 times this one, with up to 2 tablespoons of malai.

changes: Sugar is the biggest part: each teaspoon adds about 16 calories.
Malai or cream on top adds about 30 calories a tablespoon.
Thick lassi with more curd per glass has more of everything.
Mango lassi adds mango pulp; salted lassi has no sugar, see [chaas](/calories/chaas/).
method: The recipe is the sweet lassi in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 100 g curd with 20 g sugar and half a cup of water, with ice. The ice adds water, not calories, so it's left out of the volume. Curd values are from USDA's whole-milk yogurt, since IFCT 2017 has no curd; sugar from USDA.
ICMR-NIN counts a 200 ml glass of lassi with 2 teaspoons of sugar at 110 calories, close to this page's 200 ml.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 glass of sweet lassi?
faq.a: About {{kcal:glass}} for a home glass with 100 g of curd and 20 g of sugar, and about {{kcal:malai}} with a tablespoon of malai.

faq.q: How many calories are in a dhaba lassi?
faq.a: Roughly {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} for a big glass of thick lassi with malai.

faq.q: How much sugar is in sweet lassi?
faq.a: About 20 g of added sugar in this glass, close to 5 teaspoons.

faq.q: How much protein is in lassi?
faq.a: About {{protein:glass}} g in a glass, from the curd.

foods.name: Nimbu pani
foods.title: Nimbu pani calories: with sugar, without, and shikanji
foods.description: A glass of nimbu pani has about {{kcal:plain}} calories without sugar, {{kcal:two_tsp}} with 2 teaspoons of sugar and about {{kcal:textbook}} made sweet.
foods.answer: A glass of nimbu pani has about {{kcal:plain}} calories without sugar and about {{kcal:two_tsp}} with 2 teaspoons. With a teaspoon of honey it's about {{kcal:honey}}, and with the textbook's 1½ tablespoons of sugar about {{kcal:textbook}}. Sugar is the whole number: each level teaspoon adds about 16. Street shikanji or nimbu soda, made with syrup, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Nimbu pani is fresh lime or lemon juice in cold water with sugar, salt and often roasted cumin and black salt, as shikanji in north India. It's the summer drink at home, at roadside stalls and at railway stations.
Lemon juice and water have almost no calories, so each spoon of sugar decides the number.
foods.portionsCaption: One glass: half a lemon's juice in about 180 ml water.

recipe.label: Recipe for 2 glasses: the juice of 1 lemon in 360 ml water, with mint
recipe.yieldNote: no cooked weight; a glass is half the recipe, sugar added per glass

outside.label: Street shikanji or nimbu soda
outside.caption: One glass. The outside range adds 2 to 4 teaspoons of sugar.
outside.basis: No analysed value for street shikanji was found. 2 to 4 level teaspoons of sugar per glass is a stated assumption; ICMR-NIN's fresh lime juice, 60 kcal a glass, sits inside it.
text: Street shikanji and nimbu soda are usually sweet, often made with sugar syrup. Nimbu soda uses soda water, which has no calories.
No lab has measured one, so the range below allows 2 to 4 teaspoons of sugar a glass. ICMR-NIN's figure for a glass of fresh lime juice, 60 calories, falls inside it.

changes: Sugar is the whole number: each level teaspoon adds about 16 calories.
Honey adds about 21 calories a teaspoon, a little more than sugar.
Black salt, roasted cumin and mint add nothing measurable.
Ready-made lemonade and sweetened drinks can have much more sugar per glass.
method: The recipe is the lemonade in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): the juice of 1 lemon in 1.5 cups of water with mint and crushed ice, sweetened with 3 tablespoons of sugar, for 2 glasses. This page counts the sugar per glass so you can see each amount. Lemon juice values are from IFCT 2017, sugar and honey from USDA.
One lemon is taken as 48 g of juice (USDA). A level teaspoon of sugar is 4.2 g and a level tablespoon 12.5 g (USDA).

range.text: ICMR-NIN counts a glass of fresh lime juice at 60 calories, which is about 3 to 4 teaspoons of sugar. The textbook glass here, with 1½ tablespoons, is about {{kcal:textbook}}. Depending on the sugar, a glass is anywhere from about {{kcal:plain}} to {{kcal:textbook}}.
range.reason: NIN's fresh lime juice (60 kcal) is 22% below the textbook's sweet glass and well above an unsweetened one. Sugar differs. Shown as a range.

faq.q: How many calories are in nimbu pani without sugar?
faq.a: About {{kcal:plain}} for a glass with the juice of half a lemon.

faq.q: How many calories are in nimbu pani with sugar?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one_tsp}} with 1 teaspoon of sugar, {{kcal:two_tsp}} with 2, and about {{kcal:textbook}} with 1½ tablespoons.

faq.q: How many calories are in nimbu pani with honey?
faq.a: About {{kcal:honey}} with a teaspoon of honey.

faq.q: How many calories are in shikanji?
faq.a: About the same as sweet nimbu pani: {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} for a street glass with 2 to 4 teaspoons of sugar.

foods.name: Aloo gobi
foods.title: Aloo gobi calories: per katori, home and restaurant
foods.description: A 200 ml katori of home aloo gobi has about {{kcal:k200}} calories, a 150 ml katori about {{kcal:k150}}. Cauliflower and potato in a tablespoon of oil, from IFCT 2017.
foods.answer: A 200 ml katori of home aloo gobi, cooked with a tablespoon of oil for 100 g of cauliflower and 50 g of potato, has about {{kcal:k200}} calories. A 150 ml katori has about {{kcal:k150}}. The oil is most of it; cauliflower and potato are a small share. A restaurant aloo gobi runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} a katori.
intro: Aloo gobi is cauliflower and potato cooked dry with turmeric, chilli and ginger, a sabzi found in most north Indian homes and in every tiffin. Some kitchens add peas or tomato; Punjabi versions use more oil and a little garam masala at the end.
Cauliflower has very few calories, so what you taste as richness is the oil. The same katori with half the oil has close to half the calories.
foods.portionsCaption: Made as below, with all the oil counted as eaten. A textbook bowl is the whole recipe.

recipe.label: Recipe: one bowl, 100 g cauliflower and 50 g potato with 1 tablespoon of oil
recipe.yieldNote: the ingredients added together, as the Indian Nutrient Databank does
recipe.densityNote: USDA's cooked mixed vegetables: 185 g per cup (236.6 ml), as for the site's mixed veg; pieces of potato and vegetable pack about the same

foods.mealsCaption: A 200 ml katori of aloo gobi; rotis are medium, 30 g atta each.

meals.label: Aloo gobi with 2 rotis

outside.label: Restaurant or dhaba

outside.basis: No analysed value for restaurant aloo gobi was found. Restaurant sabzis are cooked in more oil or butter; 1.5 to 2.5 times this recipe's oil is a stated assumption, the same as for the site's mixed veg.
text: Restaurant and dhaba aloo gobi is usually cooked in more oil, sometimes finished with butter, and the pieces are often shallow-fried first so they hold their shape.
No lab has measured a restaurant aloo gobi, so the range below allows 1.5 to 2.5 times this recipe's oil per katori.

changes: Oil is the biggest variable. This recipe uses a tablespoon for a bowl of {{kcal:bowl}} calories; each teaspoon less or more moves it by about 40.
More potato adds more than more cauliflower: potato has {{ing:potato}} calories per 100 g, cauliflower {{ing:cauliflower}}.
Frying the cauliflower florets first, as many restaurants do, takes up extra oil that this recipe doesn't have.
Peas, tomato and onion add a little; a handful of peas is about {{ing:peas_fresh}} calories per 100 g.
A katori is a volume. A heaped 200 ml katori holds more than a level one; Slate uses your own katori size.
method: The recipe is the potato cauliflower (aloo gobhi) in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 100 g of cauliflower and 50 g of potato with half a green chilli, ginger, coriander, turmeric and chilli powder, cooked in a tablespoon of oil. Values are from IFCT 2017.

The cooked weight is the ingredients added together, as the databank does for dry sabzis. A katori is filled at 0.78 g per ml, USDA's density for cooked mixed vegetables. Garam masala and salt are left out: a quarter teaspoon of garam masala is about a calorie.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 katori of aloo gobi?
faq.a: About {{kcal:k200}} in a 200 ml katori of home aloo gobi, and about {{kcal:k150}} in a 150 ml one.

faq.q: How many calories are in aloo gobi sabzi with 2 rotis?
faq.a: About {{kcal:with_roti}} calories: a 200 ml katori of aloo gobi at {{kcal:k200}} with 2 medium [rotis](/calories/roti/) at {{kcal@roti:two}}.

faq.q: How much protein is in aloo gobi?
faq.a: About {{protein:k200}} g in a 200 ml katori. Cauliflower and potato have little protein; dal or curd on the side adds more.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of aloo gobi?
faq.a: About {{per100}} calories per 100 g of this home aloo gobi, most of it from the oil.

faq.q: Is aloo gobi low in calories?
faq.a: The vegetables are; the oil isn't. Cauliflower has {{ing:cauliflower}} calories per 100 g and potato {{ing:potato}}, while oil has {{ing:oil}}. A katori made with less oil has fewer calories, and Slate adjusts for your kitchen's oil.

foods.name: Boiled egg
foods.title: Boiled egg calories: 1 egg, 2 eggs and 3 eggs
foods.description: One boiled egg of about 50 g has about {{kcal:one}} calories and {{protein:one}} g of protein; 2 eggs about {{kcal:two}}, 3 eggs about {{kcal:three}}. From IFCT 2017's whole egg.
foods.answer: One boiled egg, about 50 g without the shell, has about {{kcal:one}} calories, with {{protein:one}} g of protein and {{fat:one}} g of fat. Two boiled eggs are about {{kcal:two}} and three about {{kcal:three}}. Boiling adds nothing: the number is the egg itself, so a bigger egg has more. ICMR-NIN counts a boiled egg at 90, which fits an egg of about 65 g.
intro: A boiled egg is the simplest thing to count on this site: there is no oil, no masala and no cooked weight to guess. The only question is the size of the egg, and that is where the sources differ.
Indian eggs sold loose are often 45 to 55 g. The 50 g egg used here is the Indian Nutrient Databank's household measure and the same as USDA's large egg.
foods.portionsCaption: Whole eggs of about 50 g each, boiled in the shell. Salt and pepper add nothing.

recipe.label: Recipe: one hen's egg, about 50 g without the shell, boiled

ingredients.note: 1 egg, as the Indian Nutrient Databank counts it

recipe.yieldNote: boiling in the shell doesn't change the weight of the egg

changes: Egg size. A 50 g egg has about {{kcal:one}} calories; an egg of 60 to 65 g has about a quarter more, which is where ICMR-NIN's 90 comes from.
The yolk holds nearly all the fat, so an egg eaten without its yolk has far fewer calories and about half the protein.
Boiling time changes nothing: soft-boiled and hard-boiled eggs have the same calories.
What goes with it does. A boiled egg in [egg curry](/calories/egg-curry/) picks up the masala's oil, about {{kcal@egg-curry:one}} per egg with gravy.
Duck eggs and desi eggs are a little larger and richer than farm hen's eggs; the values here are for the ordinary white hen's egg.
method: The recipe is the boiled egg in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): one hen's egg, which the databank counts as 50 g without the shell. Values are IFCT 2017's whole raw egg; boiling in the shell doesn't change the weight or the nutrients.
USDA's hard-boiled egg (155 calories per 100 g) and ICMR-NIN's boiled egg (90 calories) are shown as cross-checks, and the page states a range because they sit more than 15% above this value.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 boiled egg?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} calories for an egg of about 50 g without the shell, with {{protein:one}} g of protein.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 boiled eggs?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two}} calories, with {{protein:two}} g of protein and {{fat:two}} g of fat.

faq.q: How many calories are in 3 boiled eggs?
faq.a: About {{kcal:three}} calories, with {{protein:three}} g of protein.

faq.q: How much protein is in a boiled egg?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g in a 50 g egg, and about {{protein:two}} g in 2 eggs. The white and the yolk each hold roughly half of it.

faq.q: Which has more calories, a boiled egg or an omelette?
faq.a: The [omelette](/calories/omelette/), because of the oil and the second egg: about {{kcal@omelette:one}} for a 2-egg omelette against {{kcal:two}} for 2 boiled eggs. A single-egg omelette is about {{kcal@omelette:single}}.

Egg size explains most of it: a 50 g egg is a medium Indian egg, and a 60 to 65 g egg has a quarter more. A boiled egg is about {{kcal:one}} to 90 calories depending on its size.

foods.name: Omelette
foods.title: Omelette calories: 1 egg, 2 eggs, home and stall
foods.description: A plain 2-egg omelette cooked in oil has about {{kcal:one}} calories and {{protein:one}} g of protein; a single-egg omelette about {{kcal:single}}. IFCT 2017 egg, USDA for the oil taken up.
foods.answer: A plain 2-egg omelette, with a tablespoon of milk and cooked in oil, has about {{kcal:one}} calories, with {{protein:one}} g of protein and {{fat:one}} g of fat. A single-egg omelette is about {{kcal:single}}. The eggs are about two thirds of it and the oil the rest. A stall or dhaba masala omelette runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: An omelette is beaten egg cooked flat on a tawa or in a pan, plain or with onion, green chilli, tomato and coriander as a masala omelette. In India it comes with bread or pav, at home, at the railway stall and at the egg cart.
Most of the oil poured into the pan stays there. The number here counts only what the omelette takes up, set from a lab analysis, not the whole spoonful.
foods.portionsCaption: Made as below. A 3-egg omelette is one and a half times the recipe.

recipe.label: Recipe: a plain 2-egg omelette with a tablespoon of milk, cooked in oil

ingredients.note: Taken up in cooking: set from USDA's analysed omelette made with oil (15.8% fat), about 1⅔ teaspoons

recipe.yieldNote: USDA's omelette made with oil weighs 55 g per egg

outside.label: Stall or dhaba masala omelette
outside.caption: One 2-egg omelette. The outside range has 1.5 to 2.5 times the oil, plus up to 50 g of onion and tomato.
outside.basis: No analysed value for a stall omelette was found. ICMR-NIN's fried egg at 160 kcal implies roughly 10 g of oil per egg, about 2.5 times the oil taken up here, so 1.5 to 2.5 times the oil is a stated assumption. Onion and tomato up to 25 g each cover a masala omelette.
text: A stall omelette is cooked in a generous pour of oil or butter on a flat tawa, usually as a masala omelette with onion, green chilli and tomato, and often served with bread or pav.
No lab has measured an Indian stall omelette, so the range below allows 1.5 to 2.5 times the oil of this recipe, plus the onion and tomato. Bread is extra.

changes: The oil taken up. This omelette takes up about 2 teaspoons for 2 eggs; a stall omelette can take up 2 to 3 times that.
The number of eggs: about {{kcal:single}} for one egg, {{kcal:one}} for two and {{kcal:three}} for three.
Butter instead of oil changes little per teaspoon; cheese inside changes a lot.
Onion, tomato and chilli in a masala omelette add about 10 calories. Bread adds more: white bread has about {{ing:bread_white}} calories per 100 g.
An egg-white omelette drops most of the fat and about half the protein.
method: The recipe is the plain omelette in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 2 eggs beaten with a tablespoon of milk and pepper. The textbook fries it in 2 tablespoons of fat, most of which stays in the pan, so the oil eaten is set from USDA's analysed omelette made with oil, which is 15.8% fat: about 7.6 g for 2 eggs. Egg, milk and pepper values are from IFCT 2017.
The cooked weight is USDA's 55 g per egg, so a 2-egg omelette is about 110 g.

faq.q: How many calories are in a 2 egg omelette?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} calories for a plain 2-egg omelette cooked in oil, with {{protein:one}} g of protein.

faq.q: How many calories are in a 1 egg omelette?
faq.a: About {{kcal:single}} calories, half of the 2-egg omelette. ICMR-NIN's fried egg is 160, because it carries more oil.

faq.q: How many calories are in a 3 egg omelette?
faq.a: About {{kcal:three}} calories, with {{protein:three}} g of protein.

faq.q: How much protein is in an omelette?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g in a 2-egg omelette and {{protein:single}} g in a single-egg one. The milk adds a little.

faq.q: How many calories are in a masala omelette from a stall?
faq.a: About {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} for a 2-egg masala omelette, with more oil and some onion and tomato. Bread or pav is extra.

crossCheck.source: USDA FoodData Central 2707200, egg omelet made with oil
crossCheck.note: The analysis the oil is set from; USDA's eggs carry slightly more fat than IFCT's.

range.text: ICMR-NIN counts a fried egg at 160 calories, against about {{kcal:single}} for a single-egg omelette here. The gap is oil: a fried egg sits in more of it than an omelette takes up. USDA's analysed omelette made with oil agrees with this page within 2% per 100 g. Depending on the oil, a one-egg omelette is about {{kcal:single}} to 160 calories.
range.reason: ICMR-NIN's fried egg (160 kcal) has more oil than a single-egg omelette made this way; USDA's analysed omelette (192 kcal per 100 g) agrees within 2%.

judgement: The textbook fries the omelette in 2 tablespoons of fat, most of which stays in the pan; the oil eaten is set from USDA's analysed omelette instead.
An omelette is counted as 2 eggs, as in the textbook. A single-egg omelette is half.

foods.name: Egg bhurji
foods.title: Egg bhurji calories: per katori, 1 egg and 2 eggs
foods.description: Egg bhurji made with a teaspoon of butter has about {{kcal:egg}} calories per egg, {{kcal:two}} for 2 eggs and {{kcal:k200}} in a 200 ml katori. IFCT 2017 egg, USDA butter.
foods.answer: Home egg bhurji, one egg scrambled with a tablespoon of milk and a teaspoon of butter, has about {{kcal:egg}} calories per egg, with {{protein:egg}} g of protein. Two eggs come to about {{kcal:two}}, and a 200 ml katori, a little over 2 eggs, about {{kcal:k200}}. Stall anda bhurji, with more butter and onion and tomato, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} a katori.
intro: Egg bhurji is scrambled egg the Indian way: eggs broken into a pan of onion, green chilli and tomato softened in butter or oil, stirred until they set in small pieces. It's a breakfast and tiffin dish at home and a late-night one at the anda bhurji cart, eaten with pav or roti.
The textbook version counted here is plain scrambled egg with butter. Onion and tomato add little; the butter or oil in the pan is what moves the number.
foods.portionsCaption: Made as below, with the butter counted in. A 200 ml katori holds a little over 2 eggs.

recipe.label: Recipe: one egg scrambled with a tablespoon of milk and a teaspoon of butter
recipe.yieldNote: USDA's scrambled egg weighs 55 g per egg
recipe.densityNote: USDA's scrambled egg: 135 g per cup (236.6 ml)

portions.label: 1 katori of bhurji with 2 pav (43 g each)

foods.mealsCaption: A 200 ml katori of bhurji; rotis are medium, 30 g atta each; pav are 43 g each, plain.

meals.label: Egg bhurji with 2 rotis

outside.label: Anda bhurji stall or dhaba
outside.caption: One 200 ml katori. The outside range has 1.5 to 2.5 times the butter, plus up to 50 g of onion and tomato.
outside.basis: No analysed value for stall bhurji was found. Stalls cook in a generous pour of butter or oil and add onion and tomato; 1.5 to 2.5 times this recipe's butter and up to 25 g each of onion and tomato per katori are stated assumptions.
text: Anda bhurji from a cart or dhaba is cooked in a lot more butter or oil than this, usually with a good amount of onion, tomato and masala, and served with 2 pav that are often buttered too.
No lab has measured a stall bhurji, so the range below allows 1.5 to 2.5 times this recipe's butter per katori, plus the onion and tomato. The pav are extra: see the table above.

changes: The butter or oil. This recipe uses a teaspoon of butter per egg; a second teaspoon adds about 35 calories.
The number of eggs: about {{kcal:egg}} for one egg, {{kcal:two}} for two.
Pav or roti on the side. A katori of bhurji with 2 plain pav is about {{kcal:pav}}; with 2 medium rotis, about {{kcal:with_roti}}.
Onion, tomato and green chilli add about 10 calories for 50 g. Cheese on top adds far more.
Milk makes the bhurji softer and adds about {{ing:milk_cow}} calories per 100 ml, so a tablespoon is about 10.
method: The recipe is the scrambled egg (ande ki bhurji) in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): one egg with a tablespoon of milk, a teaspoon of butter and pepper. Egg, milk and pepper values are from IFCT 2017; butter from USDA, since IFCT 2017 has no butter.

The cooked weight is USDA's 55 g per scrambled egg, and a katori is filled at 0.57 g per ml, USDA's 135 g per cup of scrambled egg, so a 200 ml katori holds about {{g:k200}} g. Pav values are IFCT 2017's bread, 43 g each as on the site's vada pav page.

faq.q: How many calories are in egg bhurji?
faq.a: About {{kcal:egg}} per egg made with a teaspoon of butter, {{kcal:two}} for 2 eggs, and {{kcal:k200}} in a 200 ml katori.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 egg bhurji?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two}} calories, with {{protein:two}} g of protein and {{fat:two}} g of fat.

faq.q: How many calories are in anda bhurji with pav?
faq.a: About {{kcal:pav}} for a 200 ml katori of bhurji with 2 plain pav of 43 g each. Buttered pav and a stall's extra butter push it higher: see the outside range.

faq.q: How much protein is in egg bhurji?
faq.a: About {{protein:egg}} g per egg and {{protein:k200}} g in a 200 ml katori. With 2 rotis it's about {{protein:with_roti}} g.

faq.q: Which has more calories, egg bhurji or an omelette?
faq.a: Per egg they are close: about {{kcal:egg}} for bhurji with a teaspoon of butter, against about {{kcal@omelette:single}} for a single-egg [omelette](/calories/omelette/) cooked in oil.

crossCheck.note: USDA's eggs carry slightly more fat than IFCT's.

judgement: The textbook's bhurji (ande ki bhurji) is plain scrambled egg. Onion, tomato and green chilli, often added at home, add little: about 10 kcal for 50 g of onion and tomato.
A 200 ml katori holds about 114 g of bhurji, a little over 2 eggs.

foods.name: Chole bhature
foods.title: Chole bhature calories: per plate, home and stall
foods.description: A plate of chole bhature, 2 home bhaturas with a 200 ml katori of chole, has about {{kcal:plate}} calories; 1 bhatura with half a katori about {{kcal:half}}. IFCT 2017, USDA.
foods.answer: A plate of chole bhature, 2 home-made bhaturas with a 200 ml katori of chole, has about {{kcal:plate}} calories, with {{protein:plate}} g of protein and {{fat:plate}} g of fat. One bhatura with half a katori of chole is about {{kcal:half}}. The frying oil in the bhaturas is the largest single share. At a stall, with oilier chole, a plate runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Chole bhature is Delhi and Punjab's heavyweight breakfast: spiced kabuli chana in a thick onion and tomato gravy, with puffed, deep-fried maida bhaturas, onion rings, a green chilli and pickle on the side. It's almost always eaten out, but it's made at home on Sundays too.
This page adds up the site's own [chole](/calories/chole/) and [bhatura](/calories/bhatura/) pages into one plate, so the plate's number is exactly the sum of its parts.
foods.portionsCaption: Two bhaturas of about 27 g maida each, and one 200 ml katori of home chole. Onion, pickle and chilli add little.

recipe.label: Recipe: one plate, 2 bhaturas and a 200 ml katori of chole, each made as on the site's own page

ingredients.note: chole: taken up by the chana in soaking and cooking
bhatura: to make a soft dough: an assumption, no calories
bhatura: taken up in frying: a stated assumption, so a bhatura is about 20% fat

recipe.yieldNote: no cooked weight is known for the bhaturas, so the plate is counted as one portion

portions.label: 1 bhatura with half a katori of chole

outside.label: Chole bhature stall or restaurant
outside.caption: One plate. The outside range adds the chole page's extra oil, 1 to 2 teaspoons; the bhaturas stay as they are.
outside.basis: No analysed value for a plate of chole bhature was found. The chole page's outside range uses 1.5 to 2 times its 2 teaspoons of oil, added here as 4.5 to 9 g of oil. The bhaturas are left as they are, because the two street bhaturas measured in the lab (see the bhatura page) held the same or less fat than the home bhatura counted here.
text: Stall and restaurant chole is cooked with more oil, often with a film of it on top, while bhaturas vary from small village ones to large restaurant rounds.

No lab has measured a whole plate, so the range below adds the chole page's extra oil, 1 to 2 teaspoons, and keeps the bhaturas as they are: the street bhaturas that were measured held no more fat than this home one. A large restaurant bhatura can be bigger than either.

changes: The bhaturas. Each home bhatura is about {{kcal@bhatura:one}} calories, most of it frying oil, so a third bhatura adds about the same again.
The chole's oil. A 200 ml katori of home chole is about {{kcal@chole:k200}}; the stall version with 1.5 to 2 times the oil is about {{outLo@chole}} to {{outHi@chole}}.
The size of the bhatura. Street bhaturas measured in a lab ranged from 33 g to 52 g; a restaurant bhatura can be larger still.
The size of the katori: a 150 ml katori of chole is about {{kcal@chole:k150}}, a 250 ml one about {{kcal@chole:k250}}.
Onion, green chilli and a piece of pickle add under 20 calories. A lassi with it adds about {{kcal@lassi:glass}}.
method: The plate is 2 bhaturas and one 200 ml katori of chole, each made exactly as on its own page: the chole from the kabuli channa curry in Basic Food Preparation (40 g of dry chana per katori, with tomato, onion, ginger, a teaspoon of curd and 2 teaspoons of oil) and the bhatura from a maida and curd dough with the frying oil taken up stated as an assumption. Values are from IFCT 2017, with USDA for the curd.
No cooked weight is given for the plate, so the portions are shares of it. The arithmetic for each part is on the [chole](/calories/chole/) and [bhatura](/calories/bhatura/) pages.

faq.q: How many calories are in a plate of chole bhature?
faq.a: About {{kcal:plate}} for 2 home bhaturas with a 200 ml katori of chole, and about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} at a stall.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 bhature with chole?
faq.a: About {{kcal:plate}}: 2 bhaturas at {{kcal@bhatura:two}} plus a katori of chole at {{kcal@chole:k200}}.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 bhatura with chole?
faq.a: About {{kcal:half}} for one bhatura with half a katori of chole, or about {{sum:bhatura:one+chole:k200}} with a full 200 ml katori.

faq.q: How much protein is in chole bhature?
faq.a: About {{protein:plate}} g in a plate, most of it from the chana.

faq.q: Which has more calories, chole bhature or pav bhaji?
faq.a: Chole bhature, as a plate: about {{kcal:plate}} against about {{kcal@pav-bhaji:plate2}} for [pav bhaji](/calories/pav-bhaji/) with 2 butter pav.

useCase.label: Calories in restaurant and delivery food

judgement: A plate of 2 bhaturas and one 200 ml katori of chole is a stated assumption: no source was found for a standard plate. Onion, pickle and a green chilli on the side add little.
No independent analysed value for a plate of chole bhature was found in IFCT 2017, USDA FNDDS or NIN's Annexure 8, so there is no cross-check here. The parts are cross-checked on their own pages.

foods.name: Curd
foods.title: Curd (dahi) calories: per katori and per 100 g
foods.description: A 200 ml katori of whole-milk curd has about {{kcal:k200}} calories, 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}. With a teaspoon of sugar, about {{kcal:k200_sugar}}. From USDA's plain whole-milk yogurt.
foods.answer: A 200 ml katori of plain curd set from whole milk has about {{kcal:k200}} calories, with {{protein:k200}} g of protein and {{fat:k200}} g of fat. A 150 ml katori is about {{kcal:k150}} and 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}. With a teaspoon of sugar stirred in, a 200 ml katori is about {{kcal:k200_sugar}}. Curd from toned milk has about two thirds of the fat.
intro: Curd, dahi in most of north India, is milk set overnight with a spoon of the last batch. It's on the thali as it is, sweetened as meethi dahi, whisked into [chaas](/calories/chaas/) and [lassi](/calories/lassi/), and stirred into [raita](/calories/raita/) and [curd rice](/calories/curd-rice/).
Curd has the calories of the milk it was set from, so the milk matters: full-cream, whole or toned. The numbers here are for whole milk.
foods.portionsCaption: Plain curd from whole milk, at 1.04 g per ml. Sugar is a level teaspoon, 4.2 g.

recipe.label: Plain curd (dahi) made from whole milk
recipe.yieldNote: curd as it is
recipe.densityNote: USDA's plain whole-milk yogurt: 245 g per cup (236.6 ml)

portions.label: 1 katori (200 ml), 1 tsp sugar
portions.short: a 200 ml katori with 1 tsp sugar

changes: The milk. Whole-milk curd is about {{kcal:g100}} calories per 100 g; curd from toned milk has about two thirds of the fat, and full-cream buffalo-milk curd more.
Sugar: a level teaspoon adds about {{ing:sugar}} calories per 100 g of sugar, so about 15 to 20 per teaspoon, and most kitchen spoons are heaped.
Hung curd and Greek-style curd are thicker, so a katori of them holds more milk solids and more calories.
Packet curd marked as low fat or made from toned milk sits below these values; check the label.
A katori is a volume: a 250 ml katori of curd is about {{kcal:k250}}, a 150 ml one about {{kcal:k150}}.
method: IFCT 2017 has no entry for curd, so the values are USDA's plain whole-milk yogurt: 61 calories, 3.5 g of protein and 3.3 g of fat per 100 g, the same values the site's curd rice, raita, chaas and lassi pages use. A katori is filled at 1.04 g per ml, USDA's 245 g per cup.
Sugar values are IFCT 2017's; a level teaspoon is 4.2 g, as on the site's chai page.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 katori of curd?
faq.a: About {{kcal:k200}} in a 200 ml katori of whole-milk curd, about {{kcal:k150}} in a 150 ml one and about {{kcal:k250}} in a 250 ml one.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of curd?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}} calories, with {{protein:g100}} g of protein and {{fat:g100}} g of fat, for curd set from whole milk.

faq.q: How many calories are in curd with sugar?
faq.a: About {{kcal:k200_sugar}} for a 200 ml katori with a level teaspoon of sugar. Each extra teaspoon adds about the same again.

faq.q: How much protein is in curd?
faq.a: About {{protein:k200}} g in a 200 ml katori and {{protein:g100}} g per 100 g. Hung curd has more per katori because the water has been drained off.

faq.q: Which has fewer calories, curd or milk?
faq.a: They are about the same per 100 g, because curd is set from milk without adding anything: whole milk is about {{ing:milk_cow}} calories per 100 ml and curd about {{kcal:g100}} per 100 g. Toned milk and its curd are lower.

judgement: IFCT 2017 has no curd, so the values are USDA's plain whole-milk yogurt, as on the site's curd rice and raita pages. Curd from toned milk has about two thirds of the fat.

No cross-check is listed: the only analysed value for plain curd is USDA's yogurt, which is the value used, and IFCT 2017 and NIN's Annexure 8 have no plain curd entry that states a weight. Shop curd labels in India commonly list 60 to 100 kcal per 100 g depending on the milk, which brackets this value.
No outside range is shown: curd served with a meal outside is the same curd, set from whatever milk the kitchen uses.

foods.answer: A 200 ml katori of cucumber raita, whole-milk curd with grated cucumber, green chilli and roasted cumin, has about {{kcal:k200}} calories, with {{protein:k200}} g of protein and {{fat:k200}} g of fat. A 150 ml katori is about {{kcal:k150}}, and the textbook bowl of 100 g curd and 50 g cucumber about {{kcal:bowl}}. Boondi raita has more, because the boondi is fried.
intro: Raita is curd whisked with a vegetable or fruit and spiced with roasted cumin and chilli: cucumber, onion, tomato, boondi, pineapple, lauki. It goes with biryani, pulao, parathas and any thali, and cools a spicy plate.
Cucumber raita is mostly curd by weight and almost entirely curd by calories, so the katori has slightly fewer calories than the same katori of plain curd.
foods.portionsCaption: Two parts curd to one part cucumber, as below. A textbook bowl is the whole recipe.

recipe.label: Recipe: one bowl, 100 g curd and 50 g cucumber with roasted cumin

ingredients.note: an eighth of a teaspoon, roasted and ground

recipe.yieldNote: the ingredients added together, as the Indian Nutrient Databank does
recipe.densityNote: curd with grated cucumber taken as 1 g per ml; a stated assumption

changes: The curd. Two thirds of the raita by weight and nearly all its calories; whole-milk curd is about {{kcal@curd:g100}} per 100 g, toned-milk curd less.
Boondi. Fried besan drops take the same katori well above this; the besan and the frying oil are what add up.
The share of cucumber: more cucumber, fewer calories per katori, since cucumber has only {{ing:cucumber}} calories per 100 g.
Sugar, which some kitchens add to raita: a level teaspoon is about 15 to 20 calories.
A katori is a volume: a 150 ml katori is about {{kcal:k150}} and a 200 ml one {{kcal:k200}}.
method: The recipe is the cucumber raita in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 100 g of curd and 50 g of cucumber with half a green chilli, roasted cumin and chilli powder. Cucumber, chilli and spice values are from IFCT 2017; curd values are USDA's plain whole-milk yogurt, since IFCT 2017 has no curd.
The weight is the ingredients added together, as the databank does, and a katori is filled at 1 g per ml, a stated assumption for curd with grated cucumber.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 katori of raita?

intro: Maggi is the instant noodle India grew up on: a dried noodle cake and a masala tastemaker, cooked in a cup and a half of water for two minutes. At home it gets an egg or vegetables; at the hostel and the hill-station Maggi point it gets butter, cheese and a lot of onion.
The noodle cake is fried before it's dried, which is why a 70 g pack has more fat than the same weight of plain noodles. Water adds nothing, so the cooked bowl has the calories of the dry pack.

text: A Maggi point cooks the same pack, but starts with butter and onion in the pan, often adds tomato and chilli, and may finish with a slice of cheese or a second tastemaker.
No lab has measured a stall Maggi, so the range below adds 1 to 2 teaspoons of butter and 25 to 50 g of onion and tomato to the pack. Cheese is extra.
