The variety. Atta noodles, oats noodles and the cup versions have their own labels; the values here are for the masala pack.
Vegetables add little: a pack with 75 g of onion, carrot and capsicum is about {{kcal:veg}}, against {{kcal:pack}} plain.
Leaving some of the tastemaker out changes the salt far more than the calories.
method: The values are Nestlé India's own for Maggi 2-Minute Masala Noodles, as published on maggi.in per 100 g of the product as sold, noodle cake and tastemaker together: 384 calories, 8.2 g of protein, 59.6 g of carbohydrate and 12.5 g of fat. A single pack sold in India is 70 g, so one pack is 0.7 of those values. No cooked weight is used, because the water adds weight and no calories.
Egg, onion, carrot and capsicum values are IFCT 2017's; butter is USDA's, since IFCT 2017 has no butter.

foods.answer: One home gobi paratha (27 g atta, 33 g cauliflower, 2 teaspoons of oil) has about {{kcal:one}} calories, or about {{kcal:one_butter}} with a teaspoon of butter. Two gobi parathas with curd come to about {{kcal:two_curd}}. The cauliflower adds little; the tawa oil is nearly half the total. A dhaba gobi paratha, with butter on top, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Gobi paratha is atta dough stuffed with grated cauliflower, green chilli, ginger and onion, rolled out and cooked on the tawa with oil or ghee. It's a winter breakfast across Punjab, Haryana and Delhi, eaten with curd, pickle and butter, and it packs well in a tiffin.

The filling is mostly water: in this recipe the cauliflower is about a twentieth of the calories. The atta and the oil on the tawa make up nearly all the rest, so a gobi paratha counts a little under an [aloo paratha](/calories/aloo-paratha/).

outside.label: Dhaba or restaurant, with butter
outside.caption: One gobi paratha. The outside range is up to 1.4 times the size and half as much oil again, plus 1 to 2 teaspoons of butter.
outside.basis: No analysed value for a restaurant gobi paratha was found. Size up to 1.4 times, as for the plain and aloo parathas (USDA's paratha is 70 g against about 49 g of dough here); up to 1.5 times the oil and 1 to 2 teaspoons of butter on top are stated assumptions, the same as on the aloo paratha page.
text: At a dhaba, a gobi paratha is often larger, cooked in more ghee or oil and served with a cube of butter melting on top.
No lab figure exists for a dhaba gobi paratha, so the range below assumes one up to 1.4 times this size, with up to half as much oil again and 1 to 2 teaspoons of butter, as on the aloo paratha page.

changes: The oil on the tawa is the biggest variable. Each teaspoon adds about 40 calories to a paratha.
A teaspoon of butter on top takes one paratha from about {{kcal:one}} to {{kcal:one_butter}} calories, and a tablespoon to {{kcal:one_butter_tbsp}}.
The filling hardly matters: 50 g more cauliflower is about 10 calories. Squeezing the grated gobi dry removes water, which has no calories.
A katori of curd on the side (100 g) takes a paratha to about {{kcal:one_curd}}, and pickle in oil adds more.
Made with the same atta and oil, an [aloo paratha](/calories/aloo-paratha/) is about {{kcal@aloo-paratha:one}} and a [paneer paratha](/calories/paneer-paratha/) about {{kcal@paneer-paratha:one}}.
method: The recipe is the cauliflower paratha in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 80 g of atta, 100 g of cauliflower, 25 g of onion, 5 g of ginger, green chilli and coriander, with 2 tablespoons of oil for 3 parathas. Garam masala, chilli powder, amchur and salt, under 1 g each, are left out; together they add under 3 calories a paratha. Values are from IFCT 2017.
All the oil is counted as eaten. Curd values are from USDA, because IFCT 2017 has no curd.

faq.q: Which has more calories, gobi paratha or aloo paratha?
faq.a: The aloo paratha, by a little: about {{kcal@aloo-paratha:one}} calories against about {{kcal:one}} for a gobi paratha made with the same atta and oil. Cauliflower has fewer calories per gram than potato.

faq.q: How much protein is in a gobi paratha?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g. With a 100 g katori of curd it's about {{protein:one_curd}} g.

faq.a: About {{kcal:two_curd}} calories: 2 parathas at {{kcal:two}} plus a 100 g katori of curd.

intro: Methi paratha is atta kneaded with chopped fresh fenugreek leaves, onion, ginger and green chilli, then rolled and cooked on the tawa with a little oil. It's a winter bread across north and west India, eaten with curd and pickle, and a tiffin regular because it keeps well.

It isn't a [thepla](/calories/thepla/): a Gujarati thepla is thinner, made from mixed flours with curd, and smaller. Because the methi goes into the dough rather than a stuffing, and this textbook recipe uses only a teaspoon of oil a paratha, a methi paratha counts well under an [aloo paratha](/calories/aloo-paratha/).

foods.name: Mooli paratha
foods.title: Mooli paratha calories: homemade, with butter or curd
foods.description: A homemade mooli paratha has about {{kcal:one}} calories, or {{kcal:one_butter}} with a teaspoon of butter. Worked out from a textbook recipe and IFCT 2017.
foods.answer: One home mooli paratha (27 g atta, 33 g radish, 2 teaspoons of oil) has about {{kcal:one}} calories, or about {{kcal:one_butter}} with a teaspoon of butter. Two mooli parathas with curd come to about {{kcal:two_curd}}. The radish adds little; the tawa oil is nearly half the total. A dhaba mooli paratha, with butter on top, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Mooli paratha is atta dough stuffed with grated white radish, squeezed dry and mixed with green chilli, coriander and onion, then rolled and cooked on the tawa with oil or ghee. It's a Punjabi winter breakfast, eaten with curd, pickle and butter.

Radish is almost all water, so in this recipe the filling is about a twentieth of the calories. The atta and the oil on the tawa make up nearly all the rest, and a mooli paratha counts a little under an [aloo paratha](/calories/aloo-paratha/).
foods.portionsCaption: Made as below, with the oil counted in. Butter and curd are extra.

recipe.label: Recipe: 80 g atta, 100 g radish and 2 tablespoons of oil, making 3 parathas

ingredients.note: 4 tablespoons, to make a soft dough

recipe.yieldNote: no reliable cooked weight for a stuffed paratha

foods.mealsCaption: Curd is a 100 g katori.

outside.label: Dhaba or restaurant, with butter
outside.caption: One mooli paratha. The outside range is up to 1.4 times the size and half as much oil again, plus 1 to 2 teaspoons of butter.
outside.basis: No analysed value for a restaurant mooli paratha was found. Size up to 1.4 times, as for the plain and aloo parathas (USDA's paratha is 70 g against about 49 g of dough here); up to 1.5 times the oil and 1 to 2 teaspoons of butter on top are stated assumptions, the same as on the aloo paratha page.
text: At a dhaba, a mooli paratha is often larger, cooked in more ghee or oil and served with a cube of butter melting on top.

No lab figure exists for a dhaba mooli paratha, so the range below assumes one up to 1.4 times this size, with up to half as much oil again and 1 to 2 teaspoons of butter, as on the aloo paratha page.

changes: The oil on the tawa is the biggest variable. Each teaspoon adds about 40 calories to a paratha.
A teaspoon of butter on top takes one paratha from about {{kcal:one}} to {{kcal:one_butter}} calories, and a tablespoon to {{kcal:one_butter_tbsp}}.
The filling hardly matters: 50 g more radish is about 15 calories. Salting and squeezing the mooli removes water, which has no calories.
A katori of curd on the side (100 g) takes a paratha to about {{kcal:one_curd}}, and pickle in oil adds more.

Made with the same atta and oil, a [gobi paratha](/calories/gobi-paratha/) is about {{kcal@gobi-paratha:one}}, an [aloo paratha](/calories/aloo-paratha/) about {{kcal@aloo-paratha:one}} and a [paneer paratha](/calories/paneer-paratha/) about {{kcal@paneer-paratha:one}}.
method: The recipe is the radish paratha in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 80 g of atta, 100 g of radish, 25 g of onion, green chilli and coriander, with 2 tablespoons of oil for 3 parathas. Garam masala, chilli powder, amchur and salt, under 1 g each, are left out; together they add under 3 calories a paratha. Values are from IFCT 2017.
All the oil is counted as eaten. Curd values are from USDA, because IFCT 2017 has no curd.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 mooli paratha?
faq.a: A homemade mooli paratha made with about 27 g of atta and 2 teaspoons of oil has about {{kcal:one}} calories. Two have about {{kcal:two}}.

faq.q: Which has fewer calories, mooli paratha or aloo paratha?
faq.a: The mooli paratha, by a little: about {{kcal:one}} calories against about {{kcal@aloo-paratha:one}} for an [aloo paratha](/calories/aloo-paratha/) made with the same atta and oil. Radish is mostly water.

faq.q: How many calories are in mooli paratha with butter?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one_butter}} with a teaspoon of butter, and about {{kcal:one_butter_tbsp}} with a tablespoon. At a dhaba it can be more, because the paratha is often bigger too.

faq.q: How much protein is in a mooli paratha?
faq.a: About {{protein:one}} g, almost all from the atta. With a 100 g katori of curd it's about {{protein:one_curd}} g.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 mooli parathas with curd?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two_curd}} calories: 2 parathas at {{kcal:two}} plus a 100 g katori of curd.

judgement: No independent analysed value for mooli paratha was found: IFCT 2017 has no parathas, USDA FNDDS 2021-2023 has only a plain paratha (51300185), and NIN's Annexure 8 lists a plain paratha only. INDB's own figure (184 kcal per paratha) is from this same textbook recipe, so it agrees by design.
Coriander 'a few' sprigs taken as 2 g, green chilli 'one small' as 3.3 g, as the databank does. Spices under 1 g left out.
All 2 tbsp of oil (27.2 g) counted as eaten.
Curd from USDA FDC 171284 (whole-milk yogurt), since IFCT 2017 has no curd.

foods.name: Rajma chawal
foods.title: Rajma chawal calories: per plate, katori and with ghee
foods.description: A plate of rajma chawal, a 200 ml katori of rajma with a katori of rice, has about {{kcal:plate}} calories; with 2 katoris of rice about {{kcal:plate_big}}. IFCT 2017.
foods.answer: A plate of rajma chawal, a 200 ml katori of home rajma with a katori of plain rice, has about {{kcal:plate}} calories and {{protein:plate}} g of protein. With 2 katoris of rice it is about {{kcal:plate_big}}; a teaspoon of ghee takes it to about {{kcal:plate_ghee}}. At a dhaba, with a ghee tadka and cream, about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Rajma chawal is the Sunday lunch of Punjab, Delhi and Jammu: red kidney beans simmered in an onion and tomato masala, ladled over plain rice, with sliced onion and a wedge of lemon on the side. In Delhi it's also a street lunch, served by the plate from a steel counter.

This page adds up the site's own [rajma](/calories/rajma/) and [plain rice](/calories/plain-rice/) pages into one plate, in the proportions people actually eat, so the plate's number is exactly the sum of its parts. The rice is the easy part; how much rajma, and how much oil went into it, is what moves the total.
foods.portionsCaption: Rajma and rice are level 200 ml katoris unless the row says otherwise. Onion, lemon and salad add almost nothing.

recipe.label: One plate: a 200 ml katori of rajma and a 200 ml katori of plain rice, each made as on its own page
recipe.yieldNote: a plate of other dishes, each made as on its own page; no weight of its own

rajma chawal with a full plate of rice

outside.label: Dhaba or restaurant
outside.caption: One plate. The outside range adds the rajma page's ghee tadka and cream and the rice page's spoon of ghee.
outside.basis: The sum of the two pages' outside ranges: dhaba rajma with a 5 g ghee tadka and up to 15 g of cream (from published recipe proportions, on the rajma page) and restaurant rice with 0 to 5 g of ghee (a stated assumption, on the rice page). No analysed value for a plate of rajma chawal was found.
text: Dhaba rajma usually gets a second tadka of ghee, restaurant rajma is sometimes finished with cream, and the rice may come with a spoon of ghee on top. The plate is often bigger than a home one too.
No lab has measured a plate of rajma chawal, so the range below is the two dish pages' outside ranges added together, for the same katori of each.

changes: How much rice. A second katori of rice takes the plate from about {{kcal:plate}} to {{kcal:plate_big}} calories; a full plate cooked from 100 g of raw rice with the same rajma is about {{kcal:plate_rice}}.
Ghee on top. A teaspoon takes the plate to about {{kcal:plate_ghee}}.
The rajma's oil. The masala here takes about a teaspoon and a half of oil per katori; each extra teaspoon adds about 40 to 45 calories (see [rajma](/calories/rajma/)).
The katori. A small plate of 150 ml katoris is about {{kcal:small}}; a 250 ml katori of rajma alone is about {{kcal@rajma:k250}}.
A thick, reduced rajma holds more beans in each katori than a thin one. Sliced onion, lemon and a little salad add almost nothing.
method: The plate is a 200 ml katori of rajma and a 200 ml katori of plain rice, each made exactly as on its own page: the rajma from the kidney bean curry in The Art & Science of Cooking (30 g of dry rajma with tomato, onion and a teaspoon and a half of oil per bowl) and the rice from 100 g of raw milled rice cooked until the water is absorbed. Values are from IFCT 2017.

Nothing is re-estimated here. Each row adds the two pages' unrounded values and rounds once, so the plate always equals its parts. The recipes, the arithmetic and the cross-checks are on the [rajma](/calories/rajma/) and [plain rice](/calories/plain-rice/) pages.

faq.q: How many calories are in rajma chawal?
faq.a: About {{kcal:plate}} calories for a 200 ml katori of home rajma with a 200 ml katori of plain rice. With a teaspoon of ghee on top, about {{kcal:plate_ghee}}.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 plate rajma chawal?
faq.a: A home plate, a katori of rajma with a katori of rice, is about {{kcal:plate}} calories. A large plate with 2 katoris of rice is about {{kcal:plate_big}}, and a dhaba plate about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.

faq.q: How much protein is in rajma chawal?
faq.a: About {{protein:plate}} g in a plate, most of it from the beans. A large plate with 2 katoris of rice has about {{protein:plate_big}} g.

faq.q: How many calories are in rajma chawal with ghee?
faq.a: About {{kcal:plate_ghee}} calories with a teaspoon (5 g) of ghee on the plate.

faq.q: Which has more calories, rajma chawal or dal chawal?
faq.a: Rajma chawal: about {{kcal:plate}} calories against about {{kcal@dal-chawal:plate}} for [dal chawal](/calories/dal-chawal/) with a thin dal tadka. The rice is the same; a katori of rajma has about twice the calories of a katori of thin dal.

judgement: A plate of one 200 ml katori of rajma and one of rice is a stated assumption, matched to the meal rows on the rajma and rice pages; the large plate and the full plate of rice cover the other common ratios.

No independent analysed value for a plate of rajma chawal was found, so there is no cross-check here. The parts are cross-checked on their own pages (INDB ASC165 for the rajma; NIN, USDA, INDB and Bognár for the rice).
Sliced onion, lemon and salad on the side are left out: under 20 calories.

foods.name: Dal chawal
foods.title: Dal chawal calories: per plate, thick dal and with ghee
foods.description: A plate of dal chawal, a 200 ml katori of dal tadka with a katori of rice, has about {{kcal:plate}} calories; with thick dal about {{kcal:plate_thick}}. IFCT 2017.
foods.answer: A plate of dal chawal, a 200 ml katori of thin dal tadka with a katori of plain rice, has about {{kcal:plate}} calories. Thickness matters most: the same plate with a thick dal is about {{kcal:plate_thick}}, and with dal fry about {{kcal:plate_dal_fry}}. A teaspoon of ghee adds about 45. A dhaba plate, with thicker dal, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Dal chawal is the everyday meal of most of north, central and east India: toor dal with a tadka, poured over plain rice, often with a spoon of ghee, a pickle and some salad. It's dal bhaat in Gujarat and Bihar, dal bhat in Nepal, and the same idea with a different dal almost everywhere else.

This page adds up the site's own [dal tadka](/calories/dal-tadka/) and [plain rice](/calories/plain-rice/) pages into one plate, so the plate's number is exactly the sum of its parts. The rice is steady; the dal can vary two to one depending on how thick it is and how much ghee went into the tadka.
foods.portionsCaption: Dal and rice are level 200 ml katoris unless the row says otherwise. The dal tadka is the textbook's thin dal; the thick dal row is twice as thick.

recipe.label: One plate: a 200 ml katori of dal tadka and a 200 ml katori of plain rice, each made as on its own page
recipe.yieldNote: a plate of other dishes, each made as on its own page; no weight of its own

1 small plate (150 ml katoris of each)

outside.label: Restaurant or dhaba
outside.caption: One plate. The outside range uses the dal page's thicker restaurant dal and the rice page's spoon of ghee.
outside.basis: The sum of the two pages' outside ranges: restaurant dal tadka 1.5 to 2 times as thick as the textbook dal with the same ghee per gram of dal (a stated assumption, on the dal tadka page) and restaurant rice with 0 to 5 g of ghee (a stated assumption, on the rice page). No analysed value for a plate of dal chawal was found.
text: Restaurant and dhaba dal is thicker than everyday home dal and often finished with a second spoon of ghee or butter, and the rice may come with ghee on top. Dal fry, cooked into its masala in ghee, is richer again.
No lab has measured a plate of dal chawal, so the range below is the two dish pages' outside ranges added together, for the same katori of each.

changes: How thick the dal is. Most of a thin dal is water: the same plate with a thick dal is about {{kcal:plate_thick}} calories against {{kcal:plate}}, and with [dal fry](/calories/dal-fry/) about {{kcal:plate_dal_fry}}.
Ghee. A teaspoon on top takes the plate to about {{kcal:plate_ghee}}, and each teaspoon in the tadka adds about 45 to the pot (see [dal tadka](/calories/dal-tadka/)).
How much rice. A second katori takes the plate from about {{kcal:plate}} to {{kcal:plate_big}}.
The katori. A small plate of 150 ml katoris is about {{kcal:small}}.
Pickle in oil, papad and a fried side add more than the salad does. A roasted papad is small; a fried one takes up oil.
method: The plate is a 200 ml katori of dal tadka and a 200 ml katori of plain rice, each made exactly as on its own page: the dal from the arhar dal in Basic Food Preparation (30 g of toor dal in 300 ml of water with a 10 g ghee tadka, a thin dal) and the rice from 100 g of raw milled rice cooked until the water is absorbed. Values are from IFCT 2017.

The thick dal row uses the same dal cooked down to twice the thickness, the thick dal the Slate app counts, which matches ICMR-NIN's figure of 100 calories per half cup of plain dal; it has no page of its own. The dal fry row uses the [dal fry](/calories/dal-fry/) page.

Nothing is re-estimated here. Each row adds the pages' unrounded values and rounds once, so the plate always equals its parts. The recipes, the arithmetic and the cross-checks are on the [dal tadka](/calories/dal-tadka/) and [plain rice](/calories/plain-rice/) pages.

faq.q: How many calories are in dal chawal?
faq.a: About {{kcal:plate}} calories for a 200 ml katori of thin dal tadka with a 200 ml katori of plain rice, and about {{kcal:plate_thick}} with a thick dal. With a teaspoon of ghee on top, add about 45.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 plate dal chawal?
faq.a: A home plate, a katori of dal with a katori of rice, is about {{kcal:plate}} calories with thin dal. A large plate with 2 katoris of rice is about {{kcal:plate_big}}, and a dhaba plate about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.

faq.q: How much protein is in dal chawal?
faq.a: About {{protein:plate}} g in a plate with thin dal, and about {{protein:plate_thick}} g with a thick dal. Together, dal and rice give a more complete protein than either alone.

faq.q: How many calories are in dal chawal with ghee?
faq.a: About {{kcal:plate_ghee}} calories with a teaspoon (5 g) of ghee on the plate.

faq.q: Which has fewer calories, dal chawal or dal roti?
faq.a: They're close. A katori of dal tadka with a katori of rice is about {{kcal:plate}} calories; the same dal with 2 medium [rotis](/calories/roti/) is about {{kcal@dal-tadka:with_roti}}.

judgement: A plate of one 200 ml katori of dal and one of rice is a stated assumption, matched to the meal rows on the dal tadka and rice pages; the large plate covers the usual two-katoris-of-rice ratio.

The thick dal is the app-only dish dal-thick (data/app-foods.json): the dal tadka recipe cooked down to twice the thickness, cross-checked against NIN's 100 kcal per half cup. It is used here because thin and thick dal differ two to one, and a page that showed only the thin one would mislead.
No independent analysed value for a plate of dal chawal was found, so there is no cross-check here. The parts are cross-checked on their own pages.
Pickle, papad and salad are left out.

foods.name: Idli sambar
foods.title: Idli sambar calories: 2, 3 and 4 idlis with sambar
foods.description: 2 medium idlis with a 200 ml katori of sambar have about {{kcal:two}} calories, 4 idlis about {{kcal:four}}. Chutney not counted. From IFCT 2017 textbook recipes.
foods.answer: Two medium idlis with a 200 ml katori of sambar have about {{kcal:two}} calories and {{protein:two}} g of protein. Three idlis with the same sambar are about {{kcal:three}}, four about {{kcal:four}}. The idlis are plain; the sambar's thickness and coconut set most of the difference between kitchens. Chutney isn't counted here. A restaurant plate runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Idli sambar is the south Indian breakfast that travels everywhere: steamed rice and urad dal cakes with a katori of sambar poured over or alongside, and usually coconut chutney. In Tamil Nadu and Karnataka it's an everyday morning; in office canteens across India it's the light option.

This page adds up the site's own [idli](/calories/idli/) and [sambar](/calories/sambar/) pages into one plate, so the number is exactly the sum of its parts. Coconut chutney has no page here yet, so it isn't counted: ICMR-NIN puts 2 tablespoons at about 120 calories, which is worth adding yourself.
foods.portionsCaption: Idlis are medium, 15 g of rice and dal each; sambar is a 200 ml katori of the site's thick sambar with coconut. Chutney is not counted.

outside.basis: The sum of the two pages' outside ranges for the same plate: 2 restaurant idlis at 1 to 1.5 times the medium size with up to 5 g of ghee (a stated assumption, on the idli page) and a 200 ml katori of restaurant sambar at 0.6 to 1 times the textbook sambar (a stated assumption, on the sambar page). No analysed value for a plate of idli sambar was found.
text: Restaurant idlis are often larger than home ones, sometimes with ghee or podi oil, while restaurant and canteen sambar is usually thinner than the textbook one and refilled freely.

No lab has measured a plate of idli sambar, so the range below is the two dish pages' outside ranges added together: the low end is 2 medium idlis with a thin sambar, the high end 2 large idlis with ghee and a thick sambar.

changes: How many idlis. Each medium idli adds about {{kcal@idli:medium}} calories: 1 idli with sambar is about {{kcal:one}}, 2 about {{kcal:two}}, 3 about {{kcal:three}}, 4 about {{kcal:four}}.
The size of the idli. Two large idlis with the same sambar are about {{kcal:two_large}}; restaurant idlis are often this size.
The sambar. A thin everyday sambar without coconut is close to half this one per katori (see [sambar](/calories/sambar/)), which takes a plate of 2 idlis down to about {{outLo}}.
Chutney and ghee. Coconut chutney isn't counted here; ICMR-NIN counts 2 tablespoons at about 120 calories. A teaspoon of ghee takes the plate to about {{kcal:two_ghee}}.
Podi mixed with oil, or a fried [medu vada](/calories/medu-vada/) on the side, adds more than the idlis do.
method: The plate is 2 medium idlis and a 200 ml katori of sambar, each made exactly as on its own page: the idli from the textbook batter in The Art & Science of Cooking (parboiled rice and urad dal, 15 g of rice and dal in a medium idli) and the sambar from the same book's recipe with toor dal, vegetables, tamarind and coconut. Values are from IFCT 2017.

Nothing is re-estimated here. Each row adds the pages' unrounded values and rounds once, so the plate always equals its parts. The recipes, the arithmetic and the cross-checks are on the [idli](/calories/idli/) and [sambar](/calories/sambar/) pages. Coconut chutney is left out because the site has no chutney recipe yet; the page says so rather than guessing.

faq.q: How many calories are in idli sambar?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two}} calories for 2 medium idlis with a 200 ml katori of sambar, before chutney. One idli with the same sambar is about {{kcal:one}}.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 idli sambar?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two}} calories: 2 medium idlis at {{kcal@idli:two}} and a 200 ml katori of sambar at {{kcal@sambar:k200}}. With a thin canteen sambar it's closer to {{outLo}}.

faq.q: How many calories are in 4 idli sambar?
faq.a: About {{kcal:four}} calories for 4 medium idlis with a 200 ml katori of sambar. Three idlis with the same sambar are about {{kcal:three}}.

faq.q: How much protein is in idli sambar?
faq.a: About {{protein:two}} g in a plate of 2 idlis with sambar, from the urad dal in the idlis and the toor dal in the sambar. Four idlis with sambar have about {{protein:four}} g.

faq.q: Does idli sambar with chutney have more calories?
faq.a: Yes. Coconut chutney isn't counted on this page; ICMR-NIN counts 2 tablespoons at about 120 calories, so a plate of 2 idlis with sambar and chutney would be closer to {{kcal:two}} plus that.

faq.q: Which has fewer calories, idli sambar or dosa sambar?
faq.a: Idli sambar: about {{kcal:two}} calories for 2 idlis with a katori of sambar against about {{kcal@plain-dosa:with_sambar}} for a [plain dosa](/calories/plain-dosa/) with the same sambar, because the dosa is cooked in oil.

useCase.label: A calorie counter for Indian food

judgement: A plate of 2 medium idlis and one 200 ml katori of sambar is a stated assumption, matched to the meal row on the idli page; the 1, 3 and 4 idli rows cover the other common plates.
Coconut chutney is not counted because the site has no chutney recipe. NIN's figure of 120 kcal per 2 tablespoons is quoted from the idli page's sources so readers can add it.
No independent analysed value for a plate of idli sambar was found, so there is no cross-check here. The parts are cross-checked on their own pages (INDB, USDA FNDDS and NIN).

foods.description: A plate of poori bhaji, 4 home puris with a 200 ml katori of aloo sabzi, has about {{kcal:four}} calories; 2 puris with the sabzi about {{kcal:two}}. From IFCT 2017 recipes.
foods.answer: A plate of poori bhaji, 4 home puris with a 200 ml katori of aloo sabzi, has about {{kcal:four}} calories and {{fat:four}} g of fat. Two puris with the same sabzi are about {{kcal:two}}, six about {{kcal:six}}. The frying oil is the largest share, so puri size and old oil matter most. A halwai plate runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Poori bhaji is the festival and Sunday breakfast of north India: small puffed puris fried in oil, with a thin potato sabzi, often with a pickle and halwa on the side. It's sold by the plate from halwai counters in Delhi, Varanasi and Mathura, and it's the usual breakfast on train journeys.

This page adds up the site's own [puri](/calories/puri/) and [aloo sabzi](/calories/aloo-sabzi/) pages into one plate, so the number is exactly the sum of its parts. Most of a plate's calories are in the puris, and most of a puri's are the oil it took up in frying.
foods.portionsCaption: Puris are home puris from about 13 g of atta each, about 25 g fried; aloo sabzi is a 200 ml katori. Pickle and halwa are extra.

recipe.label: One plate: 4 puris and a 200 ml katori of aloo sabzi, each made as on its own page
recipe.yieldNote: a plate of other dishes, each made as on its own page; no weight of its own

portions.label: 1 plate (4 puris, a 200 ml katori of aloo sabzi)
2 puris and a katori of aloo sabzi
6 puris and a katori of aloo sabzi
4 large puris and a katori of aloo sabzi

outside.label: Halwai or puri-bhaji stall
outside.caption: One plate of 4 puris. The outside range uses the puri page's larger puris fried in much-used oil and the sabzi page's oilier halwai sabzi.
outside.basis: The sum of the two pages' outside ranges for the same plate: 4 halwai puris at up to 1.45 times the size (USDA's 36 g puri) with up to a fifth more oil taken up (Jain et al. 2024, on the puri page), and a 200 ml katori of halwai aloo sabzi with 1.5 to 2 times the oil (a stated assumption, on the aloo sabzi page). No analysed value for a plate of poori bhaji was found.
text: Halwai puris are often larger than home ones and fried in oil that's been used many times, which raises the fat a puri takes up, and the sabzi that comes with them is usually cooked in more oil, often with a layer of it on top.
No lab has measured a plate of poori bhaji, so the range below is the two dish pages' outside ranges added together, for 4 puris and the same katori of sabzi.

changes: How many puris. Each home puri adds about {{kcal@puri:one}} calories: 2 with the sabzi are about {{kcal:two}}, 4 about {{kcal:four}}, 6 about {{kcal:six}}.
The size of the puri. Four large puris (36 g each, USDA's puri) with the same sabzi are about {{kcal:four_large}}.
The frying oil. Oil used many times leaves about a fifth more fat in each puri, in one lab study (see [puri](/calories/puri/)).
The sabzi's oil. A 200 ml katori of home aloo sabzi is about {{kcal@aloo-sabzi:k200}}; the halwai version with 1.5 to 2 times the oil is about {{outLo@aloo-sabzi}} to {{outHi@aloo-sabzi}}.
Halwa with it is a different order of magnitude: a bowl of [gajar halwa](/calories/gajar-halwa/) alone is about {{kcal@gajar-halwa:bowl}}. Pickle adds a little oil.
method: The plate is 4 puris and a 200 ml katori of aloo sabzi, each made exactly as on its own page: the puri from the poori in The Art & Science of Cooking (80 g of atta with a teaspoon of ghee, deep-fried into 6 puris, with the oil taken up set to match USDA's analysed puri) and the sabzi from the potato curry in Basic Food Preparation (100 g of potato with tomato, onion and 2 teaspoons of oil per bowl). Values are from IFCT 2017.

Nothing is re-estimated here. Each row adds the pages' unrounded values and rounds once, so the plate always equals its parts. The recipes, the arithmetic and the cross-checks are on the [puri](/calories/puri/) and [aloo sabzi](/calories/aloo-sabzi/) pages.

faq.q: How many calories are in puri bhaji?
faq.a: About {{kcal:four}} calories for 4 home puris with a 200 ml katori of aloo sabzi, and about {{kcal:two}} for 2 puris with the same sabzi.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 puri bhaji?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two}} calories: 2 home puris at {{kcal@puri:one}} each and a 200 ml katori of aloo sabzi at {{kcal@aloo-sabzi:k200}}.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 plate poori bhaji?
faq.a: A home plate of 4 puris with a katori of aloo sabzi is about {{kcal:four}} calories. With 6 puris it's about {{kcal:six}}, and a halwai plate of 4 large puris about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.

faq.q: How much protein is in puri bhaji?
faq.a: About {{protein:four}} g in a plate of 4 puris with aloo sabzi. Most of the plate is carbohydrate and fat: about {{carbs:four}} g and {{fat:four}} g.

faq.q: Which has more calories, puri bhaji or chole bhature?
faq.a: [Chole bhature](/calories/chole-bhature/), as a plate: about {{kcal@chole-bhature:plate}} calories for 2 bhaturas with a katori of chole against about {{kcal:four}} for 4 puris with aloo sabzi.

useCase.label: Calories in restaurant and delivery food

judgement: A plate of 4 home puris and one 200 ml katori of aloo sabzi is a stated assumption, matched to the meal row on the puri page; the 2 and 6 puri rows and the large-puri row cover the other common plates.

No independent analysed value for a plate of poori bhaji was found, so there is no cross-check here. The parts are cross-checked on their own pages (NIN and USDA FNDDS for the puri, NIN for the sabzi).
Pickle and halwa are left out.

foods.name: Soan papdi
foods.title: Soan papdi calories: {{kcal:one}} per piece, {{kcal:g100}} per 100 g
foods.description: One 21 g piece of soan papdi has about {{kcal:one}} calories and 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}. A patisa recipe of besan, maida, ghee and sugar, checked against packed labels.
foods.answer: One sweet-shop piece of soan papdi, about 21 g, has about {{kcal:one}} calories; 2 pieces about {{kcal:two}}. A home piece of about 51 g is about {{kcal:home}}. Ghee and sugar make up nearly all of it, so the recipe barely changes the number; piece size does. Packed soan papdi, by its labels, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} a piece.
intro: Soan papdi, or patisa, is besan and maida roasted in ghee, beaten into a hot sugar syrup until it pulls into thousands of fine threads, then pressed flat and cut into cubes. It is the most boxed Diwali sweet in India, and the one most often passed on.
By weight it is about half sugar and a quarter ghee. The flours are a fifth. That makes it one of the richer sweets per gram, close to kaju katli, though a packed piece is small.
foods.portionsCaption: Soan papdi made as below; a sweet-shop piece is 21 g, the serving on Haldiram's packs.

recipe.label: Recipe: 115 g besan and 150 g maida roasted in 250 g ghee, set with a syrup of 500 g sugar, making 20 home pieces

ingredients.note: 1½ cups for the syrup, cooked off to a 2½-thread syrup: taken as none left (an assumption)

recipe.yieldNote: the flours, ghee, sugar and the milk's solids, with the syrup water cooked off

portions.label: 1 large home piece (a twentieth, about 51 g)

outside.label: Packed or sweet shop
outside.caption: One 21 g piece. The outside range runs from Haldiram's label to Bikaji's, per gram.
outside.basis: Packed labels per 100 g: Haldiram's 490 kcal (1% below this recipe) and Bikaji 542 (9% above). 0.99 to 1.09 times this recipe is used, for the same 21 g piece.
text: Packed soan papdi is made to much the same recipe, with refined palmolein in place of some or all of the ghee, which changes nothing: fat is fat. Haldiram's label lists 490 calories per 100 g and Bikaji's 542, either side of this page's {{kcal:g100}}.
The range below applies those labels to one 21 g piece.

changes: Piece size is the main thing: a packed cube is about 21 g, a piece cut from a home slab can be twice that or more.
Ghee is about 45% of the calories here. Recipes vary from equal weights of ghee and flour to twice as much; the sweet shop's is not on the label.
Sugar is about half the weight. A 21 g piece holds about 10 g of it.
Pista, orange, chocolate and rose soan papdi are close per gram: Haldiram's chocolate label lists 517 per 100 g against 490 for plain.
[Kaju katli](/calories/kaju-katli/) is close per gram, about {{kcal@kaju-katli:g100}} per 100 g, but a sweet-shop piece is half the weight.
method: No standard textbook in the Indian Nutrient Databank has soan papdi, so the recipe is a published Punjabi patisa recipe: 1¼ cups each of besan and maida roasted in 250 g of ghee, beaten into a syrup of 2½ cups of sugar with 2 tablespoons of milk, making 20 pieces. Cups are converted at USDA's weights (besan 92 g, flour 120 g, sugar 200 g). Values are from IFCT 2017, with sugar from USDA.

The syrup's water is cooked off to a 2½-thread syrup and is taken as gone. Cardamom and the charmagaz seeds on top, a few grams, are left out. The result is checked against two packed labels, which it matches within 10%.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 piece of soan papdi?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for a 21 g sweet-shop piece, the serving size on Haldiram's packs. A bigger home piece of about 51 g is about {{kcal:home}}.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of soan papdi?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}} for this recipe. Packed labels list 490 (Haldiram's) to 542 (Bikaji).

faq.q: How many calories are in a 250 g box of soan papdi?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g250}} for the whole box, roughly 12 pieces of 21 g.

faq.q: How much sugar is in soan papdi?
faq.a: About 10 g in a 21 g piece: sugar is close to half its weight. Haldiram's label lists 46 g of sugar per 100 g.

faq.q: Does soan papdi made with oil have fewer calories than with ghee?
faq.a: No. Palmolein and ghee have the same calories per gram, so a packed soan papdi made with oil is about the same as one made with desi ghee. The difference is taste and texture.

crossCheck.source: Haldiram's soan papdi label, per 100 g (Open Food Facts 8904004405415)
Bikaji soan papdi label, per 100 g (Open Food Facts 8906005504111)

judgement: Constructed recipe: the Indian Nutrient Databank has no soan papdi or patisa. The patisa recipe (allaboutsikhs.com) was chosen over two blog recipes because its ghee and sugar shares (25% and 49% of the finished weight) reconcile with the packed labels (fat 23 to 28 g, sugar 46 to 50 g per 100 g) and the Consumer VOICE test of branded soan papdi (sugar 37 to 40%), where the blog recipes gave 10% or 35% fat.
Cup weights: besan 92 g, maida 120 g, sugar 200 g per cup (INDB's units file, from USDA measures). Milk 2 tbsp = 30 g, its solids about 4 g, counted in the yield.

Yield 1020 g = 115 + 150 + 250 + 500 + about 4 g of milk solids, syrup water cooked off: an assumption. 20 pieces of 51 g. The 21 g shop piece is the serving size on Haldiram's labels (Open Food Facts 8904004405064 and 8904004405316).
Sugar per piece: 500 / 1020 x 21 = 10.3 g.

foods.name: Motichoor ladoo
foods.title: Motichoor ladoo calories: {{kcal:one}} per ladoo, {{kcal:g100}} per 100 g
foods.description: One 28 g motichoor ladoo has about {{kcal:one}} calories, a large 45 g one about {{kcal:large}}, 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}. Fried besan boondi in syrup, checked against labels.
foods.answer: One motichoor ladoo of about 28 g, the size on packed labels, has about {{kcal:one}} calories, and 2 about {{kcal:two}}. A large sweet-shop ladoo of about 45 g is about {{kcal:large}}. Sugar syrup is about a third of the calories and the frying ghee a third more. Sweet-shop ladoos run about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} each, mostly by size.
intro: Motichoor ladoo is tiny boondi, pearls of besan batter fried in ghee, soaked in sugar syrup and pressed into a ball. The pearls are finer than in a boondi ladoo, which is why it holds together and melts. It is the ladoo of weddings, temples and Diwali boxes across north India.
Per gram it is lighter than besan ladoo, because the syrup brings water in with the sugar. Per piece it depends almost entirely on how big the halwai rolls it.
foods.portionsCaption: Motichoor ladoo made as below; 28 g is the piece on Deep's label.

recipe.label: Recipe: 230 g besan as boondi fried in ghee, soaked in a syrup of 267 g sugar, making 25 ladoos

ingredients.note: ¼ cup, added to the syrup to clear it
Taken up in frying the boondi: set so the ladoo is about 20% fat, as packed labels show (an assumption)
3 cups in the batter, fried off, and 3 cups in the syrup, boiled to one thread; about 67 g is taken to stay in the syrup (an assumption)

recipe.yieldNote: besan, sugar, the milk's solids and the ghee taken up, plus about 67 g of syrup water left in

outside.label: Sweet shop or wedding
outside.caption: One ladoo. The outside range runs from a 28 g packed piece to a 60 g halwai ladoo.
outside.basis: Packed labels agree with this recipe per gram within 5% (Haldiram's 410 and 428, Deep 429 kcal per 100 g), so the range is size only: Deep's label piece is 28 g, the same as this recipe's, and USDA FNDDS lists a 60 g ladoo, 2.14 times.
text: Three packed labels put motichoor ladoo at 410 to 429 calories per 100 g, within 5% of this page's {{kcal:g100}}, so a sweet shop's recipe changes little. What changes is the size: a packed ladoo is about 28 g, and a halwai or wedding ladoo can be 60 g.
The range below runs from a 28 g ladoo to a 60 g one.

changes: Size is nearly everything: a 60 g wedding ladoo has more than twice the calories of a 28 g packed one.
Sugar syrup is about a third of the calories. Ladoos soaked longer are heavier and sweeter.
Frying in ghee or in oil makes no difference to the number; the boondi takes up about the same fat either way.

[Boondi ladoo](/calories/besan-ladoo/), with bigger pearls, is close per gram. A roasted [besan ladoo](/calories/besan-ladoo/) is richer, about {{kcal@besan-ladoo:g100}} per 100 g, because it holds no syrup water.
Nuts, magaz seeds and a silver leaf on top add a few calories at most.
method: No standard textbook in the Indian Nutrient Databank has motichoor or boondi ladoo, so the recipe is Sanjeev Kapoor's motichoor laddoo: 2½ cups of besan made into a thin batter, dropped through a perforated spoon into hot ghee as boondi, drained and soaked in a syrup of 1⅓ cups of sugar and ¼ cup of milk, then rolled into 25 ladoos. Cups are converted at USDA's weights (besan 92 g, sugar 200 g). Values are from IFCT 2017, with sugar from USDA.

The recipe says ghee for frying without a quantity. Fried boondi holds a lot of fat (packed khara boondi labels list 30 to 45 g per 100 g), and once soaked in syrup the finished ladoo comes to 16 to 24 g of fat per 100 g on three packed labels. This page sets the ghee taken up so the ladoo is about 20% fat, and keeps about a quarter of the sugar's weight as syrup water, as a one-thread syrup does. Both are stated assumptions; the result sits within 5% of all three labels.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 motichoor ladoo?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for a 28 g ladoo, the size on packed labels, and about {{kcal:large}} for a large 45 g sweet-shop one.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 motichoor ladoos?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two}} for two 28 g ladoos.

faq.q: How much sugar is in a motichoor ladoo?
faq.a: About 11 g in a 28 g ladoo, from the syrup. Haldiram's labels list 41 to 50 g of sugar per 100 g.

faq.q: Which has more calories, motichoor ladoo or besan ladoo?
faq.a: Besan ladoo, per gram: about {{kcal@besan-ladoo:g100}} per 100 g against {{kcal@motichoor-ladoo:g100}} for motichoor, because it holds roasted ghee and no syrup water. Per piece it depends on the size: a 35 g besan ladoo is about {{kcal@besan-ladoo:one}}, a 28 g motichoor ladoo about {{kcal:one}}.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of motichoor ladoo?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}} for this recipe. Packed labels list 410 (Haldiram's, UK pack), 428 (Haldiram's, India) and 429 (Deep).

crossCheck.source: Haldiram's motichoor ladoo label, UK pack, per 100 g (Open Food Facts 5060601190109)
Haldiram's motichoor ladoo label, 360 g pack, per 100 g (Open Food Facts 8904063281319)
Deep motichoor ladoo label, per 100 g, 28 g piece (Open Food Facts 0011433163859)

judgement: Constructed recipe: the Indian Nutrient Databank has besan ladoo (ASC343) but no boondi or motichoor ladoo.
Cup weights from INDB's units file: besan 92 g, sugar 200 g, milk ¼ cup 61 g. Milk solids about 8 g (IFCT cow milk 87% water) counted in the yield.

Ghee taken up: solved so that total fat is 20% of the finished weight: besan fat 12.2 g + milk fat 2.7 g + X = 0.2 x (572 + X), X = 124 g. Labels: 16.5 (Haldiram's UK), 24 (Haldiram's India), 21.4 (Deep) g fat per 100 g.
Syrup water left in: a one-thread syrup is about 80% sugar, so 267 / 0.8 = 334 g of syrup, 67 g of it water. Yield 696 g = 230 + 267 + 8 + 124 + 67; 25 ladoos of 27.8 g.
Sugar per ladoo: 267 / 25 = 10.7 g.
Outside high end: USDA FNDDS ladoo piece of 60 g, as on the besan ladoo page (FDC 2710351, read on 10 October).

foods.name: Rasmalai
foods.title: Rasmalai calories: {{kcal:one}} per piece, {{kcal:g100}} per 100 g
foods.description: One rasmalai with its milk, about 77 g, has about {{kcal:one}} calories; 2 about {{kcal:two}}; 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}. Textbook chhena patties in reduced sweetened milk.
foods.answer: One rasmalai with its milk, about 77 g, has about {{kcal:one}} calories, and 2 about {{kcal:two}}. The chhena patty is about half of that and the sweetened milk the rest, so the spoonfuls of ras served with it matter as much as the piece. Packed and sweet-shop rasmalai runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} a piece, by their labels.
intro: Rasmalai is a flattened rasgulla: chhena from cow's milk, kneaded, cooked in sugar syrup, then soaked in milk that has been simmered down with sugar, saffron and cardamom. It is served cold with a few spoonfuls of the milk, often with pista on top.
Unlike a rasgulla, the milk brings fat and milk sugar as well as added sugar, so a rasmalai with its ras is close to twice a rasgulla of the same patty.
foods.portionsCaption: Rasmalai made as below, each piece with about 3 tablespoons of its milk.

recipe.label: Recipe: chhena from 250 ml cow's milk cooked in syrup, soaked in 111 ml of milk reduced with sugar, making 2 rasmalai

ingredients.note: Chhena from 250 ml cow's milk, valued as IFCT paneer
Taken up from the syrup: set from market rasmalai analysed at Hisar, about 18% carbohydrate in the patty
111 ml, for the ras, simmered down by a third
In the ras, about a teaspoon per piece

recipe.yieldNote: patties of 66 g from the chhena's protein at 10.5%, as in the Hisar analysis, plus the milk reduced by a third with its sugar

outside.label: Sweet shop or packed
outside.caption: One piece with its milk. The outside range runs from Haldiram's 63 g serving to Nanak's 80 g piece.
outside.basis: Packed labels: Haldiram's Mitha Magic 190 kcal per 100 g, 63 g serving (120 per serving, 0.92 times this piece); Nanak 225 kcal per 100 g, 80 g piece (180, 1.38 times). Per gram they bracket this page's value within 6% and 32%.
text: Packed rasmalai labels run from 190 calories per 100 g (Haldiram's Mitha Magic, 63 g servings) to 225 (Nanak, 80 g pieces), against this page's {{kcal:g100}}. A thicker rabdi-style ras, or buffalo milk, pushes a sweet shop's higher.
The range below runs from Haldiram's serving to Nanak's piece.

changes: The milk served with it is half the number. Each extra tablespoon of this ras adds about 20 calories; a thick rabdi adds more.
Buffalo milk or full-cream milk in the ras adds fat; toned milk takes it off.
Sugar in the ras is about a teaspoon a piece here. Sweet shops often use more.
A [rasgulla](/calories/rasgulla/) from the same chhena, in syrup instead of milk, is about {{kcal@rasgulla:one}}.
Pista and saffron on top add nothing you can measure.
method: The chhena patties follow the rasmalai in Basic Food Preparation, a standard Indian cookery manual (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): chhena from 250 ml of cow's milk, bound with half a tablespoon of maida and cooked in sugar syrup, making 2 pieces. IFCT 2017 has no chhena, so paneer is used as the closest match, as on the rasgulla page. The chhena's weight comes from the milk's protein, taking about 80% of it as the casein that stays in the chhena.

A survey of market rasmalai in Hisar found the chhena patties about 10.5% protein and 18% carbohydrate. This page uses the chhena's protein to work out the finished weight of the patties, then sets the sugar taken up from the syrup to match. The manual gives no usable quantity for the ras, so it follows a published halwai-style recipe: a litre of milk with half a cup of sugar for 18 pieces, about 55 ml of milk and a teaspoon of sugar per piece, simmered down by a third (an assumption). Values are from IFCT 2017, with sugar from USDA.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 rasmalai?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for one piece of about 33 g with about 3 tablespoons of its milk, 77 g in all.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 rasmalai?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two}} for two pieces with their milk.

faq.q: How many calories are in rasmalai without the milk?
faq.a: About 70 for the chhena patty alone, worked out from this recipe: a 33 g piece lifted out of the ras. The milk it sits in is the other 60 or so.

faq.q: Which has more calories, rasmalai or rasgulla?
faq.a: Rasmalai, about {{kcal:one}} with its milk against about {{kcal@rasgulla:one}} for a rasgulla drained of syrup. The sweetened milk carries fat and milk sugar that syrup does not.

faq.q: How much sugar is in rasmalai?
faq.a: About 9 g of added sugar in one piece with its milk: about 3.6 g soaked into the patty and a teaspoon in the ras, plus the milk's own sugar.

crossCheck.source: Haldiram's Mitha Magic rasmalai label, per 100 g (Open Food Facts 8904004440980)

judgement: Chhena: milk protein 250 x 1.03 x 3.26% = 8.39 g; casein about 80% of milk protein (assumption, as on the rasgulla page) = 6.72 g, as paneer (IFCT L003, 18.86% protein) = 35.6 g; with the maida's protein, 36.6 g of paneer-equivalent is used so the patties' protein is 6.9 g.

Patties: 6.9 g protein at 10.5% (Hisar market rasmalai, 9.63 to 11.30%) = 66 g for 2. Carbohydrate 17.8% x 66 = 11.7 g, minus the paneer's 4.5 g = 7.2 g sugar taken up. Fat 5.4 g / 66 g = 8.2%, against 9.2 to 11.0% in the survey (the sweet shops use richer milk).

Ras: Hebbar's Kitchen's halwai-style rasmalai uses 1 litre of milk and ½ cup (100 g) of sugar for 18 pieces: 55.5 ml milk (57.2 g) and 5.6 g sugar per piece. Reduced by a third: 38 g milk + 5.6 g sugar = 43.7 g per piece. The reduction is an assumption; it changes the weight, not the calories.
Yield 153 g = 66 + 2 x 43.7. Per piece 77 g, of which the patty is 33 g (about 68 kcal) and the ras 44 g (about 63 kcal).
Per 100 g, Hisar's figures give about 204 kcal for the patties (4 x 28.3 + 9 x 10.1) and about 165 for the sweetened milk, bracketing this page's {{kcal:g100}} for piece and milk together.
The INDB's own rasmalai value (136 kcal per 100 g) counts the whole 150 g of syrup sugar and is not used. BFP393's serving count (2 pieces) is marked as guessed in INDB.
Nanak's label (225 kcal per 100 g, 80 g piece) is 32% above this page per gram and is used as the top of the outside range rather than as a cross-check.

foods.name: Kheer
foods.title: Kheer calories: {{kcal:k200}} per katori, {{kcal:g100}} per 100 g
foods.description: A 200 ml katori of rice kheer has about {{kcal:k200}} calories, a 150 ml one about {{kcal:k150}} and 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}. Worked out from a textbook recipe and IFCT 2017.
foods.answer: A 200 ml katori of home rice kheer, made with whole milk and 1½ tablespoons of sugar, has about {{kcal:k200}} calories. A small 150 ml katori is about {{kcal:k150}}, a big 250 ml one about {{kcal:k250}}. Milk is more than half of it, sugar a quarter. A sweet-shop kheer, thicker and sweeter, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} a katori.
intro: Kheer is rice simmered in milk until the milk thickens, sweetened with sugar and finished with cardamom, raisins and a few slivers of almond. It is the sweet of pujas and festival thalis across north India, and payasam, doodh pak and phirni are its cousins.
The number is set by the milk and the sugar, not the rice: a katori holds only a spoonful of rice. How far the milk is simmered down changes how much milk ends up in each katori.
foods.portionsCaption: Kheer made as below, with whole cow's milk. A katori is measured by volume.

recipe.label: Recipe: 10 g rice simmered in 250 ml milk with 1½ tablespoons of sugar, raisins and almond, making one bowl
recipe.densityNote: USDA FNDDS rice pudding: 1 cup (237 ml) = 260 g

ingredients.note: half a cup, to cook the rice; mostly simmered off

recipe.yieldNote: the milk and water simmered down to about 270 g with the rice swollen, sugar and dry fruit: an assumption, checked against USDA's rice pudding

outside.label: Sweet shop or restaurant
outside.caption: One 200 ml katori. The outside range is up to 1.33 times, as thick and sweet as USDA's firni.
outside.basis: No analysed value for a sweet-shop kheer was found. USDA FNDDS puts firni, a thicker Indian milk pudding, at 144 kcal per 100 g against 108 for its rice pudding, 1.33 times; that ratio is used for the top of the range, as a stated assumption.
text: Sweet-shop and wedding kheer is usually simmered down further, sweeter, and sometimes made with buffalo milk, khoa or condensed milk. USDA's firni, a thicker Indian milk pudding, has a third more calories per gram than its rice pudding.
The range below allows a katori up to a third richer than this recipe.

changes: Sugar is about a quarter of the number. Each tablespoon in the pot adds about 50 calories, spread over the bowls.
How far the milk is simmered down: thicker kheer puts more milk, and more calories, into the same katori.
Buffalo milk raises it by about half again on the milk's share; toned milk lowers it.
Khoa, condensed milk or cream stirred in at the end adds a lot: a tablespoon of condensed milk is about 60 calories.
Seviyan kheer and sabudana kheer are close to this per katori; [gajar halwa](/calories/gajar-halwa/) is richer, about {{kcal@gajar-halwa:small}} for a small katori.
method: The recipe is the rice kheer in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 10 g of rice cooked in half a cup of water and 250 ml of whole milk, with 1½ tablespoons of sugar, 4 to 5 raisins, a slivered almond and cardamom, for one bowl. Values are from IFCT 2017, with sugar from USDA. The cardamom, under half a gram, is left out.

The textbook does not give a finished weight. The databank's own figure for this recipe counts all the milk and water as still there, which gives a thin kheer; this page takes the milk and water as simmered down to about 270 g, so the bowl is about 300 g, an assumption. On that basis it comes out within 6% of USDA's analysed rice pudding, and a katori is measured by volume at USDA's density of 1.1 g per ml.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 katori of kheer?
faq.a: About {{kcal:k200}} for a 200 ml katori of home rice kheer made with whole milk, and about {{kcal:k150}} for a small 150 ml katori.

faq.q: How many calories are in a bowl of kheer?
faq.a: About {{kcal:bowl}} for the textbook bowl, the whole recipe of 250 ml of milk, or about {{kcal:k250}} for a big 250 ml katori.

faq.q: How much sugar is in kheer?
faq.a: About 14 g of added sugar in a 200 ml katori of this recipe, plus about 8 g of the milk's own sugar.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of kheer?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}}. USDA's analysed rice pudding is 108 per 100 g.

faq.q: Which has more calories, a katori of kheer or a gulab jamun?
faq.a: A katori of kheer, about {{kcal:k200}}, against about {{kcal@gulab-jamun:one}} for one gulab jamun. Two gulab jamuns come to about {{kcal@gulab-jamun:two}}.

crossCheck.source: USDA FNDDS 2021-2023, Pudding, rice (2705685)

judgement: Yield: 300 g is an assumption (257.5 g milk + 120 g water + 10 g rice + 18.9 g sugar + 2.6 g dry fruit = 409 g raw, simmered down by about a quarter). INDB's own value for ASC282, 75 kcal per 100 g, takes no reduction at all; USDA's analysed rice pudding is 108 per 100 g, 6% above this page's figure at 300 g.
Sugar: 1½ tbsp at 12.6 g per tbsp (INDB units, 4.2 g per tsp) = 18.9 g; per 200 ml katori 18.9 x 220 / 300 = 13.9 g added sugar; milk sugar 257.5 x 4.89% x 220 / 300 = 9.2 g.
Density 1.1 g per ml from FNDDS rice pudding (1 cup = 260 g), so a 200 ml katori is 220 g.
Cardamom ¼ tsp left out. Rice is the textbook's parboiled rice (A014).
Outside: FNDDS firni 144 kcal per 100 g / rice pudding 108 = 1.33, applied as a size factor to the katori.

foods.name: Gujiya
foods.title: Gujiya calories: {{kcal:one}} per piece, {{kcal:g100}} per 100 g
foods.description: One home gujiya of about 30 g has about {{kcal:one}} calories and 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}. Fried maida pastry with khoa, coconut and sugar, from a textbook recipe.
foods.answer: One home gujiya of about 30 g, a maida pastry filled with khoa, coconut and sugar and deep-fried, has about {{kcal:one}} calories; 2 about {{kcal:two}}. The pastry and the oil it takes up are about half of that, the sweet filling the rest. A halwai gujiya, bigger and sometimes dipped in syrup, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.
intro: Gujiya is a half-moon of maida pastry, filled with khoa, desiccated coconut, sugar and a few raisins, sealed with a crimped edge and deep-fried until crisp. Karanji in Maharashtra and ghughra in Gujarat are the same idea, often with more coconut. It is made at Holi and Diwali in north Indian homes.
The filling is sweet but small; the fried shell is where most of the calories are, as in a samosa.
foods.portionsCaption: Home gujiya made as below, fried in oil and drained.

recipe.label: Recipe: 60 g maida pastry with 12 g ghee, filled with 30 g khoa, 10 g coconut and 30 g sugar, fried, making 6 gujiyas

ingredients.note: Taken up in frying: about 14% of the raw weight, as worked out for the samosa on this site (an assumption)

recipe.yieldNote: the dough, filling and oil taken up; moisture lost in frying is not counted

outside.label: Halwai, larger or syrup-dipped
outside.caption: One gujiya. The outside range is 1.33 to 2 times the size, with up to 8 g of syrup sugar on the larger one.
outside.basis: No analysed value for gujiya was found. Halwai gujiyas of 40 to 60 g (1.33 to 2 times this recipe's 30 g) and a chashni dip of up to 8 g of sugar are stated assumptions.
text: Sweet-shop gujiyas are usually bigger than home ones, 40 to 60 g, and many are dipped in sugar syrup after frying, which adds a coat of sugar. We found no lab figure for a gujiya of either kind.
The range below assumes a gujiya 1.33 to 2 times this size, with up to 8 g of syrup sugar on the larger one.

changes: Size: a 60 g halwai gujiya has twice the calories of this 30 g one.
Frying oil taken up is about a quarter of the number. Baked gujiya skips it, about 100 calories a piece from this recipe.
A chashni dip adds sugar: a thin coat is 5 to 8 g, 20 to 30 calories.
A coconut-heavy karanji filling is a little richer per gram than khoa; a mawa-only filling a little lighter.
A [samosa](/calories/samosa/) of the same pastry is about {{kcal@samosa:one}}: the sweet filling and the savoury one come out close.
method: The recipe is the gujia in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 60 g of maida with 12 g of ghee and a tablespoon of water for the pastry, filled with 30 g of khoa, 10 g of desiccated coconut, 30 g of castor sugar and a few raisins, deep-fried, making 6 gujiyas. Values are from IFCT 2017, with sugar from USDA.

The databank counts all 480 ml of frying oil as eaten, which is far too high. This page takes the oil taken up as about 14% of the raw weight, the uptake worked out for the samosa on this site from lab-fried samosas, about 3.7 g per gujiya. No lab analysis of gujiya itself was found, so that uptake is a stated assumption.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 gujiya?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for a home gujiya of about 30 g, fried. A bigger halwai gujiya runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}}.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 gujiyas?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two}} for two home gujiyas.

faq.q: How many calories are in a baked gujiya?
faq.a: About 100 from this recipe: the same pastry and filling without the 3.7 g of frying oil, which is about 33 calories.

faq.q: How much sugar is in a gujiya?
faq.a: About 5 g of added sugar in the filling of one gujiya, plus the milk sugar in the khoa and a little from the raisins. A syrup-dipped one has more.

faq.q: Is karanji the same as gujiya?
faq.a: Close. Karanji is the Maharashtrian version, usually with a coconut and sugar filling and less or no khoa; ghughra is the Gujarati one. Per piece they are within a few calories of each other at the same size.

judgement: No analysed value for gujiya or karanji was found (IFCT 2017, NIN Annexure 8, USDA FNDDS, a web search of journals). Supplier listings and consumer databases give figures that are not lab values and are not used.
Raw weight: 60 + 12 + 15 + 30 + 10 + 1.8 + 30 = 158.8 g; oil taken up at 14% = 22.2 g, 3.7 g per gujiya. Moisture lost in frying is not counted, as on the samosa page.
INDB's gujia values (769 kcal per 100 g) count all 480 ml of frying oil and are not used.
Castor sugar valued as sugar; raisins 'a few' taken at INDB's 1.8 g.
Baked gujiya in the FAQ: 132 - 33 = 99 kcal.

foods.name: Peda
foods.title: Peda calories: {{kcal:one}} per piece, {{kcal:g100}} per 100 g
foods.description: One 28 g peda has about {{kcal:one}} calories, a small 13 g one about {{kcal:small}}, 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}. Khoa and sugar, checked against a lab survey and a label.
foods.answer: One peda of about 28 g, khoa cooked with sugar, has about {{kcal:one}} calories; 2 about {{kcal:two}}. A small packed peda of 13 g is about {{kcal:small}}. Khoa is two thirds of the calories and sugar nearly all the rest. Every sweet shop makes it the same way, so only the size moves the number: 100 g is about {{kcal:g100}}.
intro: Peda is khoa, milk reduced to solids, cooked with sugar until it holds together, then pressed into a disc and stamped. Mathura's is caramelised brown, Dharwad's darker still, and the plain white doodh peda is the one in most sweet boxes. It is the simplest of the khoa sweets, with burfi and milk cake as close relations.
Because it is only khoa and sugar, the recipe hardly varies between homes and shops. A lab survey of market pedas and a packed label both land within 5% of this page per gram.
foods.portionsCaption: Peda made as below, cooked down to about 14% moisture.

recipe.label: Recipe: 100 g khoa cooked with 35 g sugar and 2 teaspoons of milk, making 4 pedas
recipe.yieldNote: the solids of the khoa, sugar, milk and almond at 13.6% moisture, the mean of market pedas in a lab survey

changes: Size is the only real variable: packed pedas run about 13 g, a halwai's 20 to 30 g, a Mathura peda up to 35 g.
Sugar share: market pedas run from 32% to 62% sugar. Sugar and khoa are close per gram (387 and {{ing:khoa}} calories per 100 g), so a sweeter peda is a few percent more, not a lot.
Malai or kesar peda made with cream or extra ghee is a little richer; a drier, longer-cooked Mathura peda a little more per gram because there is less water.
[Kaju katli](/calories/kaju-katli/) is richer per gram, about {{kcal@kaju-katli:g100}} per 100 g, but its pieces are smaller.
Pista or silver leaf on top adds nothing you can measure.
method: The recipe is the plain burfi in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 100 g of khoa cooked with 35 g of castor sugar and 2 teaspoons of milk, with 2 almonds on top, making 4 pieces. Peda and plain khoa burfi are the same mixture shaped differently, so the burfi recipe is used for peda. Values are from IFCT 2017, with sugar from USDA. The 2 tablespoons of ghee the textbook uses to grease the tray are not counted.

Khoa is 42.5% water in IFCT 2017 and loses more as the peda cooks. The finished weight is set at the 13.6% moisture that a National Dairy Research Institute survey measured in market pedas, which also puts this recipe at 18.6% fat, 15% protein and 31.5% sugar, close to the survey's 16.7%, 15.2% and 34.4%. The result is within 5% of the survey's composition and of a packed peda label.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 peda?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for a 28 g peda, and about {{kcal:small}} for a small 13 g packed one.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 pedas?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two}} for two 28 g pedas.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of peda?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}}. A packed label (Rajhans) lists 442, and a lab survey of market pedas works out to about 419.

faq.q: How much sugar is in a peda?
faq.a: About 9 g of added sugar in a 28 g peda, plus about 4 g of the milk's own sugar from the khoa.

faq.q: Which has more calories, peda or kaju katli?
faq.a: Per piece the peda, about {{kcal:one}} against about {{kcal@kaju-katli:shop}} for a 10 g sweet-shop kaju katli. Per 100 g the kaju katli, about {{kcal@kaju-katli:g100}} against {{kcal:g100}}, because cashews are richer than khoa.

crossCheck.source: Rajhans peda label, per 100 g (Open Food Facts 8908000716476)
NDRI survey of market pedas, energy worked out from its mean composition (fat 16.74%, protein 15.23%, lactose 17.43%, sucrose 34.38%)

judgement: Peda modelled on the plain burfi recipe ASC335 (khoa, castor sugar, a little milk): the same mixture, pressed into discs instead of cut into squares. INDB's khoa ladoo (BFP404) adds coconut and nuts and was not used.

Yield from moisture: solids = khoa 57.5 (IFCT water 42.51%) + sugar 35 + milk solids 1.3 + almond 2.1 = 95.9 g; at 13.63% moisture (NDRI, other-variety market pedas, mean) = 111 g; 4 pedas of 27.8 g. The INDB's own value (408 kcal per 100 g) counts 2 tbsp of greasing ghee and no moisture loss.

Check of composition: fat 20.6 + 0.4 + 1.3 = 22.3 g / 111 = 20%; protein 16.3 + 0.3 + 0.4 = 17 g = 15.3%; sucrose 35 / 111 = 31.5%; lactose about 15%. NDRI market pedas: fat 16.74, protein 15.23, sucrose 34.38, lactose 17.43, moisture 13.63. NIFTEM's lab average: fat 20.1, protein 19.0, sucrose 30.0, lactose 18.3, moisture 10.2.
NDRI energy per 100 g: 9 x 16.74 + 4 x (15.23 + 17.43 + 34.38) = 419 kcal. NIFTEM's lab average gives 450 (+6%).
No outside range: the recipe is the same in shops and packs; only the piece size differs, and the small packed piece is a portion row.
Sugar per peda: 35 / 4 = 8.75 g; lactose 16.5 x 0.25 = 4.1 g.

foods.name: Chakli
foods.title: Chakli calories: {{kcal:one}} per piece, {{kcal:g100}} per 100 g
foods.description: One 18 g chakli has about {{kcal:one}} calories, 4 about {{kcal:four}} and 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}. A rice flour and dal spiral fried in oil, checked against packed labels.
foods.answer: One chakli of about 18 g, a spiral of rice flour and roasted gram dal fried in oil, has about {{kcal:one}} calories; 2 about {{kcal:two}} and 4 about {{kcal:four}}. The oil taken up in frying is a third of the number. Packed chakli, by its labels, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} a piece, bigger Diwali chaklis at the top.
intro: Chakli is a stiff dough of rice flour and roasted gram dal flour, with butter, sesame and chilli, pressed through a star nozzle into spirals and deep-fried until crisp. Murukku in Tamil Nadu and chakkuli in Karnataka are made the same way, sometimes with urad dal flour in place of the gram dal. It keeps for weeks, which is why it fills Diwali faral boxes.
Crisp fried snacks are light in water and heavy in oil, so per 100 g chakli sits well above most sweets. A single chakli is small, though; a handful is not.
foods.portionsCaption: Chakli made as below, fried in oil and drained.

recipe.label: Recipe: 360 g rice flour and 150 g roasted gram dal with butter and sesame, fried, making 35 chaklis

ingredients.note: ¾ cup roasted gram dal (dalia), ground; valued as Bengal gram dal
to knead a stiff dough: an assumption, cooked off in frying
Taken up in frying: about 14% of the raw weight, as worked out for the samosa on this site (an assumption)

recipe.yieldNote: the flours, dal, butter, sesame and the oil taken up, at 4% moisture, as a crisp fried snack: an assumption

outside.label: Packed or shop
outside.caption: One chakli. The outside range runs from a packed label per gram to a bigger 25 g chakli at the richest label.
outside.basis: Packed chakli labels per 100 g: Charliee masala butter chakli 474 (4% below this recipe), Palak chakli 525, Softy chakli 549 (12% above). Low end 0.96 times this 18 g chakli; high end a 25 g Diwali chakli at Softy's value per gram, 1.39 x 1.12 = 1.55 times. The 25 g size is an assumption.
text: Packed chakli labels run from 474 to 549 calories per 100 g, either side of this page's {{kcal:g100}}; one label with more oil lists 560. Shop chaklis for Diwali are often bigger than the 18 g one here, up to 25 g.
The range below runs from the lightest label for this size to a 25 g chakli at the richest common label.

changes: Oil taken up in frying is about a third of the number; a thicker spiral takes up less per gram, a thin crisp one more.
Butter in the dough is about 6% of the calories here. Butter chakli recipes with twice the butter add about 6 calories a piece.
Size: Diwali chaklis of 25 g or more are half as much again as this 18 g one.
Urad dal flour in place of the gram dal, as in murukku, changes almost nothing per gram.
[Mathri](/calories/mathri/) and [namak para](/calories/namak-para/) are richer per 100 g, about {{kcal@mathri:g100}} and {{kcal@namak-para:g100}}, because their dough carries fat before frying.
method: The Indian Nutrient Databank's standard textbooks have no chakli; its open-source recipes include a rice murukku (OSR113) whose dough is the one chakli is made from: 3 cups of rice flour, ¾ cup of roasted gram dal flour, 2 tablespoons each of butter and sesame, chilli, ajwain and salt, fried, making 35 pieces. That recipe is used here, with cups converted at USDA's weights (rice flour 120 g, roasted gram dal 150 g for ¾ cup as the databank lists). Values are from IFCT 2017, with rice flour and butter from USDA.

The databank counts all 2 cups of frying oil as eaten. This page takes the oil taken up as about 14% of the raw weight, the uptake worked out for the samosa on this site, about 3.4 g per chakli, and the finished chakli at 4% moisture as a crisp snack. Both are stated assumptions; the result, 25% fat, sits inside the 21 to 33% on packed labels and in published chakli studies, and within 12% of three labels' calories.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 chakli?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for an 18 g chakli, and about {{kcal:four}} for four.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of chakli?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}}. Packed labels list 474 to 549 per 100 g.

faq.q: Is chakli the same as murukku?
faq.a: The same dough family: rice flour with roasted gram dal or urad dal flour, butter and sesame, pressed through a nozzle and fried. The shapes and the dal differ by region; the calories per gram barely do.

faq.q: How much fat is in chakli?
faq.a: About {{fat:g100}} g per 100 g of this recipe, most of it frying oil, and about {{fat:one}} g in one chakli.

faq.q: How many calories are in a bowl of chakli?
faq.a: About {{kcal:bowl}} for a small bowl of about 50 g, 2 to 3 chaklis.

judgement: Chakli is modelled on INDB's open-source rice murukku (OSR113) because its ingredients (rice flour, roasted gram dal, butter, sesame, chilli, ajwain) are a standard chakli dough; the ASC and BFP textbooks have no chakli or murukku. Murukku is listed as an alias on that basis.

Raw weight: 360 + 150 + 28.4 + 18 + 1.3 + 300 water (assumption) = 858 g; oil taken up at 14% = 120 g, 3.4 g per chakli. Moisture: finished at 4% (assumption for a crisp fried snack): solids 317 (rice flour at 12% water) + 135 (dal at 10%) + 24 (butter fat) + 17 + 1 = 494 g, plus 120 g oil, divided by 0.96 = 640 g; 645 g used. 35 chaklis of 18.4 g.

Fat check: 1.4 + 8 + 23 + 7.7 + 120 = 160 g / 645 = 25%. Labels: Charliee 21.5, Palak 29, Softy 33, Adukale 41.6 g per 100 g. A little millet chakli study reports about 33% fat (abstract seen in search results only, not opened, not used).
Salt (¾ tsp), ajwain (½ tsp) and asafoetida left out. Roasted gram dal valued as IFCT Bengal gram dal (B001).
Adukale khara chakli (560 kcal, 41.6 g fat per 100 g) is 14% above this page and is mentioned as the oilier end rather than used as a cross-check.

foods.answer: Ten home namak para, about 50 g, have about {{kcal:ten}} calories; one 5 g diamond about {{kcal:one}}, and 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}. The ghee in the dough and the oil taken up in frying are together about half the number. Packed namak para, by its labels, runs about {{outLo}} to {{outHi}} for 50 g.
intro: Namak para is maida kneaded with ghee, ajwain and salt, rolled out, cut into diamonds and deep-fried until crisp and pale gold. It is the savoury half of a Diwali plate, next to shakarpara, and the same dough makes mathri when it is pressed into discs.
A single piece is a mouthful. Ten of them, a small bowl, are what people eat with chai, and that is the portion this page leads with.
foods.portionsCaption: Namak para made as below, fried in oil and drained. A home diamond is about 5 g; packed pieces are often smaller.

ingredients.note: to knead a stiff dough: an assumption, cooked off in frying

outside.label: Packed
outside.caption: Ten pieces, 50 g. The outside range runs from the lightest packed label to the oiliest, per gram.
outside.basis: Packed namak para labels per 100 g: Riya's 459 (12% below this recipe), Daadis 535 (3% above), Deep 607 (17% above, 42.9 g fat). 0.88 to 1.17 times this recipe is used for the same 50 g.
text: Packed namak para labels run from 459 to 607 calories per 100 g, around this page's {{kcal:g100}}. The spread is oil: the oiliest label lists 43 g of fat per 100 g against {{fat:g100}} g here. Pieces in a packet are often smaller than a home diamond, so count by weight.
The range below applies those labels to 50 g.

changes: Oil taken up in frying is about a quarter of the number. Thin, well-drained pieces take up less; re-used oil and thicker pieces more.
The ghee moyan in the dough is another fifth. Recipes run from 1 to 4 tablespoons per 2 cups of maida, about 25 calories a piece either way.
Baked namak para skips the frying oil, about 6 calories less a piece from this recipe.
Atta in place of maida adds fibre and changes the calories very little.
[Mathri](/calories/mathri/) is the same dough with more fat in it, about {{kcal@mathri:one}} a piece; [shakarpara](/calories/shakarpara/) is the sweet version, about {{kcal@shakarpara:ten}} for 10.
method: The Indian Nutrient Databank's standard textbooks have a mathri and two fortified namak para recipes (soyabean, and spinach and peanut), but no plain namak para, so the recipe is Hebbar's Kitchen's namak pare: 2 cups of maida with 3 tablespoons of ghee, ajwain, kalonji and salt, kneaded stiff, cut into diamonds and deep-fried. Cups and tablespoons are converted at USDA's weights (flour 120 g a cup, ghee 12.8 g a tablespoon). Values are from IFCT 2017. The kalonji, ajwain and salt, about 10 g together, are left out of the arithmetic.

The oil taken up is set at about 14% of the raw weight, the uptake worked out for the samosa on this site, and the finished pieces at 4% moisture as a crisp snack. Both are stated assumptions; the result, 29% fat, sits inside the 25 to 43 g on packed labels, and within 12% of two of the three labels' calories.

faq.q: How many calories are in namak para?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for one 5 g piece, {{kcal:ten}} for 10 pieces (50 g) and {{kcal:g100}} per 100 g, for home namak para fried in oil.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of namak para?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}} for this recipe. Packed labels list 459 to 607 per 100 g, depending on the oil.

faq.q: Is namak para the same as mathri?
faq.a: The same dough, cut differently. Mathri's textbook recipe carries more fat in the dough, so it is a little richer per gram: about {{kcal@mathri:g100}} per 100 g against {{kcal:g100}} here.

faq.q: How much fat is in namak para?
faq.a: About {{fat:g100}} g per 100 g, half from the ghee in the dough and half from the frying oil. That is about {{fat:ten}} g in 10 pieces.

faq.q: How many calories are in a bowl of namak para?
faq.a: About {{kcal:ten}} for a small bowl of 10 pieces, 50 g. A full katori heaped with namak para is more like 80 g, about 400.

judgement: Constructed recipe: INDB has no plain namak para (only soyabean ASC458 and spinach-peanut ASC460 versions, and BFP568 poshtik). Hebbar's Kitchen's namak pare was used; the textbook mathri dough (ASC364, 100 g maida and 2 tbsp oil) is the same idea with more fat.
Units: maida 120 g a cup (INDB units file, same as flour); ghee 12.8 g a tablespoon (INDB). Water 85 g is an assumption (a stiff dough at about 35% of the flour).
Raw weight 240 + 38.4 + 85 = 363 g; oil taken up at 14% = 52 g. Finished weight at 4% moisture: maida solids 212.8 + 38.4 + 52 = 303 / 0.96 = 316 g; about 63 pieces of 5 g.
Fat check: 1.8 + 38.4 + 52 = 92 g / 316 = 29%. Labels: Riya's 24.7, Daadis 30.6, Deep 42.9 g per 100 g.
Deep's label (607 kcal, 42.9 g fat per 100 g; 10 pieces = 28 g) is 17% above this page and is used as the top of the outside range, not as a cross-check.
A full katori in the FAQ: 80 g x 5.2 = 416 kcal.
