foods.description: One 6 g shakarpara has about {{kcal:one}} calories, 10 pieces about {{kcal:ten}} and 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}. Maida, sugar and ghee fried in oil, from a published recipe.
foods.answer: Ten home shakarpara, about 60 g, have about {{kcal:ten}} calories; one 6 g piece about {{kcal:one}}, and 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}. Sugar is a sixth of the number; the ghee in the dough and the frying oil nearly half. No lab figure or packed label was found, so the number rests on the recipe and the frying assumptions stated below.
intro: Shakarpara, or shankarpali in Maharashtra, is maida kneaded with sugar, a little rava and ghee, rolled, cut into diamonds and deep-fried until golden. It is the sweet half of a Diwali faral plate, next to namak para, and one of the few sweets that keeps for a month in a dabba.
It is a fried biscuit, so most of its calories are flour and fat; the sugar is less than people expect, about a fifth of the weight.
foods.portionsCaption: Shakarpara made as below, fried in oil and drained. A home diamond is about 6 g.

recipe.label: Recipe: 240 g maida with 100 g sugar, 21 g rava and 51 g ghee, cut into diamonds and fried, making about 79 pieces

ingredients.note: half a cup, dissolved in the water
to dissolve the sugar and knead: an assumption, cooked off in frying
Taken up in frying: about 14% of the raw weight, as worked out for the samosa on this site (an assumption)

recipe.yieldNote: the flour, rava and sugar solids, the ghee and the oil taken up, at 4% moisture, as a crisp fried snack: an assumption

changes: Oil taken up in frying is about a quarter of the number; thick pieces take up less per gram than thin ones.
Sugar: recipes run from a quarter cup to a full cup per 2 cups of maida. Each extra quarter cup adds about 2.5 calories a piece.
A chashni-coated shakarpara, dipped in syrup after frying, carries a sugar shell on top of this: a thin coat adds 5 to 10 calories a piece.
Atta or jaggery versions are close per gram.
[Namak para](/calories/namak-para/) from the same kind of dough without sugar is about {{kcal@namak-para:ten}} for 10 pieces.
method: No standard textbook in the Indian Nutrient Databank has shakarpara or shankarpali, so the recipe is Hebbar's Kitchen's shankarpali: 2 cups of maida with 2 tablespoons of rava, half a cup of sugar dissolved in water, a quarter cup of ghee and a pinch of salt, kneaded stiff, cut into diamonds and deep-fried. Cups are converted at USDA's weights (flour 120 g, sugar 200 g, semolina 167 g a cup) and ghee at 12.8 g a tablespoon. Values are from IFCT 2017, with sugar from USDA.

The oil taken up is set at about 14% of the raw weight, the uptake worked out for the samosa on this site, and the finished pieces at 4% moisture as a crisp snack. Both are stated assumptions. We found no lab analysis or packed label for shakarpara to check against; the namak para and mathri pages, made from the same kind of dough, do match their labels.

faq.q: How many calories are in shakarpara?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for one 6 g piece, {{kcal:ten}} for 10 pieces (60 g) and {{kcal:g100}} per 100 g, for home shakarpara fried in oil.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of shakarpara?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}} for this recipe, an estimate without a lab figure to check against.

faq.q: How much sugar is in shakarpara?
faq.a: About 13 g of added sugar in 10 pieces, 60 g: the sugar is about a fifth of the weight. A syrup-coated shakarpara has more.

faq.q: Which has more calories, shakarpara or namak para?
faq.a: They are close. Ten shakarpara are about {{kcal:ten}} and ten namak para about {{kcal@namak-para:ten}}; the sugar in one and the extra fat in the other roughly cancel out per piece.

faq.q: How many calories are in 10 shakarpara?
faq.a: About {{kcal:ten}} for 10 home pieces of about 6 g each.

judgement: Constructed recipe: INDB has no shakarpara, shankarpali or sweet para. Hebbar's Kitchen's shankarpali was used.

No analysed value found: Open Food Facts has no shakarpara product with values, USDA FDC returned none, and a journal search found nothing. Consumer databases disagree with each other (412 to 500 kcal per 100 g) and are not used.
Units: maida 120 g a cup, sugar 200 g, semolina 167 g (INDB units from USDA measures); ghee 12.8 g a tbsp, so ¼ cup = 51 g. Water 90 g is an assumption.
Raw weight 240 + 21 + 100 + 51 + 90 = 502 g; oil taken up at 14% = 70 g. Finished at 4% moisture: solids 212.8 + 19.1 + 100 = 332 + fats 121 = 453 / 0.96 = 472 g; about 79 pieces of 6 g.
Sugar per 10 pieces: 100 / 472 x 60 = 12.7 g.
Salt (½ tsp) left out.

foods.title: Mathri calories: {{kcal:one}} per piece, {{kcal:g100}} per 100 g
foods.description: One home mathri of about 21 g has about {{kcal:one}} calories, 2 about {{kcal:two}} and 100 g about {{kcal:g100}}. A flaky maida disc fried in oil, from a textbook recipe.
foods.answer: One home mathri of about 21 g, a flaky disc of maida with oil and ajwain, deep-fried, has about {{kcal:one}} calories, and 2 about {{kcal:two}}. The oil in the dough and the oil taken up in frying are together more than half the number, which is why mathri is richer per gram than most sweets: about {{kcal:g100}} per 100 g.
intro: Mathri is maida kneaded with a generous moyan of oil or ghee, peppercorns and ajwain, pressed into small discs, pricked and fried slowly until flaky and pale. It is a north Indian tea-time and Diwali snack, eaten plain or with achaar, and keeps for weeks.
The textbook recipe uses 2 tablespoons of oil in the dough for 100 g of flour before any frying, which is what makes it flaky and what makes it one of the richest things on this site per gram.
foods.portionsCaption: Mathri made as below, fried in oil and drained.

recipe.label: Recipe: 100 g maida with 2 tablespoons of oil, pepper and ajwain, fried, making 7 mathris

ingredients.note: to knead a stiff dough: an assumption, cooked off in frying
Taken up in frying: about 14% of the raw weight, as worked out for the samosa on this site (an assumption)

recipe.yieldNote: the maida's solids, the pepper, the dough oil and the oil taken up, at 4% moisture, as a crisp fried snack: an assumption

changes: The moyan: recipes run from 1 to 4 tablespoons of oil or ghee per 100 g of maida, about 15 calories a mathri each way.
Oil taken up in frying is about a quarter of the number. Slow frying at low heat, which mathri needs, takes up a little more than fast frying.
Size: shop mathris of 30 to 40 g are half as much again to twice this one.
Methi mathri, with dried fenugreek leaves, and atta mathri are close per gram. A baked mathri skips the frying oil, about 30 calories less a piece from this recipe.
[Namak para](/calories/namak-para/) is the same dough with less fat in it, about {{kcal@namak-para:g100}} per 100 g; [khasta kachori](/calories/kachori/) is about {{kcal@kachori:one}} a piece.
method: The recipe is the mathri in The Art & Science of Cooking, a standard Indian cookery textbook (via the Indian Nutrient Databank): 100 g of maida with 2 tablespoons of oil, 8 peppercorns, ajwain and salt, kneaded, cut into discs and deep-fried, making 7 mathris. Values are from IFCT 2017. The ajwain and salt, under 4 g, are left out.

The databank counts all 480 ml of frying oil as eaten, which is far too high. This page takes the oil taken up as about 14% of the raw weight, the uptake worked out for the samosa on this site, about 3.3 g per mathri, and the finished mathri at 4% moisture as a crisp snack. Both are stated assumptions. No lab analysis of mathri was found; the result, 35% fat, is what packed mathri labels list, though those listings were not opened for this page and are not cited.

faq.q: How many calories are in 1 mathri?
faq.a: About {{kcal:one}} for a home mathri of about 21 g. A big shop mathri of 30 to 40 g is half as much again to twice that.

faq.q: How many calories are in 2 mathris?
faq.a: About {{kcal:two}} for two home mathris, and about {{kcal:four}} for four.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of mathri?
faq.a: About {{kcal:g100}} for this recipe, with about {{fat:g100}} g of fat.

faq.q: How much fat is in a mathri?
faq.a: About {{fat:one}} g in one mathri: the 2 tablespoons of oil in the dough and the oil taken up in frying, in roughly equal shares.

faq.q: Which has more calories, mathri or samosa?
faq.a: Per piece the samosa, about {{kcal@samosa:one}} against {{kcal:one}} for a mathri, because it is three times the weight. Per 100 g the mathri, which is dry and fried, has more.

judgement: No analysed value for mathri was found (IFCT 2017, NIN Annexure 8, USDA FNDDS and branded search, Open Food Facts search returned no products, journal search). Retail listings for packed mathri seen in search results (about 560 to 570 kcal and 36 g fat per 100 g) could not be opened and are not cited.
The textbook lists no water; 35 g is an assumption for a stiff dough. Raw weight 100 + 27.2 + 2 + 35 = 164 g; oil taken up at 14% = 23 g, 3.3 g per mathri.
Finished at 4% moisture: maida solids 88.7 + pepper 1.8 + oils 50.2 = 140.7 / 0.96 = 146.6 g; 7 mathris of 21 g.
INDB's mathri values (805 kcal per 100 g) count all 480 ml of frying oil and are not used.
Baked mathri in the changes: 3.3 g oil x 8.84 = 29 kcal.
